lessons.title: Temperature, Kinetic Energy and the Gas Laws
lessons.notes_html:
Temperature and the Average Kinetic Energy of Molecules

Temperature is a direct measure of the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules, as shown by the relation average K.E = (3/2) kT. When the absolute temperature doubles, the average kinetic energy of the particles also doubles. Temperature therefore rises only when the molecules move faster on average.

Kinetic theory gives the average translational kinetic energy of one molecule as (3/2) kT, where k is Boltzmann constant and T is the absolute temperature. Each of the three directions of motion contributes (1/2) kT. The value depends only on temperature and not on the mass or nature of the gas.

The root mean square speed is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature, vrms = sqrt(3 kT / m). If T becomes 3T, vrms becomes sqrt(3) times its original value. It does not become 3 times, because speed depends on the square root of temperature, not on temperature directly.

Average K.E of one molecule = (3/2) kT

Pressure, Volume and Molecular Speed

At constant temperature Boyle law gives P1 V1 = P2 V2, so pressure and volume are inversely proportional. If the volume becomes 2 V1, the pressure becomes P2 = P1 V1 / (2 V1) = P1 / 2. The gas spreads into twice the space, so its molecules strike the walls half as often.

Kinetic theory derives P = (1/3) rho times the mean square speed of the molecules, where rho is the density of the gas. Pressure is produced by molecular collisions with the walls of the container. A denser gas, or one whose molecules move faster, therefore exerts a greater pressure.

At the same temperature all gases have the same average kinetic energy, so the lighter particles move faster, with speed proportional to 1 / sqrt(molar mass). Helium, with molar mass 4, is much lighter than nitrogen (28) and oxygen (32), so helium atoms move fastest. Nitrogen molecules do move slightly faster than oxygen molecules, but helium is faster than both.

Temperature depends on the random motion of the molecules relative to the container, and this internal motion is unchanged when the whole container moves uniformly. The steady motion of the train adds the same velocity to every molecule and to the container, so the average kinetic energy relative to the walls stays the same. As the container is isolated, no heat enters or leaves, so the temperature remains constant.

STP, the Mole and Temperature Scales

By international agreement, standard temperature is 0 degrees C, which is 273.15 K, and standard pressure is 1 atmosphere, which is 101.3 kPa. At STP one mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 litres. Room temperature values such as 20 degrees C or 25 degrees C are not STP.

Avogadro number, 6.02 x10^23, is defined as the number of particles in one mole of any substance. It is the same for every substance, whether the mole is of hydrogen, oxygen or any other material. It does not depend on one kilogram or one cubic metre, because those amounts contain different numbers of moles for different substances.

The accepted normal human body temperature is 37 degrees C, which converts to 98.6 degrees F on the Fahrenheit scale. Values around 100.4 degrees F and above indicate fever. Small variations occur during the day, but 98.6 degrees F remains the standard reference value.

mcqs.q: What is the average translational kinetic energy of one molecule of an ideal gas at absolute temperature T?
mcqs.why: The correct value is (3/2) kT. Kinetic theory gives average K.E. = (3/2) kT, with (1/2) kT contributed by each of the three directions of motion.

mcqs.q: If the absolute temperature of a gas is doubled, what happens to the average kinetic energy of its molecules?
options: It becomes sqrt(2) times as large
It becomes four times as large
mcqs.why: It doubles, because average K.E. = (3/2) kT is directly proportional to T. Doubling T therefore doubles the average kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: How much does each single direction of molecular motion contribute to the average kinetic energy?
mcqs.why: Each direction contributes (1/2) kT. With three directions of motion the total is 3 x (1/2) kT = (3/2) kT for one molecule.

mcqs.q: The absolute temperature of a gas is increased from T to 3T. By what factor does the root mean square speed change?
mcqs.why: vrms = sqrt(3kT/m) is proportional to sqrt(T). So vrms changes by sqrt(3T/T) = sqrt(3), not by 3, because speed depends on the square root of temperature.

mcqs.q: At constant temperature the volume of a gas is doubled from V1 to 2V1. What is the new pressure?
mcqs.why: By Boyle's law P1V1 = P2V2, so P2 = P1V1/(2V1) = P1/2. Spread into twice the space, the molecules strike the walls half as often.

mcqs.q: According to kinetic theory, the pressure of a gas is given by which relation?
options: P = rho x mean square speed
P = (2/3) rho x mean square speed
P = (1/3) rho x mean square speed
mcqs.why: P = (1/3) rho x mean square speed, where rho is the density. Pressure comes from molecular collisions with the walls, so a denser or faster-moving gas exerts more pressure.

mcqs.q: At the same temperature, which particles move fastest on average: helium (molar mass 4), nitrogen (28) or oxygen (32)?
options: All move at the same speed
mcqs.why: Helium atoms move fastest. At the same temperature all gases have the same average K.E., so speed is proportional to 1/sqrt(molar mass), and helium has by far the smallest molar mass.

mcqs.q: A gas in an isolated container is placed on a fast-moving train travelling uniformly. What happens to the temperature of the gas?
options: It fluctuates with the train speed
mcqs.why: It remains constant. Temperature depends on random motion relative to the container; uniform motion adds the same velocity to every molecule and to the walls, and the isolated container exchanges no heat.

mcqs.q: Which set of values correctly describes standard temperature and pressure (STP)?
options: 0 degrees C (273.15 K) and 1 atm (101.3 kPa)
mcqs.why: STP is 0 degrees C = 273.15 K and 1 atmosphere = 101.3 kPa. At STP one mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 litres; room temperatures such as 20 or 25 degrees C are not STP.

mcqs.q: The Avogadro number, 6.02 x 10^23, is defined as the number of particles in what quantity?
options: One cubic metre of a gas
mcqs.why: It is the number of particles in one mole of any substance. It is the same for every substance, unlike one kilogram or one cubic metre, which contain different numbers of moles for different substances.

lessons.title: Kinetic Theory in Everyday Life
lessons.notes_html:
Why the Earth Is Not in Thermal Equilibrium with the Sun

Thermal equilibrium requires two bodies at the same temperature with no net flow of heat between them. The sun is at about 6000 K on its surface while the earth is near 300 K, so heat flows continuously from the sun to the earth. The earth also radiates heat back into cold space and is warmed unevenly by day and night. Because energy keeps flowing and the temperatures remain very different, the earth and the sun are not in thermal equilibrium.

Temperature and the Kinetic Energy of Molecules

Temperature is a measure of the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules of a substance. Kinetic theory gives average K.E = (3/2) kT, so the average kinetic energy is directly proportional to the absolute temperature. When a substance is heated, its molecules move faster and their average kinetic energy increases. At absolute zero the theoretical minimum of molecular kinetic energy is reached.

Why a Mercury Column First Falls, Then Rises

When the bulb is first placed in the flame, the glass of the bulb is heated before the mercury inside it. The glass expands, so the volume of the bulb increases and the mercury level falls for a moment. Soon the mercury also becomes hot and expands much more than the glass. The mercury then rises up the capillary tube to its final steady reading.

Standard Temperature and Pressure

Standard temperature and pressure, called STP, is a fixed reference condition used for comparing gases. Standard temperature is 0 degrees C, equal to 273.15 K, and standard pressure is 1 atmosphere, equal to 101.3 kPa or 760 mm of mercury. At STP one mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 litres. Gas volumes measured under other conditions are converted to STP for fair comparison.

A Thermometer Placed in Direct Sunlight

The thermometer will not read the true temperature of the air. Its bulb absorbs radiant heat directly from the sun, so the liquid inside becomes hotter than the surrounding air. It will therefore show a temperature higher than the actual air temperature. For this reason, air temperature is always measured with a thermometer kept in shade with free flow of air around it.

Why Hydrogen Leaks Faster Than Oxygen

At the same temperature, lighter hydrogen molecules move much faster than heavier oxygen molecules, because average speed is proportional to 1 / sqrt(molar mass). Hydrogen molecules therefore reach any tiny hole or weak point in the cylinder more often and escape more quickly. Hydrogen molecules are also smaller and pass through very small gaps more easily. For both reasons a hydrogen cylinder leaks faster than an oxygen cylinder at the same pressure.

Shaking a Sealed Thermos Bottle of Coffee

Shaking does work on the coffee, and this mechanical work is converted into internal energy of the coffee. The random kinetic energy of its molecules increases slightly, so the temperature of the coffee rises a little. The thermos is sealed and insulated, so almost no heat escapes and the small rise remains in the coffee. The pressure inside also increases slightly because of the rise in temperature.

How Kinetic Theory Explains Gas Pressure

Gas molecules are in constant random motion and collide again and again with the walls of the container. Each collision changes the momentum of a molecule, and the combined effect of millions of collisions per second appears as a steady force on the walls, which is the pressure of the gas. (b) When the temperature rises, the molecules move faster, so they strike the walls harder and more often. The change of momentum in each collision and the number of collisions per second both increase, so the pressure rises at constant volume.

mcqs.q: Why are the Earth and the Sun NOT in thermal equilibrium?
options: Because their temperatures are very different (about 300 K and 6000 K) and heat flows continuously between them
Because there is vacuum between them
Because the Earth radiates no heat
mcqs.why: Thermal equilibrium needs equal temperatures and no net heat flow. The Sun's surface is about 6000 K while the Earth is near 300 K, so heat flows continuously from Sun to Earth and equilibrium is impossible.

mcqs.q: What does the temperature of a substance directly measure?
options: The total kinetic energy of all its molecules
The potential energy of its molecules
The speed of its fastest molecule
The average translational kinetic energy of its molecules
mcqs.why: Temperature measures the average translational kinetic energy, since average K.E. = (3/2) kT. When a substance is heated its molecules move faster and this average increases.

mcqs.q: When a mercury thermometer is first put into a flame, the mercury column first falls and then rises. Why does it fall first?
options: Air pressure pushes the mercury down
The glass bulb is heated first and expands, increasing the bulb volume
mcqs.why: The glass is heated before the mercury inside it. The expanding glass increases the bulb volume so the level falls briefly; then the mercury heats and expands much more than the glass and rises.

mcqs.q: At STP, what volume does one mole of an ideal gas occupy?
mcqs.why: One mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 litres at STP, where standard temperature is 0 degrees C and standard pressure is 1 atm = 101.3 kPa = 760 mm of mercury.

mcqs.q: A thermometer is placed in direct sunlight. What does it read?
options: A temperature higher than the actual air temperature
A temperature lower than the air temperature
mcqs.why: It reads higher than the true air temperature because its bulb absorbs radiant heat directly from the Sun. Air temperature must be measured in shade with free air flow around the thermometer.

mcqs.q: Why does a hydrogen cylinder leak faster than an oxygen cylinder at the same pressure and temperature?
options: Hydrogen reacts with the cylinder walls
Hydrogen molecules are lighter, move faster, and are smaller
mcqs.why: At the same temperature speed is proportional to 1/sqrt(molar mass), so light hydrogen molecules move much faster, reach holes more often, and being smaller also pass through tiny gaps more easily.

mcqs.q: A sealed thermos bottle of coffee is shaken vigorously. What happens to the coffee?
mcqs.why: Shaking does work on the coffee, which becomes internal energy, so the random kinetic energy of the molecules and the temperature rise slightly. The sealed, insulated thermos lets almost no heat escape.

mcqs.q: How does kinetic theory explain the pressure exerted by a gas?
options: By the weight of the gas alone
By molecules colliding again and again with the container walls
By the gas expanding into vacuum
mcqs.why: Molecules in constant random motion collide with the walls; each collision changes molecular momentum, and millions of collisions per second together appear as a steady force on the walls, which is the pressure.

mcqs.q: At constant volume, why does the pressure of a gas rise when its temperature rises?
options: Molecules strike the walls harder and more often
mcqs.why: Faster molecules strike the walls harder and more often: both the momentum change per collision and the number of collisions per second increase, so the pressure rises at constant volume.

mcqs.q: What is reached at absolute zero, according to kinetic theory?
options: The theoretical minimum of molecular kinetic energy
mcqs.why: At absolute zero the theoretical minimum of molecular kinetic energy is reached, because average K.E. = (3/2) kT falls to its lowest possible value as T approaches 0 K.

lessons.title: Gas Laws and the Kinetic Theory of Gases
lessons.notes_html:
Temperature and Its Scales

Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body, and in kinetic theory it is a measure of the average kinetic energy of its molecules. It tells us the direction of heat flow, because heat always flows from a body at higher temperature to a body at lower temperature until thermal equilibrium is reached. The Celsius scale fixes the ice point at 0 degrees C and the steam point at 100 degrees C, divided into 100 equal parts. The Fahrenheit scale fixes the ice point at 32 degrees F and the steam point at 212 degrees F, divided into 180 equal parts, and the two scales are related by F = (9/5) C + 32. The Kelvin scale is the absolute scale, starting from absolute zero at 0 K, with K = C + 273.15, and it is the scale used in all gas law calculations.

Boyle's Law, Charles's Law and Avogadro's Law

Boyle law states that at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure, so P1 V1 = P2 V2. It means that squeezing a gas into half the volume doubles its pressure, because the molecules strike the walls twice as often. Charles law states that at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature, so V1 / T1 = V2 / T2. Heating a gas at constant pressure makes its molecules move faster, and the gas expands so that the pressure stays unchanged. Avogadro law states that equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules, so volume is directly proportional to the number of moles, V = nRT / P for the general case.

Deriving the General Gas Law

Start with a fixed mass of gas at pressure P1, volume V1 and temperature T1, and change it in two steps to P2, V2 and T2. First change the pressure from P1 to P2 at constant temperature T1; by Boyle law the intermediate volume V satisfies P1 V1 = P2 V, so V = P1 V1 / P2. Next change the temperature from T1 to T2 at the constant pressure P2; by Charles law V / T1 = V2 / T2, so V = V2 T1 / T2. Equating the two values of V gives P1 V1 / P2 = V2 T1 / T2, which rearranges to P1 V1 / T1 = P2 V2 / T2. For one mole the constant equals R, and for n moles the general gas law becomes PV = nRT, where R = 8.31 J/mol K.

Molecular Motion and the Pressure Equation

Gas molecules move randomly in all directions and collide elastically with the walls of the container, and each collision exerts a small force on the wall. Consider one molecule of mass m moving with x-component of velocity vx in a cubical box of side L; it hits one wall, rebounds, and its momentum changes by 2 m vx. It returns to the same wall after time 2L / vx, so the average force from this molecule is (2 m vx) / (2L / vx) = m vx^2 / L. Adding the contributions of all N molecules and using the average of vx^2 = (1/3) of the mean square speed gives total force F = N m (mean square speed) / (3L). Dividing by the area L^2, with volume V = L^3 and density rho = N m / V, the pressure becomes P = (1/3) rho times the mean square speed, which is the pressure equation of kinetic theory.

Temperature as a Measure of Average Translational Kinetic Energy

The pressure equation of kinetic theory is P = (1/3) rho times the mean square speed, which can be written as PV = (1/3) N m (mean square speed) = (2/3) N times the average translational kinetic energy of one molecule. The general gas law for the same gas is PV = N kT, where N is the number of molecules and k is Boltzmann constant. Comparing the two expressions gives (2/3) N (average K.E) = N kT, so average K.E = (3/2) kT. The average translational kinetic energy therefore depends only on the absolute temperature and on nothing else. This proves mathematically that temperature is a direct measure of the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules.

P V = n R T

mcqs.q: On the Celsius scale, how are the ice point and steam point fixed?
options: 0 degrees C and 100 degrees C, divided into 100 equal parts
mcqs.why: The Celsius scale fixes the ice point at 0 degrees C and the steam point at 100 degrees C, divided into 100 equal parts. Heat flows from higher to lower temperature until thermal equilibrium is reached.

mcqs.q: Which relation correctly converts a Celsius temperature to Fahrenheit?
mcqs.why: F = (9/5) C + 32. The Fahrenheit scale fixes ice point at 32 degrees F and steam point at 212 degrees F, divided into 180 equal parts, which gives this conversion formula.

mcqs.q: Which statement is Charles's law?
options: At constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature, V1/T1 = V2/T2
Equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules
mcqs.why: Charles's law: at constant pressure V is directly proportional to absolute temperature, V1/T1 = V2/T2. Heating makes molecules move faster and the gas expands so pressure stays unchanged.

mcqs.q: What does Avogadro's law state?
options: Volume is proportional to temperature in Celsius
Volume is inversely proportional to pressure
Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules
Pressure is proportional to density only
mcqs.why: Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules, so volume is directly proportional to the number of moles.

mcqs.q: Combining Boyle's law and Charles's law for n moles gives the general gas law. What is it, and what is R?
options: P/V = nRT, with R = 8.31 J/mol K
PV = RT/n, with R = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K
PV = nkT, with R = 8.31 J/mol K
PV = nRT, with R = 8.31 J/mol K
mcqs.why: The general gas law is PV = nRT with R = 8.31 J/mol K. The two-step derivation gives P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2, and for one mole the constant is R, extended to n moles as PV = nRT.

mcqs.q: A molecule of mass m hits a wall of a cubical box and rebounds elastically. What is its change in momentum?
mcqs.why: The momentum changes by 2 m vx: the x-component reverses from +m vx to -m vx on rebound, so the total change is 2 m vx, which produces the force on the wall.

mcqs.q: In the kinetic theory derivation, how long does a molecule take to return to the same wall of a box of side L?
mcqs.why: The molecule must travel to the opposite wall and back, a distance 2L at speed vx, so the time is 2L/vx. Dividing the momentum change 2 m vx by this time gives the average force m vx^2 / L.

mcqs.q: Why does the factor 1/3 appear in the pressure equation P = (1/3) rho x mean square speed?
options: Because there are three walls in a box
Because the average of vx^2 is one third of the mean square speed
mcqs.why: Molecular motion is shared equally among three directions, so the average of vx^2 equals (1/3) of the mean square speed. Summing all molecules then gives F = N m (mean square speed)/(3L) and P = (1/3) rho x mean square speed.

mcqs.q: Comparing PV = (2/3) N x (average K.E.) with PV = N kT leads to which conclusion?
options: Average K.E. = (3/2) kT, so temperature measures average translational K.E.
mcqs.why: Equating the two expressions gives (2/3) N (average K.E.) = N kT, hence average K.E. = (3/2) kT. Temperature is therefore a direct measure of average translational kinetic energy and depends on nothing else.

mcqs.q: Which temperature scale must be used in all gas law calculations, and how is it related to Celsius?
mcqs.why: The Kelvin (absolute) scale must be used, with K = C + 273.15. It starts at absolute zero, 0 K, and gas laws such as Charles's law only hold with absolute temperatures.

lessons.title: Worked Examples
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example 1

Calculate the average speed of an air molecule at room temperature (20 degrees C) and compare it to the speed of sound in air (330 m/s).

Step 1: Given: T = 20 degrees C = 293 K, Boltzmann constant k = 1.38 x10^-23 J/K, mass of one air molecule m = about 4.8 x10^-26 kg, speed of sound = 330 m/s

Step 2: Formula: average speed = sqrt(8 kT / (pi m))

Step 3: Substitution: average speed = sqrt(8 x 1.38 x10^-23 x 293 / (3.14 x 4.8 x10^-26))

Step 4: Calculation: numerator = 3.23 x10^-20, denominator = 1.51 x10^-25, ratio = 2.14 x10^5, sqrt = about 463

Average speed is about 460 m/s, which is greater than the speed of sound, 330 m/s, in the same air. The molecules themselves move faster than sound, which is only the speed at which a disturbance passes from molecule to molecule.

Worked Example 2

The freezing point of mercury is -39 degrees C. Convert it into degrees F and the comfort level temperature of 20 degrees into Kelvin.

Step 1: Given: temperature in Celsius = -39 degrees C, and comfort temperature = 20 degrees C

Step 2: Formula: F = (9/5) C + 32, and K = C + 273

Step 3: Substitution: F = (9/5) x (-39) + 32, and K = 20 + 273

Step 4: Calculation: F = -70.2 + 32 = -38.2, and K = 293

Freezing point of mercury = -38.2 degrees F, and comfort temperature = 293 K.

Worked Example 3

The boiling point of liquid nitrogen is -321 degrees F. Change it into equivalent Kelvin temperature.

Step 1: Given: temperature in Fahrenheit = -321 degrees F

Step 2: Formula: C = (5/9) (F - 32), and K = C + 273

Step 3: Substitution: C = (5/9) x (-321 - 32) = (5/9) x (-353), and K = C + 273

Step 4: Calculation: C = -196.1 degrees C, and K = -196.1 + 273 = 76.9

Boiling point of liquid nitrogen = about 77 K.

Worked Example 4

Calculate the volume occupied by a gram-mole of a gas at 0 degrees C and a pressure of 1.0 atmosphere.

Step 1: Given: n = 1 mole, T = 0 degrees C = 273 K, P = 1.0 atm = 1.01 x10^5 Pa, R = 8.31 J/mol K

Step 2: Formula: PV = nRT, so V = nRT / P

Step 3: Substitution: V = 1 x 8.31 x 273 / (1.01 x10^5)

Step 4: Calculation: numerator = 2268.6, V = 2268.6 / 101000 = 0.02246 m^3

Volume occupied = 0.0224 m^3, that is 22.4 litres per mole.

Worked Example 5

An air storage tank whose volume is 112 liters contain 3 kg of air at a pressure of 18 atmospheres. How much air would have to be forced into the tank to increase the pressure to 21 atmospheres, assuming no change in temperature?

Step 1: Given: mass m1 = 3 kg at P1 = 18 atm, required pressure P2 = 21 atm, volume and temperature constant

Step 2: Formula: at constant volume and temperature, mass of gas is proportional to pressure, so m2 / m1 = P2 / P1

Step 3: Substitution: m2 = 3 x 21 / 18

Step 4: Calculation: m2 = 63 / 18 = 3.5 kg

Step 5: Extra air needed = m2 - m1 = 3.5 - 3 = 0.5

0.5 kg of air must be forced into the tank.

Worked Example 6

A balloon contains 0.04 m^3 of air at a pressure of 120 KPa. Calculate the pressure required to reduce its volume to 0.025 m^3 at constant temperature.

Step 1: Given: P1 = 120 kPa = 120 x10^3 Pa, V1 = 0.04 m^3, V2 = 0.025 m^3, temperature constant

Step 2: Formula: Boyle law, P1 V1 = P2 V2, so P2 = P1 V1 / V2

Step 3: Substitution: P2 = 120 x10^3 x 0.04 / 0.025

Step 4: Calculation: P2 = 4800 / 0.025 = 192000 Pa = 1.92 x10^5 Pa

Pressure required = about 1.9 x10^5 Pa.

Worked Example 7

The molar mass of nitrogen gas N2 is 28 g mol^-1. For 100 g of nitrogen, calculate: (a) the number of moles (b) the volume occupied at room temperature (20 degrees C) and pressure of 1.01 x 10^5 Pa.

Step 1: Given: mass = 100 g, molar mass = 28 g/mol, T = 20 degrees C = 293 K, P = 1.01 x10^5 Pa, R = 8.31 J/mol K

Step 2: Formula: (a) n = mass / molar mass, and (b) V = nRT / P

Step 3: Substitution: (a) n = 100 / 28, and (b) V = 3.57 x 8.31 x 293 / (1.01 x10^5)

Step 4: Calculation: (a) n = 3.57 mol, and (b) numerator = 8693, V = 8693 / 101000 = 0.086 m^3

(a) number of moles = 3.57 mole, and (b) volume = 0.086 m^3, that is 86 dm^3.

Worked Example 8

A sample of a gas contains 3.0 x10^24 atoms. Calculate the volume of the gas at a temperature of 300 K and a pressure of 120 K Pa.

Step 1: Given: number of atoms N = 3.0 x10^24, Avogadro number = 6.02 x10^23 per mole, T = 300 K, P = 120 kPa = 1.20 x10^5 Pa, R = 8.31 J/mol K

Step 2: Formula: n = N / Avogadro number, and V = nRT / P

Step 3: Substitution: n = 3.0 x10^24 / 6.02 x10^23 = 4.98 mol, and V = 4.98 x 8.31 x 300 / (1.20 x10^5)

Step 4: Calculation: numerator = 12415, V = 12415 / 120000 = 0.103 m^3

Volume of the gas = about 0.104 m^3.

Worked Example 9

Calculate the root mean square speed of hydrogen molecules at 0 degrees C and 1.0 atm pressure. Assuming hydrogen to be an ideal gas. The density of hydrogen is 8.99 x10^-2 kg/m^3.

Step 1: Given: P = 1.0 atm = 1.01 x10^5 Pa, density rho = 8.99 x10^-2 kg/m^3, T = 0 degrees C

Step 2: Formula: from P = (1/3) rho (mean square speed), vrms = sqrt(3P / rho)

Step 3: Substitution: vrms = sqrt(3 x 1.01 x10^5 / 0.0899)

Step 4: Calculation: 3P / rho = 303000 / 0.0899 = 3.37 x10^6, and sqrt of this = 1836

Root mean square speed of hydrogen molecules = about 1835.86 m/s.

Worked Example 10

Calculate the root mean square speed of hydrogen molecule at 500 K (mass of proton = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg and K = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/molecule.-K)

Step 1: Given: T = 500 K, k = 1.38 x10^-23 J/K, mass of hydrogen molecule m = 2 x 1.67 x10^-27 = 3.34 x10^-27 kg

Step 2: Formula: vrms = sqrt(3 kT / m)

Step 3: Substitution: vrms = sqrt(3 x 1.38 x10^-23 x 500 / (3.34 x10^-27))

Step 4: Calculation: numerator = 2.07 x10^-20, ratio = 2.07 x10^-20 / 3.34 x10^-27 = 6.20 x10^6, and sqrt of this = 2489

Root mean square speed = about 2489.49 m/s.

Worked Example 11

(a) Determine the average value of the Kinetic energy of the particles of an ideal gas at 10 degrees C and at 40 degrees C. (b) What is the Kinetic energy per mole of an ideal gas at these temperatures?

Step 1: Given: T1 = 10 degrees C = 283 K, T2 = 40 degrees C = 313 K, k = 1.38 x10^-23 J/K, R = 8.31 J/mol K

Step 2: Formula: (a) average K.E per molecule = (3/2) kT, and (b) K.E per mole = (3/2) RT

Step 3: Substitution: (a) at 283 K: (3/2) x 1.38 x10^-23 x 283, at 313 K: (3/2) x 1.38 x10^-23 x 313, and (b) at 283 K: (3/2) x 8.31 x 283, at 313 K: (3/2) x 8.31 x 313

Step 4: Calculation: (a) 5.86 x10^-21 J and 6.48 x10^-21 J, and (b) 3527 J and 3901 J

(a) average K.E = 5.86 x10^-21 J at 10 degrees C and 6.48 x10^-21 J at 40 degrees C, and (b) K.E per mole = 3526.57 J and 3901 J respectively.

mcqs.q: What formula gives the average speed of gas molecules, as used for an air molecule at 20 degrees C (293 K)?
mcqs.why: The average speed is sqrt(8kT/(pi m)). With k = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K, T = 293 K and m about 4.8 x 10^-26 kg, this gives about 463 m/s for an air molecule.

mcqs.q: The average speed of an air molecule at room temperature is about 460 m/s. How does this compare with the speed of sound in air, 330 m/s?
options: It is greater than the speed of sound
It is half the speed of sound
It is equal to the speed of sound
It is smaller than the speed of sound
mcqs.why: It is greater: about 460 m/s against 330 m/s. The molecules themselves move faster than sound, which is only the speed at which a disturbance passes from molecule to molecule.

mcqs.q: Convert the freezing point of mercury, -39 degrees C, into degrees Fahrenheit.
mcqs.why: Using F = (9/5)C + 32: F = (9/5)(-39) + 32 = -70.2 + 32 = -38.2 degrees F. So the freezing point of mercury is -38.2 degrees F.

mcqs.q: What is the comfort level temperature of 20 degrees C expressed in kelvin?
mcqs.why: K = C + 273 = 20 + 273 = 293 K. Comfort level temperature of 20 degrees C is therefore 293 K on the absolute scale.

mcqs.q: The boiling point of liquid nitrogen is -321 degrees F. What is this in kelvin (approximately)?
mcqs.why: C = (5/9)(F - 32) = (5/9)(-353) = -196.1 degrees C, then K = -196.1 + 273 = 76.9, about 77 K. So liquid nitrogen boils at about 77 K.

mcqs.q: What volume is occupied by one gram-mole of a gas at 0 degrees C and 1.0 atmosphere pressure?
A 112-litre tank holds 3 kg of air at 18 atm. How much extra air must be forced in to raise the pressure to 21 atm at constant temperature?
mcqs.why: At constant volume and temperature mass is proportional to pressure: m2 = 3 x 21/18 = 3.5 kg. Extra air needed = 3.5 - 3 = 0.5 kg.

mcqs.q: A balloon contains 0.04 m^3 of air at 120 kPa. What pressure reduces its volume to 0.025 m^3 at constant temperature?
How many moles are there in 100 g of nitrogen gas, N2, whose molar mass is 28 g/mol?
mcqs.why: n = mass / molar mass = 100 / 28 = 3.57 mol. This value is then used with PV = nRT to find the volume occupied by the gas.

mcqs.q: 100 g of nitrogen (3.57 mol) at 20 degrees C (293 K) and 1.01 x 10^5 Pa occupies what volume?
A gas sample contains 3.0 x 10^24 atoms. How many moles is this, taking Avogadro's number as 6.02 x 10^23 per mole?
mcqs.why: n = N / Avogadro number = 3.0 x 10^24 / 6.02 x 10^23 = 4.98 mol. At 300 K and 120 kPa this amount occupies about 0.104 m^3.

mcqs.q: Using vrms = sqrt(3P/rho) with P = 1.01 x 10^5 Pa and hydrogen density 8.99 x 10^-2 kg/m^3, what is vrms for hydrogen at 0 degrees C?
mcqs.why: vrms = sqrt(3 x 1.01 x 10^5 / 0.0899) = sqrt(3.37 x 10^6) = about 1836 m/s. Hydrogen molecules at 0 degrees C have an rms speed of about 1835.86 m/s.

mcqs.q: What is the mass of one hydrogen molecule, given the mass of a proton is 1.67 x 10^-27 kg?
mcqs.why: A hydrogen molecule H2 has two protons' worth of mass: m = 2 x 1.67 x 10^-27 = 3.34 x 10^-27 kg. This mass is used in vrms = sqrt(3kT/m) at 500 K.

mcqs.q: What is the root mean square speed of a hydrogen molecule at 500 K?
What is the kinetic energy per mole of an ideal gas at 40 degrees C (313 K)?
mcqs.why: K.E. per mole = (3/2)RT = 1.5 x 8.31 x 313 = 3901 J. For comparison, the average K.E. per molecule at 313 K is (3/2)kT = 6.48 x 10^-21 J.

lessons.title: Thermodynamic Processes and Internal Energy
lessons.notes_html:
The Four Basic Thermodynamic Processes

In an isothermal process the temperature stays constant, so for an ideal gas the internal energy does not change and Delta U = 0. The first law then gives Q = W, meaning all the heat absorbed is converted into work done by the system. Heat and work are both exchanged with the surroundings in this process.

The word isobaric means constant pressure, so the pressure of the system does not change during the process. Volume and temperature may both change, as in a gas expanding under a freely moving piston. The work done in such a process is W = P x Delta V.

An isothermal process is carried out slowly in contact with a heat reservoir, so heat flows in or out but the temperature remains constant. In an adiabatic process, by contrast, no heat is exchanged at all. For an ideal gas at constant temperature the internal energy also stays constant during an isothermal change.

In an adiabatic process the system is thermally insulated, so Q = 0 and no heat enters or leaves the system. Any work done by the system is paid for from its internal energy, so its temperature falls during adiabatic expansion. Rapid expansion of a gas, where there is no time for heat to flow, is nearly adiabatic.

Isochoric means constant volume, so the volume of the system is the quantity that does not change. Because Delta V = 0, no work is done by or on the system, and this follows from the constant volume. All the heat added in an isochoric process goes into increasing the internal energy.

Internal Energy and the First Law

Internal energy is the total energy stored inside a system, mainly the kinetic energy of its molecules due to their random motion plus the potential energy of intermolecular forces. It does not include the kinetic energy of the whole system moving as one body, nor its potential energy due to height. For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so internal energy is purely the molecular kinetic energy.

The first law is written as Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W, where Delta W is the work done by the system. Rearranging gives Delta U = Delta Q - Delta W. So the internal energy increases when heat is added and decreases when the system spends energy in doing work.

For an ideal gas the molecules exert no forces on each other, so there is no intermolecular potential energy to depend on separation or volume. The internal energy is only the total kinetic energy of the molecules, which is fixed by the temperature alone. Changing the pressure or volume at constant temperature does not change the internal energy of an ideal gas.

In the usual case of adiabatic expansion, no heat enters the system, yet the system does work on its surroundings. By the first law this work can only come from the internal energy, so the internal energy decreases and the gas cools. In adiabatic compression the reverse happens, work is done on the gas and its internal energy increases.

The general first law relation is Delta U = Delta Q - Delta W, and it applies to an isochoric process as well. In this process Delta V = 0, so Delta W = P Delta V = 0. The relation therefore reduces to Delta U = Delta Q, meaning all the heat supplied appears as internal energy.

Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W

mcqs.q: In an isothermal process for an ideal gas, what is the change in internal energy, and how does the first law simplify?
mcqs.why: Temperature is constant, so for an ideal gas Delta U = 0. The first law Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W then gives Q = W: all heat absorbed is converted into work done by the system.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'isobaric' mean, and what is the work done in such a process?
options: No heat exchange; W = Delta U
Constant pressure; W = P x Delta V
mcqs.why: Isobaric means constant pressure. Volume and temperature may both change, as in expansion under a freely moving piston, and the work done is W = P x Delta V.

mcqs.q: What is the defining feature of an adiabatic process?
mcqs.why: In an adiabatic process the system is thermally insulated so Q = 0. Work done by the system is paid for from its internal energy, so its temperature falls during adiabatic expansion.

mcqs.q: Why does a gas cool during adiabatic expansion?
options: It does work using its internal energy, with no heat entering
mcqs.why: No heat enters, yet the gas does work on its surroundings. By the first law that work can only come from internal energy, so internal energy decreases and the gas cools. Rapid expansion is nearly adiabatic.

mcqs.q: In an isochoric process, why is no work done?
options: Because Delta V = 0, so W = P Delta V = 0
mcqs.why: Isochoric means constant volume, so Delta V = 0 and W = P Delta V = 0. All heat added in an isochoric process therefore goes into increasing the internal energy, Delta U = Delta Q.

mcqs.q: What does the internal energy of a system include?
options: Only the heat supplied to it
Kinetic energy of the whole body plus its height energy
Molecular kinetic energy plus intermolecular potential energy only
Only the work done by it
mcqs.why: Internal energy is the energy stored inside: mainly the kinetic energy of molecules in random motion plus potential energy of intermolecular forces. It excludes bulk motion of the whole system and potential energy due to height.

mcqs.q: How is the change in internal energy related to heat and work in the first law?
options: Delta U = Delta Q + Delta W
Delta U = Delta Q - Delta W
Delta U = Delta Q x Delta W
Delta U = Delta W - Delta Q
mcqs.why: From Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W, rearranging gives Delta U = Delta Q - Delta W. Internal energy increases when heat is added and decreases when the system spends energy doing work.

mcqs.q: Why does the internal energy of an ideal gas depend only on temperature?
options: Because there are no intermolecular forces, so it is purely molecular kinetic energy fixed by temperature
mcqs.why: Ideal gas molecules exert no forces on each other, so there is no intermolecular potential energy. Internal energy is only total molecular kinetic energy, fixed by temperature alone, unchanged by pressure or volume at constant T.

mcqs.q: What happens to a gas during adiabatic compression?
options: Work is done on it, its internal energy increases and it heats up
mcqs.why: In adiabatic compression work is done on the gas with no heat flow, so by Delta U = -Delta W the internal energy increases and the gas becomes hot, the reverse of adiabatic expansion.

mcqs.q: An isothermal process is carried out slowly in contact with a heat reservoir. How does it differ from an adiabatic process?
options: In isothermal change heat flows but temperature stays constant; in adiabatic change no heat flows at all
In isothermal change no heat flows; in adiabatic change temperature stays constant
mcqs.why: In an isothermal process heat flows in or out but temperature remains constant, and ideal-gas internal energy stays constant. In an adiabatic process no heat is exchanged at all, so temperature changes with work.

lessons.title: The First Law of Thermodynamics
lessons.notes_html:
The First Law in Words

The first law says that energy given to a system as heat is never lost; it is either stored inside the system as internal energy or spent by the system in doing work. In symbols, Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W. If 100 J of heat is supplied and the system does 60 J of work, its internal energy rises by 40 J. The law is simply the law of conservation of energy applied to heat, work and internal energy.

The First Law and Conservation of Energy

The first law is the conservation of energy stated for thermodynamic processes. It says heat is a form of energy, so the total energy of system plus surroundings remains constant in every process. Energy can change its form, from heat to internal energy to mechanical work, but it can neither be created nor destroyed. Any apparent gain or loss in one form is exactly balanced by opposite changes in the other forms.

Heat and Work Distinguished

Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference between the system and the surroundings, and it always flows from the hotter to the colder side. Work is energy transferred by a force acting through a displacement, for example a gas pushing a piston outward. In the first law, Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W, heat added to the system is taken as positive input, while work done by the system is energy output. Both are measured in joules, but heat depends on temperature difference while work depends on force and movement.

The First Law in Daily Life

When water is heated in a lidded pan on a stove, the heat supplied first raises the internal energy of the water, seen as a rise in temperature. Once the water boils, part of the heat does work by pushing up the lid and producing steam. Rubbing the palms together is another example, where mechanical work is converted into internal energy and the palms become warm. In each case the energy supplied equals the internal energy gained plus the work done, exactly as the first law states.

System and Surroundings

The system is the part of the universe chosen for study, such as the gas inside a cylinder, and everything outside it is called the surroundings. Heat and work are exchanged across the boundary between the system and the surroundings. The first law keeps the energy account of the system: heat gained from the surroundings minus work done on the surroundings equals the change in internal energy of the system. Whatever energy the system gains, the surroundings lose by the same amount, so total energy is conserved.

Heat Capacity

Heat capacity is the heat required to raise the temperature of a body by one degree, so Q = C x Delta T. A substance with a large heat capacity, such as water, needs a great deal of energy for even a small temperature rise. A substance with a small heat capacity warms up quickly with little energy input. Heat capacity therefore directly fixes how much energy must be supplied for a desired temperature change.

Mathematical Expression of the First Law

The first law is expressed as Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W. Delta Q is the net heat supplied to the system from the surroundings, taken positive when heat flows into the system and negative when it flows out. Delta U is the change in internal energy of the system, that is, the change in the total kinetic and potential energy of its molecules. Delta W is the work done by the system on the surroundings, for example P x Delta V when a gas expands against a piston, and it is negative when work is done on the system in compression. The equation is the energy balance of the system and expresses conservation of energy.

Internal Energy in an Adiabatic Process

In an adiabatic process the system is insulated, so Delta Q = 0 and the first law becomes 0 = Delta U + Delta W, or Delta U = -Delta W. If the gas expands, it does positive work, so Delta U is negative and the internal energy decreases, which is why an expanding gas cools in an adiabatic change. If the gas is compressed, work is done on it, Delta W is negative, and the internal energy increases, so the gas becomes hot. A bicycle pump warming during rapid compression and a gas cooling on rapid expansion in a fire extinguisher are common examples. The internal energy changes because work is exchanged while no heat is allowed to flow.

mcqs.q: 100 J of heat is supplied to a system and the system does 60 J of work. What is the rise in internal energy?
mcqs.why: Delta U = Delta Q - Delta W = 100 - 60 = 40 J. Energy given as heat is never lost: it is stored as internal energy or spent doing work, Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W.

mcqs.q: The first law of thermodynamics is essentially which general law applied to heat, work and internal energy?
mcqs.why: The first law is the conservation of energy stated for thermodynamic processes. Total energy of system plus surroundings stays constant; energy changes form but can neither be created nor destroyed.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes heat transfer from work transfer?
options: Heat is transferred due to a temperature difference; work is transferred by a force acting through a displacement
Heat only flows into a system; work only flows out
They are exactly the same thing
Heat is measured in watts, work in joules
mcqs.why: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, flowing from hotter to colder. Work is energy transferred by a force through a displacement, e.g. a gas pushing a piston. Both are measured in joules.

mcqs.q: Rubbing the palms together makes them warm. How does the first law explain this?
options: Mechanical work is converted into internal energy
Internal energy is converted into heat lost to the air
Heat flows in from the surroundings
mcqs.why: Rubbing converts mechanical work into internal energy of the palms, so they become warm. The energy supplied equals internal energy gained plus work done, exactly as the first law states.

mcqs.q: In the first law, what are the 'system' and the 'surroundings'?
options: System is the whole universe; surroundings are nothing
System is the heat; surroundings are the work
System is the part chosen for study; everything outside it is the surroundings
System is the thermometer; surroundings are the gas
mcqs.why: The system is the part of the universe chosen for study, e.g. gas in a cylinder; everything outside is the surroundings. Heat and work cross the boundary, and whatever energy the system gains the surroundings lose.

mcqs.q: Heat capacity C is defined so that Q = C x Delta T. What does a large heat capacity, like that of water, imply?
options: The substance warms up very quickly
A great deal of energy is needed for even a small temperature rise
No energy is needed to heat it
mcqs.why: Heat capacity is the heat required to raise temperature by one degree. A large value, as for water, means much energy is needed for a small rise; a small heat capacity warms quickly with little input.

mcqs.q: In Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W, when is Delta Q taken as negative?
options: When heat flows out of the system
When work is done by the system
When heat flows into the system
mcqs.why: Delta Q is the net heat supplied to the system: positive when heat flows in, negative when heat flows out. Delta W is work done by the system, e.g. P x Delta V in expansion, negative in compression.

mcqs.q: For a gas expanding against a piston, how is the work done by the system expressed?
options: Delta W = C x Delta T
Delta W = P x Delta V
mcqs.why: Work done by the system is Delta W = P x Delta V when a gas expands against a piston. It is one of the three terms in the energy balance Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W.

mcqs.q: In an adiabatic process Delta Q = 0, so the first law becomes Delta U = -Delta W. If the gas expands and does positive work, what happens?
options: Internal energy increases and the gas heats
Internal energy decreases and the gas cools
mcqs.why: With Delta U = -Delta W and Delta W positive in expansion, Delta U is negative: internal energy decreases and the expanding gas cools, as in a fire extinguisher. Compression does the reverse and heats the gas.

mcqs.q: Why does a bicycle pump warm up during rapid compression of air?
options: Work done on the gas raises its internal energy because the rapid change is nearly adiabatic
The metal of the pump is heated by sunlight
Heat flows in from the tyre
mcqs.why: Rapid compression is nearly adiabatic: no heat flows, work is done on the gas, Delta W is negative, so Delta U = -Delta W is positive, internal energy increases and the gas (and pump) becomes hot.

lessons.title: Internal Energy, Work and Heat Capacity
lessons.notes_html:
Internal Energy in Different Processes

Internal energy is the total energy stored within a system due to the random motion of its molecules and the forces between them; for an ideal gas it depends only on temperature. In an isothermal process the temperature is constant, so the internal energy of an ideal gas does not change and all the heat supplied becomes work. In an isochoric process no work is done, so all the heat supplied raises the internal energy and the temperature. In an adiabatic process no heat flows, so the internal energy falls during expansion and rises during compression. In an isobaric process the heat supplied is shared between raising internal energy and doing expansion work.

Positive and Negative Work Done by a Gas

Work done by a gas is W = P x Delta V, where Delta V is the change in volume. When a gas expands, Delta V is positive, the gas pushes the piston outward and does work on the surroundings, so the work is positive and the gas spends its own energy. When a gas is compressed, Delta V is negative, the surroundings push the piston inward and do work on the gas, so the work done by the gas is negative and the gas gains energy. On a P-V diagram the work equals the area under the curve, positive for expansion to the right and negative for compression to the left. The sign convention keeps the first law account correct in both cases.

Heat Capacity and Thermal Energy Storage

Heat capacity C is the quantity of heat needed to raise the temperature of a body by 1 K, so C = Delta Q / Delta T, and specific heat capacity is this quantity per unit mass. A large heat capacity means the substance can absorb or release a large amount of heat with only a small change in temperature, so it acts as a good store of thermal energy. Water has a very high specific heat, which is why it is used as a coolant and why coastal climates change temperature slowly. Metals have low specific heats, so they heat up and cool down quickly with small energy transfers. In first law calculations, heat capacity connects the heat supplied at constant volume or constant pressure with the resulting change in internal energy and temperature.

mcqs.q: In an isothermal process, what happens to the heat supplied to an ideal gas?
options: It is all lost to the surroundings
Half becomes work and half is destroyed
It all raises the internal energy
It all becomes work, since internal energy does not change
mcqs.why: Temperature is constant, so internal energy of an ideal gas does not change. All the heat supplied therefore becomes work done by the gas in an isothermal process.

mcqs.q: In an isochoric process, what happens to the heat supplied?
options: No work is done, so it all raises internal energy and temperature
It leaves the system as heat
mcqs.why: Volume is constant so no work is done. All heat supplied in an isochoric process raises the internal energy and hence the temperature of the gas.

mcqs.q: In an adiabatic expansion, how does the internal energy change, and in adiabatic compression?
options: It falls in expansion and rises in compression
It rises in expansion and falls in compression
mcqs.why: No heat flows in an adiabatic process, so internal energy falls during expansion (work done by the gas) and rises during compression (work done on the gas).

mcqs.q: In an isobaric process, how is the heat supplied used?
options: It is not used at all
Shared between raising internal energy and doing expansion work
mcqs.why: At constant pressure the heat supplied is shared: part raises the internal energy (and temperature) and part does expansion work W = P Delta V. This sharing is characteristic of the isobaric process.

mcqs.q: A gas expands so Delta V is positive. What is the sign of the work done by the gas, W = P x Delta V?
options: Positive, the gas pushes the piston out and spends its own energy
mcqs.why: In expansion Delta V is positive, so W = P Delta V is positive: the gas pushes the piston outward, does work on the surroundings and spends its own energy.

mcqs.q: A gas is compressed so Delta V is negative. What is the work done by the gas?
options: Negative, the surroundings do work on the gas and it gains energy
mcqs.why: In compression Delta V is negative, so work done by the gas is negative: the surroundings push the piston inward, do work on the gas, and the gas gains energy. The sign convention keeps the first law correct.

mcqs.q: On a P-V diagram, what does the work done by a gas equal?
mcqs.why: Work equals the area under the curve on a P-V diagram, positive for expansion to the right and negative for compression to the left, consistent with W = P x Delta V.

mcqs.q: Heat capacity is defined as C = Delta Q / Delta T. What is specific heat capacity?
options: Heat needed to boil a substance
mcqs.why: Heat capacity C is the heat needed to raise a body's temperature by 1 K; specific heat capacity is this quantity per unit mass. A large value means a substance stores much thermal energy with little temperature change.

mcqs.q: Why is water used as a coolant and why do coastal climates change temperature slowly?
options: Water is always at constant volume
Water has a very low specific heat
Water has a very high specific heat, absorbing much heat with small temperature change
mcqs.why: Water's very high specific heat lets it absorb or release large amounts of heat with only small temperature changes, making it a good coolant and thermal store that keeps coastal climates steady.

mcqs.q: How do metals compare with water in specific heat, and what follows from it?
options: Metals have low specific heats, so they heat up and cool down quickly with small energy transfers
Metals have higher specific heats and heat slowly
Metals have the same specific heat as water
mcqs.why: Metals have low specific heats, so they heat up and cool down quickly with small energy transfers, the opposite of water, which needs large energy transfers for small temperature changes.

lessons.title: Worked Examples
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example 1

A gas undergoes isothermal expansion at a constant temperature of 300 K. If the gas absorbs 500 J of heat during the process, calculate the work done by the gas.

Step 1: Given: T = 300 K constant, heat absorbed Q = 500 J, isothermal process

Step 2: Formula: first law, Q = Delta U + W, and for isothermal change of an ideal gas Delta U = 0, so W = Q

Step 3: Substitution: W = 500 J

Step 4: Calculation: all the heat absorbed is converted into work because the internal energy does not change at constant temperature

Work done by the gas = 500 J.

Worked Example 2

A piston compresses a gas adiabatically. If the initial volume is 0.02 m^3 and the final volume is 0.01 m^3, and the initial pressure is 200 kPa, determine the final pressure. Assume the gas behaves ideally.

Step 1: Given: V1 = 0.02 m^3, V2 = 0.01 m^3, P1 = 200 kPa, gas ideal

Step 2: Formula: for the gas, pressure is inversely proportional to volume for a fixed mass, P1 V1 = P2 V2, so P2 = P1 V1 / V2 (no value of gamma is given in the book, so this ideal gas relation is the one intended)

Step 3: Substitution: P2 = 200 x 0.02 / 0.01

Step 4: Calculation: P2 = 200 x 2 = 400

Final pressure = 400 kPa.

Worked Example 3

A system undergoes an isobaric process where the pressure is kept constant at 150 kPa. If the volume increases from 0.05 m^3 to 0.08 m^3, calculate the heat added to the system.

Step 1: Given: P = 150 kPa = 150 x10^3 Pa constant, V1 = 0.05 m^3, V2 = 0.08 m^3, so Delta V = 0.03 m^3

Step 2: Formula: work done at constant pressure, W = P x Delta V, and first law, Q = Delta U + W

Step 3: Substitution: W = 150 x10^3 x 0.03

Step 4: Calculation: W = 4500 J

The expansion work is 4500 J, and the heat added is Q = Delta U + 4500 J, so the heat cannot be fixed from the given data alone because the change in internal energy is not given. Note: the answer 600 J printed in the book does not follow from the data given in this question.

Worked Example 4

During an isochoric process, the internal energy of a gas increases by 300 J. If no work is done, determine the heat added to the system.

Step 1: Given: Delta U = 300 J, isochoric process so Delta V = 0 and W = 0

Step 2: Formula: first law, Q = Delta U + W

Step 3: Substitution: Q = 300 + 0

Step 4: Calculation: Q = 300 J

Heat added to the system = 300 J, and it appears entirely as internal energy.

Worked Example 5

A gas undergoes a cyclic process, starting at point A with a volume of 0.02 m^3, going to B (isochoric heating), then to C (isothermal expansion), and finally back to A. If the heat added during isothermal expansion is 1000 J and the heat rejected during isochoric heating is 500 J, calculate the net work done by the system.

Step 1: Given: cyclic process, heat taken in Q1 = 1000 J, heat rejected Q2 = 500 J

Step 2: Formula: for a complete cycle Delta U = 0, so first law gives net work W = net heat = Q1 - Q2

Step 3: Substitution: W = 1000 - 500

Step 4: Calculation: W = 500 J

Net work done by the system = 500 J per cycle.

Worked Example 6

A gas expands from 0.03 m^3 to 0.06 m^3 against a constant pressure of 100 kPa. Calculate the work done in both a reversible and an irreversible process, and compare the results.

Step 1: Given: V1 = 0.03 m^3, V2 = 0.06 m^3, so Delta V = 0.03 m^3, constant pressure P = 100 kPa = 100 x10^3 Pa

Step 2: Formula: work against a constant pressure, W = P x Delta V

Step 3: Substitution: W = 100 x10^3 x 0.03

Step 4: Calculation: W = 3000 J

The work is 3000 J; with only a constant opposing pressure given, the same value is obtained for the expansion whether it is described as reversible or irreversible, because the temperature data needed for a separate reversible isothermal calculation is not given. Note: the answers 300 J and 600 J printed in the book do not follow from the data given in this question.

Worked Example 7

A 50 g piece of copper at 100 degrees C is placed in 200 g of water at 20 degrees C. If the final temperature of the system is 30 degrees C, calculate the specific heat capacity of copper. (Specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 J/g degrees C)

Step 1: Given: mass of copper = 50 g, copper cools from 100 degrees C to 30 degrees C, so its temperature fall = 70 degrees C, mass of water = 200 g, water warms from 20 degrees C to 30 degrees C, so its temperature rise = 10 degrees C, c of water = 4.18 J/g degrees C

Step 2: Formula: heat lost by copper = heat gained by water, m(copper) x c(copper) x 70 = m(water) x c(water) x 10

Step 3: Substitution: 50 x c x 70 = 200 x 4.18 x 10

Step 4: Calculation: heat gained by water = 8360 J, so c = 8360 / 3500 = 2.39

From the data as printed, c of copper = 2.39 J/g degrees C. Note: the value 0.39 J/g degrees C printed in the book is the standard tabulated value for copper, but it does not agree with the final temperature of 30 degrees C stated in this question.

Worked Example 8

How much heat is required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of lead from 25 degrees C to 100 degrees C? (Specific heat capacity of lead = 0.128 J/g degrees C).

Step 1: Given: mass m = 1 kg = 1000 g, temperature rise Delta T = 100 - 25 = 75 degrees C, c of lead = 0.128 J/g degrees C

Step 2: Formula: Q = m c Delta T

Step 3: Substitution: Q = 1000 x 0.128 x 75

Step 4: Calculation: Q = 128 x 75 = 9600 J

Heat required = 9600 J. Note: the answer printed in the book does not follow from the data given in this question.

mcqs.q: A gas expands isothermally at 300 K and absorbs 500 J of heat. How much work does the gas do?
mcqs.why: For isothermal change of an ideal gas Delta U = 0, so the first law Q = Delta U + W gives W = Q = 500 J. All heat absorbed is converted into work at constant temperature.

mcqs.q: A gas is compressed adiabatically from 0.02 m^3 to 0.01 m^3 starting at 200 kPa. Using P1V1 = P2V2, what is the final pressure?
mcqs.why: P2 = P1V1/V2 = 200 x 0.02/0.01 = 200 x 2 = 400 kPa. Halving the volume doubles the pressure for a fixed mass of ideal gas in this relation.

mcqs.q: At constant pressure 150 kPa a gas expands from 0.05 m^3 to 0.08 m^3. What is the expansion work?
mcqs.why: Delta V = 0.08 - 0.05 = 0.03 m^3, so W = P Delta V = 150 x 10^3 x 0.03 = 4500 J. This is the work done by the gas in the isobaric expansion.

mcqs.q: For the same isobaric expansion (P = 150 kPa, W = 4500 J), why can the total heat added Q not be fixed from the data given?
options: Because Q = Delta U + W and the change in internal energy Delta U is not given
Because the first law does not apply
mcqs.why: Q = Delta U + 4500 J, but Delta U is not given, so Q cannot be fixed. Note the 600 J printed in the book does not follow from the data given in the question.

mcqs.q: In an isochoric process the internal energy of a gas increases by 300 J and no work is done. How much heat was added?
mcqs.why: Q = Delta U + W = 300 + 0 = 300 J. In an isochoric process Delta V = 0 so W = 0, and all heat added appears entirely as internal energy.

mcqs.q: A cyclic process takes in 1000 J of heat and rejects 500 J. What is the net work done per cycle?
mcqs.why: For a complete cycle Delta U = 0, so net work = net heat = Q1 - Q2 = 1000 - 500 = 500 J per cycle, by the first law.

mcqs.q: Why is Delta U = 0 for any complete cyclic process?
options: Because the system returns to its starting state, so its internal energy is unchanged
Because no heat is exchanged in a cycle
Because work is always zero in a cycle
mcqs.why: Internal energy depends only on the state of the system. After a complete cycle the system is back at its starting state, so Delta U = 0 and net work equals net heat absorbed.

mcqs.q: A gas expands from 0.03 m^3 to 0.06 m^3 against constant pressure 100 kPa. What is the work done?
mcqs.why: Delta V = 0.06 - 0.03 = 0.03 m^3, so W = P Delta V = 100 x 10^3 x 0.03 = 3000 J. The book's printed 300 J and 600 J do not follow from the data given.

mcqs.q: For that expansion against a constant opposing pressure of 100 kPa, how do the reversible and irreversible work values compare?
options: Both give the same value, 3000 J, from the data given
mcqs.why: With only a constant opposing pressure given, W = P Delta V = 3000 J either way. Temperature data needed for a separate reversible isothermal calculation is not given, so no different value can be obtained.

mcqs.q: 200 g of water warms from 20 degrees C to 30 degrees C (c = 4.18 J/g degrees C). How much heat does the water gain?
mcqs.why: Heat gained = m c Delta T = 200 x 4.18 x 10 = 8360 J. The water's temperature rise is 30 - 20 = 10 degrees C, and this heat is supplied by the hot copper cooling down.

mcqs.q: 50 g of copper cools from 100 degrees C to 30 degrees C while the water gains 8360 J. From this data, what is the specific heat capacity of copper?
mcqs.why: Heat lost by copper = heat gained by water: 50 x c x 70 = 8360, so c = 8360/3500 = 2.39 J/g degrees C from the data as printed. The book's 0.39 is the tabulated value but disagrees with the stated 30 degrees C final temperature.

mcqs.q: In the copper-water experiment, what are the temperature changes of the copper and of the water?
options: Copper falls 100 degrees C; water rises 20 degrees C
Copper falls 10 degrees C; water rises 70 degrees C
Copper falls 70 degrees C; water rises 10 degrees C
mcqs.why: Copper cools from 100 to 30 degrees C, a fall of 70 degrees C; water warms from 20 to 30 degrees C, a rise of 10 degrees C. These changes enter heat lost = heat gained: 50 x c x 70 = 200 x 4.18 x 10.

mcqs.q: How much heat raises 1 kg of lead from 25 degrees C to 100 degrees C? (c of lead = 0.128 J/g degrees C)
mcqs.why: Delta T = 100 - 25 = 75 degrees C and m = 1000 g, so Q = m c Delta T = 1000 x 0.128 x 75 = 128 x 75 = 9600 J. The answer printed in the book does not follow from the data given.

mcqs.q: Which formula is used to calculate the heat in the lead and copper-water examples?
mcqs.why: Q = m c Delta T gives heat from mass, specific heat capacity and temperature change. It gives 9600 J for the lead and 8360 J gained by the water in the copper experiment.

mcqs.q: In the isothermal expansion example at 300 K with Q = 500 J, why is Delta U exactly zero?
options: Because the temperature is constant and ideal-gas internal energy depends only on temperature
mcqs.why: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. The expansion is isothermal at 300 K, so temperature and internal energy are unchanged, Delta U = 0, and W = Q = 500 J.

lessons.title: Heat Engines, Entropy and the Second Law
lessons.notes_html:
Heat Engines and Efficiency

Carnot efficiency is eta = 1 - T2 / T1, where T2 is the exhaust or sink temperature in kelvin. The efficiency becomes 1, that is 100 percent, only when T2 = 0 K. Absolute zero cannot be reached in practice, so even a frictionless engine cannot be 100 percent efficient.

A diesel engine has no sparking plug, because the fuel is ignited by the high temperature of air compressed strongly inside the cylinder. The injector sprays diesel fuel into this hot air and it burns at once. A sparking plug is used only in a petrol engine, where the mixture is ignited by an electric spark.

The Kelvin statement of the second law says no cyclic engine can convert all the heat it absorbs into work; some heat must always be rejected to a colder sink. Even an ideal Carnot engine rejects heat because its sink is above 0 K. Complete conversion in a single non-cyclic change is possible, but not in a working cycle.

A diesel engine compresses air to a much higher ratio than a petrol engine, and higher compression gives higher efficiency. Typical diesel efficiencies are about 35 to 40 percent, compared with about 25 to 30 percent for petrol engines. Neither engine can have efficiency 1, because some heat is always rejected to the sink.

Entropy and the Direction of Natural Change

For a reversible change, the entropy change is Delta S = Delta Q(rev) / T, where Delta Q(rev) is the heat absorbed reversibly at absolute temperature T. Its unit is J/K. Heat absorbed increases entropy, while heat rejected decreases it.

Natural processes are irreversible and proceed in the direction of increasing disorder. The second law states that the entropy of the universe, system plus surroundings, increases in every natural process. It can remain constant only in the ideal reversible case, which does not occur in nature.

One form of the second law is that the entropy of an isolated system, and of the universe as a whole, increases with time in all natural processes. Heat flows by itself from hot to cold, never from cold to hot. Energy is certainly converted between forms, as the first law describes, but the second law fixes the direction of the change.

Heat flowing by itself from a cold body to a hot body would decrease the total entropy and contradicts the Clausius statement of the second law. A refrigerator does move heat from cold to hot, but only because external work is supplied, so it does not violate the law. Working heat engines and the mixing of gases both agree with the second law.

Delta S = Delta Q(rev) / T

Refrigerators and Irreversible Change

A refrigerator removes heat from its inside and rejects a larger amount of heat to the room from its back coils, because the rejected heat includes the work done by the motor. With the door open, the heat removed from the room air returns to the same room, while the electrical work is added as extra heat. The net effect is that the room slowly becomes warmer.

A chemical explosion takes place suddenly, with friction, turbulence and heat loss, and it cannot be run backwards to restore both the system and the surroundings. Slow, frictionless changes such as the slow compression of a spring or a gas can be reversed by an equal opposite change. Explosions, free expansion and mixing are standard examples of irreversible processes.

mcqs.q: Carnot efficiency is eta = 1 - T2/T1. When would the efficiency become 1 (100 percent)?
options: When T2 is half of T1
mcqs.why: eta = 1 only when T2/T1 = 0, i.e. T2 = 0 K. Absolute zero cannot be reached in practice, so even a frictionless engine cannot be 100 percent efficient.

mcqs.q: Why does a diesel engine have no sparking plug?
options: Fuel is ignited by the high temperature of strongly compressed air, sprayed in by an injector
It uses an electric heater instead
mcqs.why: Air compressed strongly in the cylinder becomes very hot; the injector sprays diesel into this hot air and it burns at once. A sparking plug is used only in a petrol engine, where a spark ignites the mixture.

mcqs.q: What does the Kelvin statement of the second law say?
options: No cyclic engine can convert all the heat it absorbs into work; some heat must be rejected to a colder sink
Energy can be created in a cycle
Heat flows by itself from cold to hot
mcqs.why: The Kelvin statement says no cyclic engine converts all absorbed heat into work; some heat must always be rejected to a colder sink. Even an ideal Carnot engine rejects heat because its sink is above 0 K.

mcqs.q: How do typical diesel and petrol engine efficiencies compare?
options: Diesel about 35-40 percent, petrol about 25-30 percent
mcqs.why: A diesel compresses air to a much higher ratio, giving higher efficiency: typically 35-40 percent for diesel against 25-30 percent for petrol. Neither can reach efficiency 1 because some heat is always rejected.

mcqs.q: For a reversible change, the entropy change is Delta S = Delta Q(rev)/T. What is the unit of entropy change?
mcqs.why: Delta S = Delta Q(rev)/T has unit joules per kelvin, J/K. Heat absorbed increases entropy, while heat rejected decreases it, at absolute temperature T.

mcqs.q: What does the second law say about the entropy of the universe in every natural process?
options: It increases; it can stay constant only in the ideal reversible case
mcqs.why: The entropy of the universe (system plus surroundings) increases in every natural process, since natural processes are irreversible and increase disorder. Constancy occurs only in the ideal reversible limit, which does not occur in nature.

mcqs.q: Which event would violate the second law (Clausius statement)?
options: Heat flowing by itself from a cold body to a hot body
mcqs.why: Heat flowing by itself from cold to hot would decrease total entropy and contradicts the Clausius statement. A refrigerator moves heat cold-to-hot only because external work is supplied, so it does not violate the law.

mcqs.q: A refrigerator runs with its door open in a closed room. What happens to the room temperature?
options: It falls to the refrigerator temperature
mcqs.why: The refrigerator rejects more heat from its back coils than it removes inside, because rejected heat includes the motor's work. With the door open both stay in the same room, so the room slowly becomes warmer.

mcqs.q: Which of the following processes is irreversible?
mcqs.why: A chemical explosion is sudden, with friction, turbulence and heat loss, and cannot be run backwards to restore system and surroundings. Slow frictionless changes like compressing a spring can be reversed; explosions, free expansion and mixing cannot.

mcqs.q: Why can complete conversion of heat into work not happen in a working cycle, even though it can in a single change?
options: Because a cycle must return to its start and reject heat to a sink above 0 K
Because work is always zero in a cycle
mcqs.why: In a single non-cyclic change (e.g. isothermal expansion) all heat can become work. But a cyclic engine must repeat its cycle and, by the Kelvin statement, must reject some heat to a colder sink, so complete conversion in a cycle is impossible.

lessons.title: The Second Law in Daily Life
lessons.notes_html:
Factors Affecting the Efficiency of Automobile Engines

The efficiency of an automobile engine depends strongly on the compression ratio, because a higher ratio between the source and sink temperatures gives a higher possible efficiency. Friction between moving parts, heat lost to the cooling system and exhaust gases, and incomplete burning of fuel all reduce the actual efficiency. The temperature of the burning gases and the temperature at which heat is rejected also matter. Good lubrication, correct fuel-air mixture and proper maintenance therefore improve efficiency.

An Air Conditioner Standing Inside the Room

The room will become warmer, not cooler. An air conditioner removes heat from the air at its front and rejects that heat, plus the electrical work consumed, from its back. When the unit stands inside the room, both the removed heat and the rejected heat stay in the same room. The work done by its motor and compressor is added as extra heat, so the average temperature of the room rises slowly.

Adding Heat Without Changing the Temperature

Heat can be added without a temperature change during an isothermal process, where the system expands while in contact with a heat reservoir and all the heat supplied is converted into work. Heat is also added without temperature change during a change of state, such as melting ice or boiling water at constant pressure. In that case the energy is used to break intermolecular bonds and increase internal potential energy. In both cases the internal kinetic energy, and hence the temperature, stays constant.

Can an Open Refrigerator Cool a Room?

No, a room cannot be cooled by leaving the refrigerator door open. The refrigerator takes heat from the air near its open door but rejects a greater quantity of heat to the same room from the coils at its back. The extra rejected heat is the electrical work done by the compressor. As a result the room actually warms up slowly instead of cooling.

When Does the Entropy of a System Decrease?

The entropy of a system decreases when heat is removed from it in an orderly way, for example when a gas is compressed isothermally and rejects heat, or when water freezes into ice. In such cases the system itself becomes more ordered and its entropy falls. However, the entropy of the surroundings increases by a larger amount, so the entropy of the universe still increases. A local decrease of entropy is therefore allowed by the second law.

Can an Engine Be Free of Thermal Pollution?

No, such an engine is impossible according to the second law. Every cyclic heat engine must reject some heat to a colder sink, and this rejected heat warms the environment, which is thermal pollution. Only an engine with a sink at 0 K could convert all heat into work, and absolute zero cannot be attained. Better design can reduce the rejected heat but can never remove it completely.

Can Heat Be Completely Converted into Work?

In a single non-cyclic process, such as the isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, heat can be completely converted into work because the internal energy does not change. But no cyclic engine, which must return again and again to its starting state to work continuously, can do this. The second law requires a working engine to reject part of the heat to a sink. So complete conversion is possible once, but not in a continuous cycle.

Entropy as the Arrow of Time

Entropy is called the arrow of time because it gives a direction to natural change: the entropy of the universe always increases as time passes. We remember the past, where entropy was lower, and move towards the future, where entropy is higher. Processes such as mixing, cooling of hot bodies and breaking of objects can be told apart from their reverse by the entropy change alone. Just as an arrow points one way, increasing entropy points from past to future.

mcqs.q: Which factor most strongly affects the efficiency of an automobile engine through the temperature ratio?
options: The type of engine oil brand only
mcqs.why: Efficiency depends strongly on compression ratio, because a higher ratio between source and sink temperatures gives a higher possible efficiency. Friction, cooling and exhaust losses, and incomplete burning then reduce the actual value.

mcqs.q: Which of the following REDUCE the actual efficiency of an automobile engine?
options: Friction, heat lost to cooling and exhaust, and incomplete burning of fuel
mcqs.why: Friction between moving parts, heat lost to the cooling system and exhaust gases, and incomplete burning of fuel all reduce actual efficiency. Good lubrication, correct mixture and proper maintenance improve it.

mcqs.q: An air conditioner stands on a table inside a closed room and runs. What happens to the room?
options: It becomes warmer, because rejected heat plus electrical work stay in the room
Only the air near it cools permanently
mcqs.why: The unit removes heat at its front but rejects that heat plus the electrical work consumed from its back. Both stay in the same room, so the work is added as extra heat and the room temperature rises slowly.

mcqs.q: During which process can heat be added to a system without changing its temperature by expansion against a reservoir?
options: Isothermal process, where all heat supplied becomes work
Free expansion into vacuum with heating
mcqs.why: In an isothermal process the system expands in contact with a heat reservoir and all heat supplied is converted into work, so internal kinetic energy and temperature stay constant while heat is added.

mcqs.q: Heat is also added without a temperature change during a change of state, such as melting ice. Where does the energy go?
options: It breaks intermolecular bonds and increases internal potential energy
It becomes work on the surroundings only
mcqs.why: During melting or boiling at constant pressure the energy breaks intermolecular bonds and increases internal potential energy. Internal kinetic energy, and hence temperature, stays constant during the change of state.

mcqs.q: Can a room be cooled by leaving the refrigerator door open?
options: Yes, if the room is small
No, because refrigerators produce no cooling at all
No, the refrigerator rejects more heat to the room than it removes, so the room warms slowly
mcqs.why: No. The refrigerator takes heat from air near its door but rejects a greater quantity from its back coils; the extra is the compressor's electrical work. The room therefore warms up slowly instead of cooling.

mcqs.q: When does the entropy of a system itself decrease?
options: When heat is removed in an orderly way, e.g. isothermal compression rejecting heat, or water freezing
When heat is added to it
mcqs.why: Entropy of a system falls when heat is removed orderly, a gas compressed isothermally rejecting heat, or water freezing into ice, as the system becomes more ordered. The surroundings gain more entropy, so the universe still increases.

mcqs.q: Why is an engine completely free of thermal pollution impossible?
options: Because every cyclic engine must reject heat to a colder sink; only a 0 K sink would avoid it, and 0 K cannot be attained
mcqs.why: Every cyclic heat engine must reject some heat to a colder sink, and that rejected heat warms the environment, thermal pollution. Only a sink at 0 K would remove it, and absolute zero cannot be attained; design can only reduce it.

mcqs.q: Can heat be completely converted into work?
options: Yes, in a single non-cyclic process such as isothermal expansion, but not in a continuous cycle
mcqs.why: In isothermal expansion of an ideal gas internal energy is unchanged, so heat is completely converted into work, once. A cyclic engine must return to its start repeatedly and must reject part of the heat to a sink, so it cannot do this continuously.

mcqs.q: Why is entropy called the 'arrow of time'?
options: Because entropy decreases as time passes
Because time flows from hot to cold
Because entropy measures clock time directly
Because the entropy of the universe always increases with time, giving direction from past (lower entropy) to future (higher entropy)
mcqs.why: Entropy gives direction to natural change: universe entropy was lower in the past and increases towards the future. Mixing, cooling and breaking can be told from their reverses by entropy change alone, like an arrow pointing one way.

lessons.title: Engines, Refrigerators and Entropy
lessons.notes_html:
Statements of the Second Law and the Concept of Entropy

The Kelvin statement says it is impossible to construct a cyclic engine that absorbs heat from a single reservoir and converts it completely into work without any other change.
