The Clausius statement says it is impossible for heat to flow by itself from a colder body to a hotter body without external work being done. Entropy is a measure of the disorder or randomness of a system, defined by Delta S = Delta Q(rev) / T for a reversible change. When heat is absorbed, the molecules become more disordered and entropy increases; when heat is rejected in an orderly way, entropy decreases. In terms of entropy, the second law states that the entropy of the universe increases in every natural process, Delta S(universe) is greater than zero, and remains constant only in the ideal reversible limit.

The Heat Engine and Its Efficiency

A heat engine is a cyclic device that absorbs heat Q1 from a hot reservoir, converts part of it into work W, and rejects the remaining heat Q2 to a cold reservoir. A steam engine and a petrol engine work on this principle, using a working substance that returns to its initial state after each cycle. By the first law for a complete cycle, Delta U = 0, so W = Q1 - Q2. Efficiency is defined as useful work output divided by heat input, eta = W / Q1. Substituting for W gives eta = (Q1 - Q2) / Q1 = 1 - Q2 / Q1, which is always less than 1 because Q2 can never be zero.

Reversible and Irreversible Processes

A reversible process is an ideal process carried out infinitely slowly, through a series of equilibrium states, so that it can be reversed by an infinitesimal change and both the system and surroundings return exactly to their initial states. There is no friction, no turbulence and no heat flow across a finite temperature difference in such a process. An irreversible process cannot be reversed in this way; it leaves a permanent change in the surroundings, and all natural processes are of this type. Friction, free expansion, conduction across a large temperature difference, and chemical explosions are irreversible. Reversible processes are useful as a standard because they give the maximum possible efficiency or work for given conditions.

The Carnot Engine and the Carnot Cycle

A Carnot engine is an ideal reversible engine working between two temperatures, and no real engine working between the same temperatures can be more efficient. Its cycle has four reversible steps: isothermal expansion at the hot temperature T1, adiabatic expansion down to the cold temperature T2, isothermal compression at T2, and adiabatic compression back to the starting state. For this cycle Q2 / Q1 = T2 / T1, so the efficiency is eta = 1 - T2 / T1. Since T2 is never 0 K in practice, T2 / T1 is always positive and eta is always less than 1. Even the Carnot engine therefore rejects heat to the sink and cannot reach 100 percent efficiency.

The Refrigerator: A Heat Engine in Reverse

A refrigerator takes heat Q2 from a cold body, receives work W from an external source such as an electric motor, and rejects the total heat Q1 = Q2 + W to the warmer surroundings. This is exactly the heat engine cycle run backwards: instead of heat flowing down and producing work, work is supplied to push heat up from cold to hot. Its performance is measured by the coefficient of performance, COP = Q2 / W, which plays the role of efficiency for a refrigerator. Using Q1 = Q2 + W, COP = Q2 / (Q1 - Q2), and for an ideal reversible refrigerator COP = T2 / (T1 - T2), where T2 is the cold temperature and T1 is the hot temperature in kelvin.

Entropy Change When Heat Is Added or Removed

Entropy change is given by Delta S = Delta Q(rev) / T, where T is the absolute temperature and is always positive. When heat is added, Delta Q is positive, so Delta S is positive and the entropy of the system increases, because the molecules gain energy and their motion becomes more random. When heat is removed, Delta Q is negative, so Delta S is negative and the entropy decreases, because the molecules lose energy and become more ordered. Melting of ice is an example of entropy increase on heating, while freezing of water shows entropy decrease on cooling. The sign of the entropy change of a system is therefore fixed by the direction of heat flow.

Increase of Entropy and Degradation of Energy

Degradation of energy means energy becoming less available for doing useful work, even though the total amount of energy is conserved. In every irreversible process, such as friction, conduction and mixing, organised energy like mechanical work or a high temperature difference is spread out as random molecular energy. Once energy is spread uniformly at a low temperature, it cannot be gathered back to do the same work again. This loss of availability is measured by the increase of entropy, through the relation unavailable energy = T0 x Delta S for surroundings at T0. Increasing entropy therefore means steady degradation of the quality of energy in the universe.

eta = 1 - T2 / T1

mcqs.q: What does the Clausius statement of the second law say?
options: A cyclic engine can convert all heat into work
Work can be created from nothing
Heat cannot flow by itself from a colder body to a hotter body without external work
mcqs.why: The Clausius statement says heat cannot flow by itself from cold to hot without external work being done. This complements the Kelvin statement, which forbids a cyclic engine converting all absorbed heat into work.

mcqs.q: Entropy is best described as a measure of what, and how is its change defined?
options: Disorder or randomness; Delta S = Delta Q(rev)/T for a reversible change
Pressure; Delta S = P Delta V
mcqs.why: Entropy measures disorder or randomness, defined by Delta S = Delta Q(rev)/T. Heat absorbed makes molecules more disordered (entropy up); heat rejected orderly makes entropy decrease.

mcqs.q: A heat engine absorbs Q1 from a hot reservoir and rejects Q2 to a cold reservoir. What are its work and efficiency?
options: W = Q1 - Q2; eta = W/Q1 = 1 - Q2/Q1
W = Q1 x Q2; eta = 1 always
mcqs.why: For a complete cycle Delta U = 0, so W = Q1 - Q2 by the first law. Efficiency eta = W/Q1 = (Q1 - Q2)/Q1 = 1 - Q2/Q1, always less than 1 because Q2 can never be zero.

mcqs.q: What is a reversible process?
options: An ideal process carried out infinitely slowly through equilibrium states, reversible by an infinitesimal change with system and surroundings restored exactly
A process that increases entropy greatly
mcqs.why: A reversible process proceeds infinitely slowly through equilibrium states, with no friction, turbulence or heat flow across a finite temperature difference, so an infinitesimal change reverses it and restores system and surroundings exactly.

mcqs.q: Which list contains only irreversible processes?
options: Friction, free expansion, conduction across a large temperature difference, chemical explosions
Slow spring compression, slow gas compression
mcqs.why: Friction, free expansion, conduction across a large temperature difference and chemical explosions are irreversible, they leave permanent change in the surroundings. All natural processes are irreversible; reversible ones are an ideal standard giving maximum efficiency.

mcqs.q: What are the four reversible steps of the Carnot cycle, in order?
options: Isothermal expansion at T1, adiabatic expansion to T2, isothermal compression at T2, adiabatic compression back to start
Two isobaric and two isochoric steps
Isothermal compression, adiabatic compression, isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion
mcqs.why: The Carnot cycle is: isothermal expansion at hot T1, adiabatic expansion down to cold T2, isothermal compression at T2, adiabatic compression back to the start. It is the ideal reversible cycle between two temperatures.

mcqs.q: Why is even the Carnot engine's efficiency less than 100 percent?
options: Because of friction in its parts
Because eta = 1 - T2/T1 and T2 is never 0 K in practice, so T2/T1 is positive and heat is rejected to the sink
mcqs.why: For the Carnot cycle Q2/Q1 = T2/T1, so eta = 1 - T2/T1. Since T2 is never 0 K in practice, eta is always less than 1 and even the Carnot engine rejects heat to the sink.

mcqs.q: A refrigerator takes Q2 from a cold body with work input W. How much heat Q1 does it reject, and what is its COP?
mcqs.why: A refrigerator is a heat engine in reverse: it rejects Q1 = Q2 + W to the warmer surroundings. Its coefficient of performance is COP = Q2/W = Q2/(Q1 - Q2), and ideally COP = T2/(T1 - T2).

mcqs.q: Heat is added to a system reversibly. What happens to its entropy, and what example illustrates it?
options: Entropy increases; e.g. melting of ice
Entropy is unchanged; e.g. adiabatic change
Entropy decreases; e.g. freezing of water
mcqs.why: Delta S = Delta Q(rev)/T with T always positive: heat added (Delta Q positive) gives positive Delta S, molecules gain energy and move more randomly. Melting of ice illustrates entropy increase; freezing shows the decrease on heat removal.

mcqs.q: What is meant by degradation of energy, and how is the unavailable energy measured?
options: Energy becomes less available for useful work though total energy is conserved; unavailable energy = T0 x Delta S
Energy is destroyed; measured by Delta U
Energy increases in quality; measured by work done
Energy changes into mass; measured by Q1 - Q2
mcqs.why: Degradation means organised energy spreads out as random molecular energy in irreversible processes and can no longer do the same work, though total energy is conserved. Unavailable energy = T0 x Delta S for surroundings at T0, so rising entropy means steady degradation.

lessons.title: Worked Examples
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example 1

A Carnot engine takes 2000J of heat from a reservoir at 500K does some work, and discards some heat to a reservoir at 350K. How much heat is discarded, how much work does the engine do, and what is the efficiency?

Step 1: Given: heat absorbed Q1 = 2000 J, hot reservoir T1 = 500 K, cold reservoir T2 = 350 K

Step 2: Formula: for a Carnot engine Q2 / Q1 = T2 / T1, work W = Q1 - Q2, and efficiency eta = 1 - T2 / T1

Step 3: Substitution: Q2 = 2000 x 350 / 500, and eta = 1 - 350 / 500

Step 4: Calculation: Q2 = 1400 J, W = 2000 - 1400 = 600 J, and eta = 1 - 0.70 = 0.30

Heat discarded = 1400 J, work done = 600 J, and efficiency = 30 percent.

Worked Example 2

One kilogram of ice at 0 degrees C is melted and converted to water at 0 degrees C. Compute its change in entropy.

Step 1: Given: mass m = 1 kg, T = 0 degrees C = 273 K, latent heat of fusion of ice Lf = 3.34 x10^5 J/kg

Step 2: Formula: heat absorbed Q = m Lf, and entropy change Delta S = Q / T

Step 3: Substitution: Q = 1 x 3.34 x10^5 = 3.34 x10^5 J, and Delta S = 3.34 x10^5 / 273

Step 4: Calculation: Delta S = 1223 J/K

Increase in entropy = about 1220 J/K.

Worked Example 3

In a high-pressure steam turbine engine, the steam is heated to 600 degrees C and exhausted at about 90 degrees C. What is the highest possible efficiency of any engine that operates between these two temperatures?

Step 1: Given: T1 = 600 degrees C = 873 K, T2 = 90 degrees C = 363 K

Step 2: Formula: highest possible efficiency is the Carnot efficiency, eta = 1 - T2 / T1

Step 3: Substitution: eta = 1 - 363 / 873

Step 4: Calculation: 363 / 873 = 0.416, and eta = 1 - 0.416 = 0.584

Highest possible efficiency = 58.4 percent, and a real engine will always be less efficient than this.

Worked Example 4

Temperature difference between the surface water and bottom water in Manchester Lake might be 5 degrees C. Assuming the surface water to be at 20 degrees C. What highest efficiency a steam engine could have if it operates between these two temperatures?

Step 1: Given: surface temperature T1 = 20 degrees C = 293 K, temperature difference = 5 degrees C, so bottom temperature T2 = 15 degrees C = 288 K

Step 2: Formula: Carnot efficiency, eta = 1 - T2 / T1 = (T1 - T2) / T1

Step 3: Substitution: eta = 5 / 293

Step 4: Calculation: eta = 0.0171

Highest possible efficiency = 1.71 percent, which is too small to be useful in practice.

Worked Example 5

A heat engine works at the rate of 500kW. The efficiency of the engine is 30 percent. Calculate the loss of heat per hour.

Step 1: Given: work output rate = 500 kW = 500 x10^3 W, efficiency eta = 30 percent = 0.30, time = 1 hour = 3600 s

Step 2: Formula: input power = work rate / eta, loss rate = input power - work rate, and heat lost in one hour = loss rate x 3600

Step 3: Substitution: input power = 500 x10^3 / 0.30 = 1.667 x10^6 W, and loss rate = 1.667 x10^6 - 500 x10^3 = 1.167 x10^6 W

Step 4: Calculation: heat lost = 1.167 x10^6 x 3600 = 4.2 x10^9 J

Loss of heat per hour = 4.2 x10^9 J.

Worked Example 6

A heat engine performs work of 0.4166 watts in one hour and rejects 4500J of heat to the sink. What is the efficiency of engine?

Step 1: Given: work rate = 0.4166 W, time = 1 hour = 3600 s, heat rejected Q2 = 4500 J

Step 2: Formula: work W = rate x time, heat absorbed Q1 = W + Q2, and efficiency eta = W / Q1

Step 3: Substitution: W = 0.4166 x 3600 = 1500 J, and Q1 = 1500 + 4500 = 6000 J

Step 4: Calculation: eta = 1500 / 6000 = 0.25, that is about 25 percent

Efficiency of the engine = about 24.9 percent.

Worked Example 7

A Carnot engine operates between the temperatures 850K and 300K. the engine performs 1200J of work in each cycle, which takes 0.25 sec (a) What is the efficiency of this engine? (b) What is the average power of this engine? (c) How much energy is extracted as heat from the high temperature reservoir? (d) How much energy is delivered as heat to the low temperature reservoir?

Step 1: Given: T1 = 850 K, T2 = 300 K, work per cycle W = 1200 J, time per cycle t = 0.25 s

Step 2: Formula: (a) eta = 1 - T2 / T1, (b) power P = W / t, (c) heat absorbed Q1 = W / eta, and (d) heat rejected Q2 = Q1 - W

Step 3: Substitution: (a) eta = 1 - 300 / 850, (b) P = 1200 / 0.25, (c) Q1 = 1200 / 0.647, and (d) Q2 = Q1 - 1200

Step 4: Calculation: (a) eta = 0.647, about 65 percent, (b) P = 4800 W = 4.8 kW, (c) Q1 = 1855 J, and (d) Q2 = 655 J

(a) efficiency = about 65 percent (b) average power = 4.8 kW (c) heat extracted = 1855 J (d) heat delivered to the low temperature reservoir = 655 J.

Worked Example 8

A Carnot engine absorbs 52kJ as heat and exhaust 36kJ as heat in each cycle. Calculate: (a) The engine efficiency (b) The work done per cycle in kilojoules.

Step 1: Given: heat absorbed Q1 = 52 kJ, heat exhausted Q2 = 36 kJ

Step 2: Formula: work W = Q1 - Q2, and efficiency eta = W / Q1

Step 3: Substitution: W = 52 - 36, and eta = 16 / 52

Step 4: Calculation: W = 16 kJ, and eta = 0.3076

(a) engine efficiency = 30.76 percent, and (b) work done per cycle = 16 kJ.

mcqs.q: A Carnot engine takes 2000 J from a reservoir at 500 K and discards heat to a reservoir at 350 K. How much heat is discarded?
mcqs.why: For a Carnot engine Q2/Q1 = T2/T1, so Q2 = 2000 x 350/500 = 1400 J. The remaining 600 J becomes work done by the engine.

mcqs.q: For the same Carnot engine (Q1 = 2000 J, Q2 = 1400 J), how much work does it do?
mcqs.why: W = Q1 - Q2 = 2000 - 1400 = 600 J. This is the work done per cycle by the Carnot engine operating between 500 K and 350 K.

mcqs.q: What is the efficiency of that Carnot engine between 500 K and 350 K?
How much heat is absorbed when 1 kg of ice at 0 degrees C melts? (Lf = 3.34 x 10^5 J/kg)
mcqs.why: Q = m Lf = 1 x 3.34 x 10^5 = 3.34 x 10^5 J. This heat is absorbed at constant temperature 273 K during melting.

mcqs.q: What is the entropy change when 1 kg of ice melts at 0 degrees C (273 K)?
mcqs.why: Delta S = Q/T = 3.34 x 10^5 / 273 = 1223 J/K, about 1220 J/K. Entropy increases because the melted water is more disordered than ice.

mcqs.q: Steam is heated to 600 degrees C and exhausted at 90 degrees C. What is the highest possible (Carnot) efficiency?
mcqs.why: Convert to kelvin: T1 = 873 K, T2 = 363 K. eta = 1 - 363/873 = 1 - 0.416 = 0.584, i.e. 58.4 percent. A real engine between these temperatures will always be less efficient.

mcqs.q: Surface water at 20 degrees C (293 K) and bottom water 5 degrees C colder (288 K): what is the highest possible efficiency?
mcqs.why: eta = 1 - T2/T1 = (T1 - T2)/T1 = 5/293 = 0.0171, i.e. 1.71 percent. Such a small temperature difference gives an efficiency too small to be useful in practice.

mcqs.q: A heat engine does work at 500 kW with 30 percent efficiency. What is its heat input power?
mcqs.why: Input power = work rate / eta = 500 x 10^3 / 0.30 = 1.667 x 10^6 W. The loss rate is then input minus work rate, used to find heat lost per hour.

mcqs.q: For that engine (input 1.667 x 10^6 W, work 500 kW), how much heat is lost per hour?
mcqs.why: Loss rate = 1.667 x 10^6 - 500 x 10^3 = 1.167 x 10^6 W. In one hour: 1.167 x 10^6 x 3600 = 4.2 x 10^9 J of heat is lost.

mcqs.q: An engine works at 0.4166 W for one hour. How much work does it perform in that hour?
mcqs.why: W = rate x time = 0.4166 x 3600 = 1500 J (about 1499.8 J). Together with the 4500 J rejected, this gives heat absorbed Q1 = 6000 J.

mcqs.q: That engine rejects 4500 J and does 1500 J of work. What is its efficiency?
mcqs.why: Q1 = W + Q2 = 1500 + 4500 = 6000 J, so eta = W/Q1 = 1500/6000 = 0.25, about 25 percent (24.9 percent as printed in the book).

mcqs.q: A Carnot engine operates between 850 K and 300 K. What is its efficiency?
mcqs.why: eta = 1 - T2/T1 = 1 - 300/850 = 1 - 0.353 = 0.647, about 65 percent. No real engine between these temperatures can exceed this Carnot value.

mcqs.q: That Carnot engine does 1200 J of work per cycle, each cycle taking 0.25 s. What is its average power?
mcqs.why: Power P = W/t = 1200/0.25 = 4800 W = 4.8 kW. Power is the work per cycle divided by the time taken for each cycle.

mcqs.q: For the 850 K / 300 K Carnot engine doing 1200 J per cycle at eta = 0.647, how much heat is extracted from the hot reservoir per cycle?
mcqs.why: Q1 = W/eta = 1200/0.647 = 1855 J extracted as heat from the high temperature reservoir per cycle. The rest of the accounting gives Q2 = Q1 - W = 655 J.

mcqs.q: A Carnot engine absorbs 52 kJ and exhausts 36 kJ per cycle. What are the work done and the efficiency?
mcqs.why: W = Q1 - Q2 = 52 - 36 = 16 kJ, and eta = W/Q1 = 16/52 = 0.3076, i.e. 30.76 percent efficiency with 16 kJ of work done per cycle.

lessons.title: Magnetic Fields and Forces
lessons.notes_html:
Field of a Current-Carrying Conductor

The magnetic field around a current carrying conductor is directly tied to the direction of the current, as shown by the right hand rule. If the current is reversed, every field line reverses its sense of circulation. The strength of the field stays the same, only its direction is reversed.

Magnetic levitation trains use powerful magnetic fields to lift the train above the track and to push it forward, removing friction with the rails. Microwave ovens use electromagnetic waves, electrolysis uses electric current in a liquid, and photosynthesis is a biological process. Maglev trains are therefore the direct application of strong magnetic fields.

Inside a long, closely wound solenoid the field lines are straight, parallel and equally spaced, so the field is uniform and given by B = mu0 n I. It has nearly the same value at all points well inside the solenoid. Outside the solenoid the field is very weak and falls off rapidly near the ends.

B = mu0 n I (inside a solenoid)

Force on Conductors and Moving Charges

The simple form F = BIL is the maximum force and holds when the conductor is at right angles to the magnetic field, so that sin theta = 1 with theta = 90 degrees. In general the force is F = BIL sin theta. If the conductor is parallel to the field, theta = 0 and the force becomes zero.

The magnetic force on a moving charge is F = q v B sin theta, so the force is directly proportional to the charge q. If q is doubled while v, B and theta stay the same, the force is also doubled. It would become four times only if both the charge and another factor such as velocity were doubled together.

The magnetic force F = q v B sin theta always acts at right angles to both the velocity of the charge and the magnetic field. This is found from Fleming left hand rule or the right hand rule for a positive charge. Because the force is always perpendicular to the motion, the proton moves in a circle and its speed does not change.

The force is F = q v B sin theta, and for motion parallel to the field theta = 0 degrees, so sin theta = 0. The magnetic force is therefore zero whatever the speed of the electron. The electron continues in a straight line with constant velocity as if no field were present.

F = B I L sin theta ; F = q v B sin theta

Parallel Currents and Measuring Instruments

For a solenoid B = mu0 n I, where n is the number of turns per unit length, so increasing the number of turns increases the field strength directly. Increasing the current and inserting an iron core also strengthen the field, because the core has a large permeability. Decreasing the number of turns would weaken the field, so it is the one change that does not help.

Each current carrying conductor produces a magnetic field around itself, and this field exerts a force on the current in the other conductor. Parallel currents in the same direction attract each other, while currents in opposite directions repel. This force is a direct result of the magnetic effect of current and is used to define the ampere.

A voltmeter must have a high resistance so that it draws very little current and does not disturb the circuit it is measuring. To measure a higher voltage range, a high resistance is connected in series with the galvanometer, which increases the total internal resistance. Most of the voltage then drops across this series resistance and only a safe fraction reaches the coil.

mcqs.q: If the current in a conductor is reversed, what happens to the magnetic field around it?
options: Every field line reverses its sense of circulation, while the strength stays the same
mcqs.why: Reversing the current reverses the field direction given by the right hand rule; every field line circulates the other way, but the field strength is unchanged.

mcqs.q: Which device is a direct application of strong magnetic fields, lifting a vehicle above its track to remove friction?
mcqs.why: Maglev trains use powerful magnetic fields to lift the train above the track and push it forward, removing friction with the rails.

mcqs.q: Inside a long, closely wound solenoid, the magnetic field is:
options: Uniform, with straight, parallel, equally spaced field lines, given by B = mu0 n I
mcqs.why: Well inside a long solenoid the field lines are straight, parallel and equally spaced, so the field is uniform and B = mu0 n I; outside it is very weak.

mcqs.q: The simple form F = BIL gives the maximum force on a conductor. This holds when the conductor is:
options: At right angles to the magnetic field, so theta = 90 degrees and sin theta = 1
mcqs.why: F = BIL sin theta is maximum when sin theta = 1, that is theta = 90 degrees, with the conductor at right angles to the field.

mcqs.q: A current-carrying conductor is placed parallel to a magnetic field (theta = 0 degrees). The magnetic force on it is:
mcqs.why: Using F = BIL sin theta with theta = 0 degrees gives sin theta = 0, so the force is zero when the conductor is parallel to the field.

mcqs.q: The charge on a moving particle is doubled while v, B and theta stay the same. The magnetic force F = q v B sin theta becomes:
mcqs.why: F = q v B sin theta is directly proportional to q, so doubling q alone doubles the force; it would quadruple only if another factor such as v were also doubled.

mcqs.q: The magnetic force on a moving positive charge always acts:
options: At right angles to both its velocity and the magnetic field
mcqs.why: F = q v B sin theta acts at right angles to both the velocity and the field, as found from Fleming's left hand rule or the right hand rule for a positive charge.

mcqs.q: A proton moves perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. What happens to its motion and speed?
options: It speeds up in a straight line
It moves in a circle and its speed does not change
It moves in a circle and keeps speeding up
mcqs.why: The force is always perpendicular to the motion, so it changes only the direction of motion: the proton moves in a circle and its speed stays constant.

mcqs.q: An electron moves parallel to a uniform magnetic field at high speed. The magnetic force on it is:
options: Zero, whatever its speed, because sin theta = 0
Maximum because its speed is high
mcqs.why: For motion parallel to the field theta = 0 degrees, so sin theta = 0 and F = q v B sin theta = 0 whatever the speed; it continues in a straight line at constant velocity.

mcqs.q: Two parallel conductors carry currents in the same direction. They:
options: Exert no force on each other
mcqs.why: Each conductor's magnetic field exerts a force on the current in the other; parallel currents in the same direction attract, while opposite currents repel, and this force defines the ampere.

lessons.title: Solenoids, Toroids and the Galvanometer
lessons.notes_html:
Identifying the Sign of Charged Particles in a Vacuum Tube

Yes, it is possible by applying a known magnetic or electric field across the tube and observing the direction of deflection on the fluorescent screen. A positive particle deflects to one side while a negative particle deflects to the opposite side under the same field. The direction of the spot shift, compared with the known field direction, tells the sign of the charge. This is how the negative charge of cathode ray particles was first established.

Solenoid and Simple Coil of Wire

A solenoid is a long coil of wire wound in the form of a helix on a cylindrical frame, with many closely spaced turns. When current passes through it, it behaves like a bar magnet with a nearly uniform field inside and poles at its ends. A simple coil has only a few turns, usually in one plane, and produces a much weaker and less uniform field. The solenoid is designed to concentrate a strong, uniform field along its axis, while an ordinary coil is not.

Can a Solenoid Produce a Field Without Current?

No, an ordinary solenoid cannot produce a magnetic field without current. Its field is produced only by the current flowing in its turns, as given by B = mu0 n I, so when I = 0 the field is zero. The wire itself is not magnetic and has no field of its own. Only if a permanent magnet or a magnetised iron core is placed inside can a field exist without current, and then the field belongs to the magnet, not to the solenoid.

Why a Toroid Is Often Preferred

A toroid is a solenoid bent into a closed ring, so its magnetic field is confined almost entirely inside the core. Very little flux leaks into the surrounding space, so it does not disturb or get disturbed by nearby components. This closed path also gives a stronger, better controlled field for a given current. For these reasons toroids are preferred in transformers, inductors and sensitive electronic circuits where stray magnetic fields must be avoided.

Ampere's Circuital Law and the Field Inside a Toroid

Ampere circuital law says the line integral of B around a closed path equals mu0 times the total current passing through the path. Applying it to a circular path inside a toroid of N turns carrying current I gives B x 2 pi r = mu0 N I, so B = mu0 N I / (2 pi r). The law shows that the field inside depends on the total turns and current and falls slightly with radius r. It also shows that the field outside the toroid is zero, because the net enclosed current outside is zero.

The Galvanometer and Its Function

A galvanometer is a sensitive instrument in which a current carrying coil placed in a magnetic field is deflected by the torque produced on it. Its primary function is to detect small electric currents and to indicate their direction. The deflection of its pointer is proportional to the current passing through the coil. With suitable series or shunt resistances it is converted into a voltmeter or an ammeter for actual measurements.

mcqs.q: Charged particles fired through a vacuum tube hit a fluorescent screen. How can their sign be found?
options: By applying a known magnetic or electric field and observing the direction of deflection of the spot
By measuring the brightness of the spot only
mcqs.why: A positive particle deflects to one side and a negative particle to the opposite side under the same known field, so the direction of the spot shift compared with the field direction tells the sign of the charge.

mcqs.q: Observing the deflection of cathode ray particles in a known field first established that they are:
mcqs.why: Cathode ray particles deflect to the side expected for negative charge under a known field, which is how their negative charge was first established.

mcqs.q: A solenoid is best described as:
options: A single loop of wire in one plane
A long coil of wire wound as a helix on a cylindrical frame, with many closely spaced turns
mcqs.why: A solenoid is a long coil wound in the form of a helix on a cylindrical frame with many closely spaced turns; it behaves like a bar magnet with a nearly uniform field inside.

mcqs.q: Compared with a solenoid, a simple coil of wire produces a field that is:
mcqs.why: A simple coil has only a few turns, usually in one plane, so its field is much weaker and less uniform; a solenoid is designed to concentrate a strong, uniform field along its axis.

mcqs.q: An ordinary solenoid carries no current (I = 0). Its magnetic field is:
options: Zero, because B = mu0 n I gives B = 0 when I = 0
mcqs.why: The solenoid's field is produced only by the current in its turns: B = mu0 n I, so with I = 0 the field is zero and the wire itself has no field of its own.

mcqs.q: A field exists inside a current-free solenoid only if a permanent magnet or magnetised core is placed inside. In that case the field belongs to:
mcqs.why: Without current the solenoid produces no field; any field present comes from the permanent magnet or magnetised iron core inside, so it belongs to the magnet, not the solenoid.

mcqs.q: A toroid is often preferred over a straight solenoid mainly because:
options: Its field is confined almost entirely inside the core, with very little flux leaking out
mcqs.why: A toroid is a solenoid bent into a closed ring, so very little flux leaks into the surrounding space; it neither disturbs nor is disturbed by nearby components, suiting transformers, inductors and sensitive circuits.

mcqs.q: Applying Ampere's circuital law to a circular path of radius r inside a toroid of N turns carrying current I gives the field:
options: B = mu0 N I / (2 pi r)
B = mu0 I / (2 pi r) only, independent of N
mcqs.why: Ampere's law gives B x 2 pi r = mu0 N I, so B = mu0 N I / (2 pi r); the field falls slightly with radius r, and outside the toroid the enclosed current is zero so the field is zero.

mcqs.q: Ampere's circuital law states that the line integral of B around a closed path equals:
options: mu0 times the total current passing through the path
The magnetic flux through the path
mcqs.why: Ampere's circuital law says the line integral of B around a closed path equals mu0 times the total current passing through that path.

mcqs.q: The primary function of a galvanometer is to:
options: Detect small electric currents and indicate their direction
mcqs.why: In a galvanometer a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field is deflected by the torque on it; its deflection is proportional to the current, so it detects small currents and their direction, and with series or shunt resistances it becomes a voltmeter or ammeter.

lessons.title: Measuring Instruments: Ammeter and Voltmeter
lessons.notes_html:
Can a Galvanometer Measure AC?

A moving coil galvanometer measures direct current well, because the torque on its coil is in one direction and the deflection is proportional to the current. With alternating current the torque reverses direction many times per second, following the current. The pointer cannot follow these rapid reversals because of its inertia, so it stays near zero and only shows the average value, which is zero for a complete cycle. It therefore cannot measure ordinary AC directly. AC is measured instead with moving iron or rectifier type instruments, or the alternating current is first converted to DC.

Why an Ammeter Must Have Very Low Resistance

An ammeter is connected in series, so the full circuit current must pass through it. If its resistance were large, it would reduce the very current it is meant to measure and would also cause a large voltage drop and heating. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance, so it leaves the circuit completely unchanged. In practice a galvanometer is converted into an ammeter by connecting a very low resistance, called a shunt, in parallel with it. This keeps the total resistance very small while the deflection remains proportional to the total current.

Using a Voltmeter Correctly

Note: a voltmeter is in fact designed to have a high internal resistance, because it is connected in parallel and must draw as little current as possible; the real risk described in this question arises when its resistance is not high enough compared with the component, or when the chosen range is wrong, so that it loads the circuit and reads a voltage lower than the true value. There is also a risk of damaging the coil if the applied voltage is far above the selected range. This risk is mitigated by using a voltmeter whose resistance is much greater than that of the component being measured, by adding a suitable series multiplier resistance, and by always starting from the highest voltage range and coming down. Used in this way the voltmeter disturbs the circuit negligibly and stays safe.

Working Principle of a Voltmeter

A voltmeter is a galvanometer with a high resistance connected in series with its coil, and it is always connected in parallel with the component across which the voltage is to be measured. Because its resistance is very high, only a tiny current passes through it, and this current is proportional to the potential difference between its terminals. The current produces a torque on the coil, and the deflection of the pointer is calibrated directly in volts. The high series resistance also fixes the maximum voltage range of the instrument. In this way the voltmeter reads the voltage across a component without appreciably changing the circuit conditions.

mcqs.q: A moving coil galvanometer connected to ordinary AC shows almost no deflection because:
options: The average torque over a complete cycle is zero and the pointer cannot follow the rapid reversals
mcqs.why: With AC the torque reverses many times per second; the pointer's inertia stops it following, so it stays near zero, showing the average value, which is zero over a complete cycle.

mcqs.q: How is ordinary AC measured if a moving coil galvanometer cannot measure it directly?
options: By using the galvanometer at night
With moving iron or rectifier type instruments, or by first converting the AC to DC
mcqs.why: The notes state that AC is measured with moving iron or rectifier type instruments, or the alternating current is first converted to DC, because a moving coil galvanometer only responds correctly to DC.

mcqs.q: An ammeter must have very low resistance because it is connected:
options: In parallel, so it must draw all the current
In series, so a large resistance would reduce the very current it is meant to measure
Across the supply, so it must block current
In series, so it must produce a large voltage drop
mcqs.why: An ammeter is connected in series and the full circuit current passes through it; a large resistance would reduce that current and cause a large voltage drop and heating, so an ideal ammeter has zero resistance.

mcqs.q: A galvanometer is converted into an ammeter by connecting:
options: A high resistance in series with it
A capacitor in series with it
A very low resistance, called a shunt, in parallel with it
mcqs.why: A very low resistance shunt connected in parallel with the galvanometer keeps the total resistance very small while the deflection stays proportional to the total current, making it an ammeter.

mcqs.q: An ideal ammeter has a resistance of:
mcqs.why: An ideal ammeter has zero resistance so that, connected in series, it leaves the circuit completely unchanged and measures the true current.

mcqs.q: A voltmeter is always connected:
options: In parallel with the component across which the voltage is to be measured
mcqs.why: A voltmeter is a galvanometer with a high resistance in series with its coil, and it is always connected in parallel with the component whose potential difference is to be measured.

mcqs.q: A voltmeter draws only a tiny current because:
options: It is switched off while reading
A high resistance is connected in series with its coil, and this current is proportional to the potential difference at its terminals
mcqs.why: The high series resistance makes the voltmeter's total resistance very high, so only a tiny current passes, proportional to the potential difference; the torque from this current deflects the pointer, calibrated directly in volts.

mcqs.q: If a voltmeter's resistance is not high enough compared with the component, or the wrong range is chosen, the reading will be:
options: Lower than the true value, because the meter loads the circuit
Unchanged but the meter heats up only
mcqs.why: A voltmeter whose resistance is not much greater than the component's loads the circuit and reads a voltage lower than the true value; there is also a risk of damaging the coil if the applied voltage is far above the selected range.

mcqs.q: To use a voltmeter safely and accurately, you should:
options: Start from the highest voltage range and come down, using a meter resistance much greater than the component's
Always start from the lowest voltage range
mcqs.why: The risk is mitigated by using a voltmeter of resistance much greater than the component, adding a suitable series multiplier resistance, and always starting from the highest voltage range and coming down.

mcqs.q: In a voltmeter, the high series resistance also determines:
options: The maximum voltage range of the instrument
mcqs.why: The high series resistance fixes the maximum voltage range of the voltmeter: most of an applied voltage drops across it and only a safe fraction reaches the coil, whose deflection is calibrated in volts.

lessons.title: Worked Examples
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example 1

An aluminum window has a width of 60 cm and length of 85 cm as shown in the figure. a. When the window is closed the magnetic flux density is 1.8 x 10^-4 T is normal to window. b. Calculate the magnetic flux through the window.

Step 1: Given: width = 60 cm = 0.60 m, length = 85 cm = 0.85 m, flux density B = 1.8 x10^-4 T normal to the window, so theta = 0 degrees

Step 2: Formula: area A = length x width, and magnetic flux Phi = B A cos theta

Step 3: Substitution: A = 0.85 x 0.60 = 0.51 m^2, and Phi = 1.8 x10^-4 x 0.51 x 1

Step 4: Calculation: Phi = 0.918 x10^-4 = 9.18 x10^-5

Magnetic flux through the window = 9.18 x10^-5 Wb.

Worked Example 2

The poles of a horse shoe magnet measures 8Cm x 3.2cm. the magnetic flux density between the magnet poles is 80mT. Outside of the magnet the magnetic flux density is zero. Calculate the magnetic flux between the poles of a magnet.

Step 1: Given: pole face = 8 cm x 3.2 cm, B = 80 mT = 80 x10^-3 T = 0.080 T

Step 2: Formula: area A = 0.08 m x 0.032 m, and flux Phi = B A

Step 3: Substitution: A = 0.00256 m^2, and Phi = 0.080 x 0.00256

Step 4: Calculation: Phi = 2.048 x10^-4

Magnetic flux between the poles = 2.048 x10^-4 Wb.

Worked Example 3

A wire 1.80 m long carries a current of 13.0 A and makes an angle of 35.0 degrees with a uniform magnetic field of magnitude B = 1.50T. Calculate the magnetic force on the wire.

Step 1: Given: L = 1.80 m, I = 13.0 A, B = 1.50 T, theta = 35.0 degrees

Step 2: Formula: F = B I L sin theta

Step 3: Substitution: F = 1.50 x 13.0 x 1.80 x sin 35 degrees, with sin 35 degrees = 0.574

Step 4: Calculation: 1.50 x 13.0 x 1.80 = 35.1, and F = 35.1 x 0.574 = 20.1

Magnetic force on the wire = about 20.1 N. Note: the answer 19.46 N printed in the book does not follow exactly from the data given in this question.

Worked Example 4

A solenoid has length L = 1.23 m and inner diameter d = 3.55 cm, and it carries a current I= 5.57 A. It consists of five close-packed layers, each with 850 turns along length L. What is B at its center?

Step 1: Given: L = 1.23 m, I = 5.57 A, total turns N = 5 x 850 = 4250, mu0 = 4 pi x10^-7

Step 2: Formula: turns per unit length n = N / L, and field at the centre B = mu0 n I

Step 3: Substitution: n = 4250 / 1.23 = 3455 turns per m, and B = 4 pi x10^-7 x 3455 x 5.57

Step 4: Calculation: B = 4 pi x10^-7 x 19244 = 0.0242 T

Magnetic field at the centre = 0.0242 T, that is 24.2 mT.

Worked Example 5

A moving coil galvanometer has resistance of 50 ohm and it gives full scale deflection at 4mA current. A voltmeter is made using this galvanometer and a 5K ohm resistance. Calculate the maximum voltage that can be measured using this voltmeter.

Step 1: Given: galvanometer resistance G = 50 ohm, full scale current Ig = 4 mA = 0.004 A, series resistance R = 5k ohm = 5000 ohm

Step 2: Formula: total resistance = G + R, and maximum voltage V = Ig x (G + R)

Step 3: Substitution: V = 0.004 x (50 + 5000) = 0.004 x 5050

Step 4: Calculation: V = 20.2

Maximum voltage that can be measured = 20.2 V.

Worked Example 6

Compute the magnitude of the magnetic field of a long, straight wire carrying a current of 1A at distance of 1m from it. Compare it with Earth magnetic field.

Step 1: Given: I = 1 A, distance r = 1 m, mu0 = 4 pi x10^-7, Earth magnetic field = about 5.0 x10^-5 T

Step 2: Formula: field of a long straight wire, B = mu0 I / (2 pi r) = (2 x10^-7 x I) / r

Step 3: Substitution: B = 2 x10^-7 x 1 / 1

Step 4: Calculation: B = 2 x10^-7 T, and ratio = 5.0 x10^-5 / 2 x10^-7 = 250

Field of the wire = 2 x10^-7 T, which is very much weaker than the Earth magnetic field; the Earth field is roughly one hundred to two hundred and fifty times stronger, depending on the value taken for it.

Worked Example 7

Find the current in a long straight wire that would produce a magnetic field twice the strength of the Earth at a distance of 5.0cm from the wire. (Magnetic field of Earth =5.0 x 10^-5 T).

Step 1: Given: required field B = 2 x 5.0 x10^-5 = 1.0 x10^-4 T, distance r = 5.0 cm = 0.05 m

Step 2: Formula: B = (2 x10^-7 x I) / r, so I = B r / (2 x10^-7)

Step 3: Substitution: I = 1.0 x10^-4 x 0.05 / (2 x10^-7)

Step 4: Calculation: numerator = 5.0 x10^-6, and I = 5.0 x10^-6 / 2 x10^-7 = 25

Current required = 25 A.

Worked Example 8

What is flux density at a distance of 0.1m in air from a long straight conductor carrying a current of 6.5 A. calculate the force per on a similar parallel conductor at a distance of 0.1m from the first and carrying a current of 3A.

Step 1: Given: I1 = 6.5 A, I2 = 3 A, distance r = 0.1 m

Step 2: Formula: flux density B = (2 x10^-7 x I1) / r, and force per unit length on the second conductor F/L = B I2

Step 3: Substitution: B = 2 x10^-7 x 6.5 / 0.1, and F/L = B x 3

Step 4: Calculation: B = 1.3 x10^-5 T = 13 x10^-6 Wb/m^2, and F/L = 1.3 x10^-5 x 3 = 3.9 x10^-5 N per m

Flux density = 13 x10^-6 Wb/m^2, and force per unit length = 39 x10^-6 N/m, attractive if the currents are in the same direction.

mcqs.q: An aluminium window 0.60 m wide and 0.85 m long has a flux density of 1.8 x 10^-4 T normal to it. The magnetic flux through the window is:
mcqs.why: Area A = 0.85 x 0.60 = 0.51 m^2 and theta = 0, so Phi = B A cos theta = 1.8 x 10^-4 x 0.51 x 1 = 9.18 x 10^-5 Wb.

mcqs.q: The poles of a horseshoe magnet measure 8 cm x 3.2 cm with flux density 80 mT between them. The flux between the poles is:
A wire 1.80 m long carrying 13.0 A makes an angle of 35 degrees with a uniform field of 1.50 T (sin 35 degrees = 0.574). The magnetic force on the wire is about:

mcqs.q: For the same wire (L = 1.80 m, I = 13.0 A, B = 1.50 T) placed at right angles to the field, the force would be:
mcqs.why: At right angles sin theta = 1, so F = B I L = 1.50 x 13.0 x 1.80 = 35.1 N, the maximum force for this wire.

mcqs.q: A solenoid consists of five close-packed layers, each with 850 turns. The total number of turns N is:
mcqs.why: Total turns N = 5 layers x 850 turns per layer = 4250 turns, the value used in the worked example for this solenoid.

mcqs.q: That solenoid has length L = 1.23 m and N = 4250 turns. The number of turns per unit length n is about:
mcqs.why: n = N / L = 4250 / 1.23 = 3455 turns per metre, which is then used in B = mu0 n I for the field at the centre.

mcqs.q: For that solenoid carrying I = 5.57 A, the field at its centre is:
A galvanometer of resistance 50 ohm gives full scale deflection at 4 mA. With a 5000 ohm series resistance it becomes a voltmeter whose maximum measurable voltage is:
mcqs.why: V = Ig (G + R) = 0.004 x (50 + 5000) = 0.004 x 5050 = 20.2 V, the maximum voltage this voltmeter can measure.

mcqs.q: In that voltmeter conversion, the total resistance in the meter branch at full scale deflection is:
mcqs.why: The galvanometer resistance and series resistance add: G + R = 50 + 5000 = 5050 ohm, and multiplying by Ig = 0.004 A gives the 20.2 V range.

mcqs.q: The magnetic field of a long straight wire carrying 1 A, at a distance of 1 m from it, is:
mcqs.why: B = mu0 I / (2 pi r) = (2 x 10^-7 x I) / r = 2 x 10^-7 x 1 / 1 = 2 x 10^-7 T, far weaker than the Earth's field.

mcqs.q: Taking the Earth's magnetic field as 5.0 x 10^-5 T, it is stronger than the field of that 1 A wire at 1 m (2 x 10^-7 T) by a factor of about:
mcqs.why: Ratio = 5.0 x 10^-5 / 2 x 10^-7 = 250, so the Earth's field is about 250 times stronger than the wire's field in this comparison.

mcqs.q: What current in a long straight wire produces a field twice the Earth's field (2 x 5.0 x 10^-5 T) at a distance of 5.0 cm?
The flux density at 0.1 m in air from a long straight conductor carrying 6.5 A is:
A similar parallel conductor 0.1 m away carries 3 A in that field of 1.3 x 10^-5 T. The force per unit length on it is:
mcqs.why: F/L = B I2 = 1.3 x 10^-5 x 3 = 3.9 x 10^-5 N per metre, that is 39 x 10^-6 N/m, attractive if the currents are in the same direction.

mcqs.q: Magnetic flux through an area A is calculated with Phi = B A cos theta. For the window example theta = 0 degrees because:
options: The field is parallel to the window surface
The window is made of aluminium
The flux density is normal (perpendicular) to the window, so cos theta = 1
mcqs.why: Theta is the angle between B and the normal to the area; the field is normal to the window, so theta = 0 degrees and cos theta = 1, giving Phi = B A.

lessons.title: Faraday's Law, Lenz's Law and Inductance
lessons.notes_html:
Inducing an EMF: The Generator and Transformer Effects

In a generator, coils of conductor are moved or rotated within magnetic fields, which changes the magnetic flux through them and induces an emf. This converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. Chemical conversion takes place in cells, static electricity is not used for bulk power, and photovoltaic cells convert light energy, not magnetism.

Faraday law covers both methods, because in each case the magnetic flux linking a coil changes with time. Relative movement changes the flux in the generator effect, while a changing current in a nearby coil changes the flux in the transformer effect. A truly static magnetic field with no movement produces no induced emf at all.

By Faraday law, emf = -N x (rate of change of flux), so the induced emf is directly proportional to the number of turns N in the coil. More turns mean each turn contributes its own emf and the total adds up. Slower motion, a weaker field or a smaller area all reduce the rate of change of flux and so reduce the emf.

Faraday law states that the magnitude of the induced emf equals the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage, emf = -N Delta Phi / Delta t. The opposition of the induced current to the change is Lenz law, which is a separate statement giving the direction. The law is the working principle of generators, transformers and induction coils.

emf = -N x (rate of change of flux)

Lenz's Law and Eddy Currents

Lenz law states that the induced current flows in such a direction that it opposes the change in flux that produced it. If the flux through a coil is increasing, the induced current makes a field opposing that increase, and if the flux is decreasing, it acts to maintain it. This opposition is required by the law of conservation of energy.

Eddy currents are loops of induced current set up in a bulk conductor when the flux through it changes. By Lenz law their magnetic field opposes the change that produced them. Because they flow through the resistance of the material, they waste energy as heat, which is why transformer cores are laminated to reduce them.

A laminated core is made of thin iron sheets insulated from each other, which breaks up the paths of eddy currents and greatly increases their resistance. This reduces eddy current losses and the heating of the core, improving efficiency. Lamination does not aim at reducing weight or changing permeability, which is fixed by the iron itself.

Self-Induction, Mutual Induction and Transformers

When the current in a coil changes, its own magnetic flux changes, and an emf is induced in the same coil, given by emf = -L dI/dt. This self induced emf opposes the change in current, so a coil resists both growth and decay of current. Induction between two different coils is mutual induction, not self-induction.

An inductor stores energy in the magnetic field built up around and within its coil when current flows through it. The stored energy is U = (1/2) L I^2. It is not stored as heat, which is an energy loss, and an inductor has no significant capacitance or electric field storage like a capacitor.

A transformer works by mutual induction: the alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing flux in the iron core, and this changing flux induces an emf in the secondary coil. The voltage ratio equals the turns ratio, Vs / Vp = Ns / Np. It works only with AC, because a steady DC produces no changing flux and no induced emf.

mcqs.q: In a generator, an emf is induced because:
options: Coils of conductor move or rotate in a magnetic field, changing the flux through them
Chemical energy is converted in a cell
Light falls on a photovoltaic cell
Static electricity is used for bulk power
mcqs.why: In the generator effect, relative movement changes the magnetic flux linking a coil and induces an emf, converting mechanical energy into electrical energy.

mcqs.q: The transformer effect induces an emf by:
options: A changing current in a nearby coil changing the flux linking the second coil
mcqs.why: In the transformer effect a changing current in one coil changes the flux linking a nearby coil and induces an emf there; a truly static field with no movement produces no induced emf at all.

mcqs.q: By Faraday's law, emf = -N x (rate of change of flux). The induced emf is therefore directly proportional to:
options: The number of turns N in the coil
The steady value of the flux
mcqs.why: Each turn contributes its own emf and the total adds up, so the induced emf is directly proportional to N; slower motion, a weaker field or a smaller area all reduce the emf.

mcqs.q: Faraday's law itself states that:
options: The induced current always opposes the change in flux
A changing electric field produces a magnetic field
Only electric currents can produce magnetic fields
The magnitude of the induced emf equals the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage, emf = -N Delta Phi / Delta t
mcqs.why: Faraday's law gives the magnitude: emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage. The opposition to the change is Lenz's law, a separate statement giving the direction.

mcqs.q: According to Lenz's law, if the flux through a coil is increasing, the induced current:
options: Flows only in one fixed direction always
Makes a field opposing that increase
mcqs.why: Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change that produced it: if flux is increasing it makes a field opposing the increase, and if flux is decreasing it acts to maintain it.

mcqs.q: The opposition required by Lenz's law is a consequence of:
options: The law of conservation of energy
The law of conservation of charge
mcqs.why: This opposition is required by conservation of energy: work must be done against it, and that work is converted into the electrical energy produced.

mcqs.q: Eddy currents in a bulk conductor waste energy as heat. Transformer cores are laminated in order to:
options: Reduce the weight of the core
Increase the permeability of the iron
Break up the eddy current paths, greatly increasing their resistance and reducing the losses
mcqs.why: A laminated core of thin insulated iron sheets breaks up the paths of eddy currents and greatly increases their resistance, reducing eddy current losses and heating and improving efficiency.

mcqs.q: Self-induction in a coil is described by emf = -L dI/dt. The self-induced emf:
options: Helps the current to grow and decay faster
Opposes the change in current, so the coil resists both growth and decay of current
Occurs only between two different coils
mcqs.why: When a coil's own current changes, its flux changes and an emf is induced in the same coil opposing the change, so the coil resists both growth and decay of current; induction between two different coils is mutual induction.

mcqs.q: The energy stored in an inductor carrying current I is:
options: U = (1/2) L I^2, stored in the magnetic field around and within the coil
Stored as heat in its resistance
Stored in an electric field like a capacitor
mcqs.why: An inductor stores energy in the magnetic field built up around and within its coil, U = (1/2) L I^2; it is not stored as heat, which would be an energy loss.

mcqs.q: A transformer, which works by mutual induction, has voltage ratio Vs / Vp = Ns / Np and works only with AC because:
options: A steady DC produces no changing flux and so no induced emf in the secondary
mcqs.why: AC in the primary produces a changing flux in the iron core which induces an emf in the secondary; a steady DC produces no changing flux, so no emf is induced.

lessons.title: Faraday's Law and Its Applications
lessons.notes_html:
Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction

Faraday law states that an emf is induced in a circuit whenever the magnetic flux through it changes, and the magnitude of the emf is proportional to the rate of change of flux. In symbols, emf = -N Delta Phi / Delta t for a coil of N turns, where Phi = B A cos theta. The change of flux may be produced by moving a magnet, moving the coil, or changing the current in a neighbouring coil. The negative sign is included from Lenz law and shows the opposition to the change.

Lenz's Law and Its Significance

Lenz law states that the direction of an induced current is such that it opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it. Its significance is that it gives the direction of the induced emf, which Faraday law alone does not give. It is also a statement of conservation of energy: work must be done against this opposition, and that work is converted into electrical energy. Without this opposition, a tiny change could produce energy from nothing.

Step-Up and Step-Down Transformers

A step-up transformer increases the voltage, so its secondary coil has more turns than its primary coil, Ns greater than Np. A step-down transformer decreases the voltage, so its secondary has fewer turns than its primary. In both, the current changes in the inverse ratio, so the power ideally stays the same. Step-up transformers are used at power stations for transmission, while step-down transformers supply homes and appliances.

Principle of Operation of an AC Generator

An AC generator works on electromagnetic induction: a coil is rotated in a magnetic field, so the flux through the coil changes continuously. The flux is Phi = B A cos(omega t), and the induced emf is emf = N B A omega sin(omega t), which alternates in direction every half turn. Slip rings and brushes take the alternating current out to the external circuit. Mechanical energy supplied to rotate the coil is thus converted into electrical energy.

Self-Induction and How It Occurs in a Coil

Self-induction is the induction of an emf in a coil by the change of its own current and flux. When the current through a coil increases, the magnetic flux through the coil also increases, and the induced emf acts to oppose the increase. When the current decreases, the induced emf acts to maintain it. The effect is measured by the self inductance L in emf = -L dI/dt, and depends on the number of turns, the area and the core of the coil.

Mutual Induction

Mutual induction is the production of an emf in one coil due to a changing current in a neighbouring coil, because part of the flux of the first coil links with the second. The induced emf is emf2 = -M dI1/dt, where M is the mutual inductance. The transformer is the standard example: a changing current in the primary coil induces an emf in the secondary coil through the common iron core. Wireless chargers and induction coils also work by mutual induction.

Arrangement of Coils and the Degree of Mutual Induction

Mutual induction is greatest when the two coils are close together, wound on the same iron core, and their axes are aligned so that maximum flux from one coil passes through the other. It decreases rapidly as the coils are separated or turned at an angle, because less flux links the second coil. A soft iron core increases mutual induction greatly by guiding the flux. More turns in both coils also increase the linkage and hence the mutual inductance.

Motional Electromotive Force

Motional emf is the emf induced in a conductor when it moves through a magnetic field and cuts the field lines. For a straight conductor of length L moving with speed v at right angles to a field B, the motional emf is emf = B L v. The magnetic force separates the free charges towards the ends of the conductor, creating a potential difference between them. It is the basic emf produced in the moving conductors of a generator.

Motional EMF and Electromagnetic Induction

Motional emf arises from the magnetic force on the free charges of a conductor that is physically moving through a magnetic field, emf = B L v. General electromagnetic induction arises whenever the magnetic flux through a circuit changes, even if the circuit is at rest, as in a transformer where the field itself changes. Motional emf is therefore a special case of flux change caused by motion. In the transformer effect there is no motion, while in the generator effect the changing area or angle causes the flux change.

AC and DC in Long-Distance Power Transmission

DC flows steadily in one direction at constant value, while AC reverses direction regularly and can easily be stepped up or down by transformers. For long-distance transmission, AC is stepped up to a very high voltage, which reduces the current and hence the I^2 R loss in the lines for the same power. DC cannot be transformed by an ordinary transformer, so changing its voltage is difficult and costly. For this reason power grids use AC for long-distance transmission and distribution.

mcqs.q: For a coil of N turns, Faraday's law is written emf = -N Delta Phi / Delta t, where the flux is:
mcqs.why: The flux through one turn is Phi = B A cos theta, and the emf is proportional to the rate of change of this flux, with the negative sign from Lenz's law showing opposition to the change.

mcqs.q: A change of magnetic flux through a circuit can be produced by:
options: Using a static field with no movement
Moving a magnet, moving the coil, or changing the current in a neighbouring coil
mcqs.why: The notes list three ways flux changes: moving a magnet, moving the coil, or changing the current in a neighbouring coil; in each case the changing flux induces an emf.

mcqs.q: The significance of Lenz's law is that it:
options: Gives the magnitude of the induced emf
Gives the direction of the induced emf, which Faraday's law alone does not give, and expresses conservation of energy
Measures the resistance of the coil
mcqs.why: Faraday's law gives the size of the emf; Lenz's law gives its direction and is a statement of conservation of energy, since work done against the opposition is converted into electrical energy.

mcqs.q: In a step-up transformer compared with a step-down transformer:
options: The turns do not affect the voltage
A step-up has Ns less than Np
A step-up has Ns greater than Np, while a step-down has Ns less than Np
mcqs.why: A step-up transformer increases voltage so its secondary has more turns than its primary (Ns > Np); a step-down decreases voltage so Ns < Np, with current changing in the inverse ratio so power ideally stays the same.

mcqs.q: Step-up transformers are used at power stations for transmission, while step-down transformers are used to:
options: Supply homes and appliances at lower voltage
mcqs.why: Step-up transformers raise voltage for transmission from power stations, and step-down transformers lower it again to supply homes and appliances, as stated in the lesson.

mcqs.q: In an AC generator the flux through the rotating coil is Phi = B A cos(omega t), and the induced emf is:
options: emf = N B A omega sin(omega t), alternating in direction every half turn
Constant, equal to N B A
mcqs.why: As the coil rotates the flux changes continuously, giving emf = N B A omega sin(omega t), which alternates every half turn; slip rings and brushes take this AC out to the external circuit.

mcqs.q: In an AC generator, the alternating current is taken out to the external circuit by:
mcqs.why: Slip rings and brushes take the alternating current out of the rotating coil to the external circuit, so the mechanical energy used to rotate the coil becomes electrical energy.

mcqs.q: Self-induction is measured by the self inductance L in emf = -L dI/dt, and L depends on:
options: Only the colour of the wire
The number of turns, the area and the core of the coil
The frequency of the mains only
mcqs.why: Self-induction is the induction of an emf in a coil by the change of its own current and flux; L depends on the number of turns, the area and the core of the coil.

mcqs.q: Mutual induction between two coils is greatest when they are:
options: Close together, wound on the same iron core, with their axes aligned so maximum flux links both
Far apart and at right angles
mcqs.why: Mutual induction, emf2 = -M dI1/dt, is greatest when the coils are close, on the same iron core and aligned, so maximum flux from one passes through the other; it falls rapidly as they are separated or turned.

mcqs.q: For long-distance transmission, AC is stepped up to a very high voltage mainly because this:
options: Increases the current in the lines
Reduces the current and hence the I^2 R loss in the lines for the same power
mcqs.why: At high voltage the same power P = V I needs a smaller current, so the I^2 R heating loss in the lines falls sharply; DC cannot be transformed by an ordinary transformer, so grids use AC.

lessons.title: What Controls the Size of the Induced EMF
lessons.notes_html:
Magnetic Field Strength and the Induced EMF

Magnetic flux is Phi = B A cos theta, so flux is directly proportional to the field strength B. Faraday law gives emf = -N Delta Phi / Delta t, so for the same rate of movement or the same area, a stronger field produces a faster rate of change of flux and a larger induced emf. Doubling B doubles the emf when all other factors stay the same. This is why generator coils are placed in the strongest possible field, close to powerful magnets or electromagnets. A weak field gives only a small emf even if the coil rotates quickly.

Area of the Coil and the Induced EMF

The flux through a coil is the product of field strength and area, Phi = B A cos theta, so a coil of larger area intercepts more field lines. When the field or the angle changes, a larger area gives a larger total change of flux in the same time. By Faraday law, emf = -N Delta Phi / Delta t, so the induced emf increases in proportion to the area. This is why practical generator and transformer coils enclose as large an area as is convenient. Doubling the area, other things equal, doubles the induced emf.

Orientation of the Coil and the Number of Turns

Flux depends on the angle theta between the field and the normal to the coil, Phi = B A cos theta. When the coil is perpendicular to the field the flux is maximum but momentarily not changing, while as it rotates the flux changes fastest when the coil is parallel to the field, and that is where the induced emf is greatest. Changing the orientation therefore changes the rate of change of flux and controls the emf throughout the cycle of an AC generator. The total emf is also proportional to the number of turns N, because the flux change takes place in every turn and the emfs of all turns add in series. Increasing the number of turns therefore increases the induced emf in the same proportion, which is why transformer and generator coils have many turns.

Rate of Change of Magnetic Flux

Faraday law states that emf equals the rate of change of flux, emf = -N Delta Phi / Delta t, so it is the speed of the change, not the size of the flux itself, that matters. A very large but steady flux induces no emf at all, because Delta Phi = 0. Moving a magnet quickly into or out of a coil changes the flux in a short time and produces a large emf, while slow movement gives a small emf. Similarly, in a transformer, a rapidly changing primary current induces more emf than a slowly changing one. Doubling the speed of change doubles the induced emf.

Resistance of the Conductor and the Induced Current

The induced emf is fixed by the rate of change of flux, but the induced current is I = emf / R, so a higher resistance gives a smaller induced current for the same emf. Resistance also converts part of the induced electrical energy into heat, reducing the useful output. It becomes significant in circuits carrying large induced currents, such as generator windings, transformer secondaries and eddy current paths in solid cores. In high frequency circuits and long coils the resistance can also limit the current and the response of the circuit. Low resistance copper windings are therefore used where large induced currents are expected.

Frequency of the Changing Field and the Induced EMF

A field that changes more frequently produces a greater rate of change of flux, so the induced emf increases with frequency. For a sinusoidal field the maximum flux change occurs more often each second when the frequency is higher, and emf(max) = N B A omega, where omega = 2 pi f. Doubling the frequency therefore doubles the maximum induced emf for the same flux amplitude. This is why transformers and generators are designed for a particular supply frequency. It is also why the output voltage of an AC generator rises as its speed of rotation increases.

Material Properties of the Coil

The induced emf itself depends on flux change, turns and area, but the current it can drive depends on the conductivity of the wire: a highly conducting material like copper has low resistance, so a larger useful current flows for a given emf. A poor conductor wastes energy as heat and reduces the output of a generator or transformer. The core material matters as well: a high permeability core such as soft iron concentrates the flux and greatly increases the induced emf. Magnetic materials with large hysteresis loss heat up under rapidly changing fields, so low loss materials are chosen for high frequency work. Material choice therefore decides both the size of the induced effect and the efficiency of the device.

The Core Material of a Transformer

The iron core guides almost all the flux produced by the primary coil through the secondary coil, so the flux linkage and the induced emf are far greater than they would be in air. A core of high permeability, such as soft iron or silicon steel, gives strong linkage and allows the turns ratio to fix the voltage ratio accurately. Cores are laminated to reduce eddy current losses, and materials with a narrow hysteresis loop are chosen to reduce hysteresis loss. A poor core material leaks flux, heats up and lowers the efficiency of the transformer. With a good core, transformer efficiency can exceed 95 percent.
