mcqs.why: Flux Phi = B A cos theta is directly proportional to B, so by emf = -N Delta Phi / Delta t a stronger field gives a faster rate of change of flux; doubling B doubles the emf.

mcqs.q: Doubling the area of a coil, other things being equal, does what to the induced emf?
options: Doubles it, because a larger area intercepts more field lines and gives a larger change of flux
mcqs.why: Phi = B A cos theta, so a larger area intercepts more field lines and produces a larger total change of flux in the same time, increasing the emf in proportion to the area.

mcqs.q: For a rotating coil, the induced emf is greatest when:
options: The coil is perpendicular to the field and flux is maximum
The coil is parallel to the field, where the flux is changing fastest
mcqs.why: Flux is maximum when the coil is perpendicular to the field but is momentarily not changing there; as the coil rotates the flux changes fastest when the coil is parallel to the field, and that is where the induced emf is greatest.

mcqs.q: The total induced emf is proportional to the number of turns N because:
options: More turns increase the resistance only
The flux change takes place in every turn and the emfs of all the turns add in series
mcqs.why: Each turn experiences the same flux change and contributes its own emf, and these emfs add in series, so increasing N increases the total induced emf in the same proportion.

mcqs.q: A very large but perfectly steady magnetic flux through a coil induces:
options: No emf at all, because Delta Phi = 0
An emf equal to the flux
mcqs.why: Faraday's law depends on the rate of change of flux, not the size of the flux itself; a steady flux has Delta Phi = 0, so no emf is induced however large the flux is.

mcqs.q: Moving a magnet quickly into a coil produces a larger emf than moving it slowly because:
options: The same change of flux takes place in a shorter time, so the rate of change of flux is greater
mcqs.why: emf = -N Delta Phi / Delta t: a quick movement changes the flux in a short time, giving a large rate of change and a large emf; doubling the speed of change doubles the emf.

mcqs.q: The induced emf is fixed by the rate of change of flux, but the induced current is I = emf / R, so a higher circuit resistance gives:
options: A smaller induced current for the same emf
mcqs.why: With I = emf / R, increasing R reduces the induced current for the same emf, and the resistance also converts part of the induced electrical energy into heat, reducing the useful output.

mcqs.q: For a sinusoidal field, emf(max) = N B A omega with omega = 2 pi f. Doubling the frequency therefore:
mcqs.why: A field that changes more frequently produces a greater rate of change of flux; since emf(max) = N B A omega and omega = 2 pi f, doubling f doubles the maximum induced emf.

mcqs.q: Copper is used for generator and transformer windings mainly because:
options: Its high conductivity gives low resistance, so a larger useful current flows for a given emf and less energy is wasted as heat
It is the cheapest metal of all
It increases the flux by itself
mcqs.why: The emf depends on flux change, turns and area, but the current it can drive depends on conductivity; copper's low resistance gives a larger useful current and less heating, while a high permeability core concentrates the flux.

mcqs.q: With a good core material, a transformer's efficiency can exceed:
mcqs.why: The core is laminated to reduce eddy current losses and made of material with a narrow hysteresis loop to reduce hysteresis loss; with a good core, transformer efficiency can exceed 95 percent.

lessons.title: Generators, Motors and Worked Examples
lessons.notes_html:
Slip Rings in AC Generators and the Commutator in DC Generators

In an AC generator the emf induced in the rotating coil naturally reverses every half turn, and slip rings simply connect the two ends of the coil continuously to the external circuit through brushes. Each slip ring stays connected to the same end of the coil, so the alternating emf appears unchanged at the output. A DC generator uses a split ring commutator instead, which reverses the connections of the coil to the brushes every half turn. This switching converts the alternating emf inside the coil into a one-way, direct output. Slip rings therefore pass AC out as AC, while a commutator rectifies it into DC.

Why a Commutator Is Necessary in a DC Motor

In a DC motor the torque on the coil reverses whenever the coil passes the vertical position, because the current direction relative to the field is then wrong for continued rotation in the same sense. The commutator reverses the current in the coil at exactly this moment, every half turn. This keeps the torque acting in the same rotational direction at all times. Without a commutator the coil would only oscillate about its equilibrium position and stop. The commutator therefore makes continuous rotation of a DC motor possible.

Applications of DC Motors in Everyday Devices

DC motors are used wherever a compact motor must run from a battery or low voltage DC supply with easy speed control. Common examples are the starter motor and windscreen wipers of cars, electric toothbrushes, hair dryers with DC motors, and cooling fans in computers. They also drive toys, model trains, electric shavers, cordless drills and the vibration motors of mobile phones. In homes they are found in mixer grinders with universal motors and in tape and disc players. Their simple speed control by changing the supply voltage makes them ideal for such devices.

Worked Example 1

Two coils are placed adjacent to each other, and a change in current in the first coil induces an emf of 0.5 V in the second coil. If the mutual inductance is 0.2 H, calculate the rate of change of current in the first coil.

Step 1: Given: induced emf in second coil = 0.5 V, mutual inductance M = 0.2 H

Step 2: Formula: emf = M x (rate of change of current), so rate of change = emf / M

Step 3: Substitution: rate of change = 0.5 / 0.2

Step 4: Calculation: rate of change = 2.5

Rate of change of current in the first coil = 2.5 A/s.

Worked Example 2

A coil with an inductance of 0.5 H experiences a rate of change of current of 2 A/s. Calculate the induced EMF in the coil.

Step 1: Given: self inductance L = 0.5 H, rate of change of current dI/dt = 2 A/s

Step 2: Formula: self induced emf = -L x dI/dt, the negative sign showing opposition by Lenz law

Step 3: Substitution: emf = -0.5 x 2

Step 4: Calculation: emf = -1

Induced emf in the coil = -1 V, the magnitude being 1 V opposing the change of current.

Worked Example 3

Two coils are placed close to each other. If a change in current of 3 A/s in the first coil induces an EMF of 4 V in the second coil, calculate the mutual inductance.

Step 1: Given: induced emf = 4 V, rate of change of current = 3 A/s

Step 2: Formula: emf = M x (rate of change of current), so M = emf / (rate of change of current)

Step 3: Substitution: M = 4 / 3

Step 4: Calculation: M = 1.33

Mutual inductance = 1.33 H.

Worked Example 4

A transformer has 200 turns in the primary coil and 400 turns in the secondary coil. If the primary voltage is 120 V, calculate the secondary voltage for a step-up transformer.

Step 1: Given: primary turns Np = 200, secondary turns Ns = 400, primary voltage Vp = 120 V

Step 2: Formula: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np, so Vs = Vp x Ns / Np

Step 3: Substitution: Vs = 120 x 400 / 200

Step 4: Calculation: Vs = 120 x 2 = 240

Secondary voltage = 240 V, confirming a step-up transformer.

Worked Example 5

An inductor with an inductance of 0.02H has a current flowing through it of 2 A. Calculate the energy stored in the inductor.

Step 1: Given: inductance L = 0.02 H, current I = 2 A

Step 2: Formula: energy stored U = (1/2) L I^2

Step 3: Substitution: U = 0.5 x 0.02 x (2)^2

Step 4: Calculation: U = 0.5 x 0.02 x 4 = 0.04

Energy stored in the inductor = 0.04 J, stored in its magnetic field.

Worked Example 6

A coil stores energy in form of electric potential energy of 0.2J when it carries a current of 2A. Calculate the inductance of coil.

Step 1: Given: stored energy U = 0.2 J, current I = 2 A

Step 2: Formula: U = (1/2) L I^2, so L = 2U / I^2

Step 3: Substitution: L = 2 x 0.2 / (2)^2 = 0.4 / 4

Step 4: Calculation: L = 0.1

Inductance of the coil = 0.1 H.

Worked Example 7

An AC generator produces an alternating current with a maximum voltage of 240 V. If the frequency of the generated AC is 50 Hz, calculate the peak value of the voltage.

Step 1: Given: the stated voltage 240 V is the rms value of the supply (as the book answer shows), frequency f = 50 Hz

Step 2: Formula: peak value V0 = Vrms x sqrt(2)

Step 3: Substitution: V0 = 240 x 1.414

Step 4: Calculation: V0 = 339.4

Peak value of the voltage = about 339 V; the frequency fixes the time period but does not change the peak value.

Worked Example 8

A transformer has 1000 turns in its primary coil and 200 turns in its secondary coil. If the primary voltage is 120 V, calculate the secondary voltage for a step-down transformer.

Step 1: Given: primary turns Np = 1000, secondary turns Ns = 200, primary voltage Vp = 120 V

Step 2: Formula: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np, so Vs = Vp x Ns / Np

Step 3: Substitution: Vs = 120 x 200 / 1000

Step 4: Calculation: Vs = 120 x 0.2 = 24

Secondary voltage = 24 V, confirming a step-down transformer.

Worked Example 9

A conductor of length 0.4 m moves at a velocity of 5 m/s perpendicular to a magnetic field of 0.3 T. Calculate the motional EMF induced in the conductor.

Step 1: Given: length L = 0.4 m, speed v = 5 m/s, field B = 0.3 T, motion perpendicular to the field

Step 2: Formula: motional emf = B L v

Step 3: Substitution: emf = 0.3 x 0.4 x 5

Step 4: Calculation: emf = 0.6

Motional emf induced in the conductor = 0.6 V.

mcqs.q: In an AC generator, slip rings are used because they:
options: Keep each end of the coil continuously connected to the same brush, so the alternating emf appears unchanged at the output
Stop the current every half turn
mcqs.why: Each slip ring stays connected to the same end of the rotating coil, so the emf that naturally reverses every half turn is passed out unchanged as AC.

mcqs.q: A DC generator uses a split ring commutator instead of slip rings in order to:
options: Reverse the connections of the coil to the brushes every half turn, converting the alternating emf inside the coil into a one-way direct output
mcqs.why: The commutator reverses the coil connections every half turn, so the alternating emf inside the coil is rectified into a direct, one-way output.

mcqs.q: A commutator is necessary in a DC motor because it:
options: Reverses the current in the coil every half turn, just as the coil passes the vertical position, keeping the torque in the same rotational direction
Increases the resistance of the coil
Turns the motor into a generator
mcqs.why: Without reversal the torque would reverse as the coil passes the vertical position; the commutator reverses the current at exactly that moment so the torque always acts in the same sense and rotation continues.

mcqs.q: Without a commutator, the coil of a DC motor would:
options: Only oscillate about its equilibrium position and stop
mcqs.why: The lesson states that without a commutator the torque reverses each half turn, so the coil would only oscillate about its equilibrium position and stop instead of rotating continuously.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an everyday application of a DC motor given in the lesson?
options: The starter motor and windscreen wipers of a car
mcqs.why: DC motors run compact devices from battery or low voltage DC with easy speed control; examples in the lesson include car starter motors and windscreen wipers, electric toothbrushes, computer cooling fans, toys and cordless drills.

mcqs.why: emf = M x (rate of change of current), so rate of change = emf / M = 0.5 / 0.2 = 2.5 A/s.

options: -1 V, with magnitude 1 V opposing the change
mcqs.why: Self-induced emf = -L dI/dt = -0.5 x 2 = -1 V; the magnitude is 1 V and the negative sign shows it opposes the change of current, by Lenz's law.

mcqs.q: A change of current of 3 A/s in a first coil induces an emf of 4 V in a second coil. The mutual inductance M is:
mcqs.why: M = emf / (rate of change of current) = 4 / 3 = 1.33 H, as calculated in the worked example.

mcqs.why: Vs = Vp x Ns / Np = 120 x 400 / 200 = 120 x 2 = 240 V, confirming a step-up transformer.

mcqs.why: U = (1/2) L I^2 = 0.5 x 0.02 x (2)^2 = 0.5 x 0.02 x 4 = 0.04 J, stored in its magnetic field.

mcqs.q: A coil stores 0.2 J of energy when it carries a current of 2 A. Its inductance is:
An AC supply has an rms voltage of 240 V. Its peak value of voltage is about:
mcqs.why: Peak value V0 = Vrms x sqrt(2) = 240 x 1.414 = 339.4 V, about 339 V; the 50 Hz frequency fixes the period but does not change the peak value.

mcqs.q: In that generator example, changing the frequency of the generated AC would change:
options: The peak value of the voltage
The time period of the wave, but not its peak value
mcqs.why: The lesson notes that the frequency fixes the time period but does not change the peak value, which is set by V0 = Vrms x sqrt(2).

mcqs.why: Vs = Vp x Ns / Np = 120 x 200 / 1000 = 120 x 0.2 = 24 V, confirming a step-down transformer.

lessons.title: Alternating Current and Its Values
lessons.notes_html:
Alternation, Frequency and Phase

Alternation is the correct term for one half cycle in which the current flows in one direction before reversing. Alternating current repeats this reversal continuously, first flowing one way and then the opposite way. One complete set of two alternations makes a full cycle. Oscillation and cycle describe the repetition in general, but the specific reversal phenomenon named in the book is alternation.

50 Hz is the standard mains frequency used in Pakistan. This means the current reverses its direction 100 times per second and completes 50 full cycles in one second. The value 60 Hz is used in countries such as the USA, but Pakistani household supply is generated and distributed at 50 Hz. All domestic AC appliances in Pakistan are designed for this frequency.

Frequency measures how rapidly the alternating current or voltage repeats its cycle with time. It is the number of complete cycles completed in one second and is measured in hertz. Amplitude and peak voltage describe the maximum size of the wave, not its rate of change. Phase angle describes the position of the wave in its cycle, so frequency is the correct parameter.

In a purely resistive circuit the voltage and the current rise, fall and reverse together, so the phase difference is 0 degrees. Both reach their peak values at the same instant and cross zero at the same instant. This is why a resistor is said to have voltage and current in phase. A 90 degrees difference occurs only in a purely inductive or purely capacitive circuit.

RMS Values and the Sine Wave

An AC voltmeter is calibrated so that its scale reads the RMS value of the alternating voltage directly. The RMS value is the value that produces the same heating effect as the equivalent DC voltage. An oscilloscope displays the waveform and shows the peak value, from which RMS must be calculated. Ordinary AC meters used in the laboratory are therefore RMS-reading instruments.

The peak-to-peak voltage is measured from the top of the positive peak to the bottom of the negative peak of the wave. Since the positive peak is +Vo and the negative peak is -Vo, the total swing is Vo - (-Vo) = 2Vo. It is therefore exactly double the peak voltage. This value is commonly read directly from an oscilloscope screen.

The power factor is cos phi, where phi is the phase angle between voltage and current. In a purely resistive circuit phi = 0 degrees, and cos 0 degrees = 1, so the power factor is 1. This is the maximum possible value and means all the supplied power is usefully dissipated in the resistor. No power is wasted in such a circuit.

Vrms = Vo / sqrt(2) = 0.707 Vo

Reactance, Resonance and Transformers

Reactance is the opposition offered to alternating current by inductance and capacitance in the circuit. Inductive reactance XL = 2 pi f L is offered by a coil, and capacitive reactance XC = 1 / (2 pi f C) is offered by a capacitor. Unlike resistance, reactance does not dissipate energy as heat; it stores and returns energy. Total opposition including resistance is called impedance, not reactance.

The book treats the balanced condition of the reactances in an RLC circuit as the resonant condition of the circuit. At resonance the inductive reactance and the capacitive reactance are equal, XL = XC, and they cancel each other. The impedance then becomes minimum and equal to the resistance alone, and the current becomes maximum and in phase with the voltage. Such a circuit is therefore called a resonant circuit.

A transformer is used to step up or step down alternating voltage in a power distribution system. It raises the voltage for long-distance transmission so that current and line losses fall, and it lowers the voltage again for safe domestic use. It works only on AC because it depends on mutual induction between its two coils. It does not convert AC to DC and does not store energy.

mcqs.q: In AC terminology, an alternation is:
options: One half cycle in which the current flows in one direction before reversing
The peak value of the wave
mcqs.why: An alternation is one half cycle in which the current flows in one direction before reversing; one complete set of two alternations makes a full cycle.

mcqs.q: The mains frequency in Pakistan is 50 Hz. This means the current:
options: Has a peak value of 50 V
Completes 50 full cycles in one second and reverses its direction 100 times per second
Is the same as the 60 Hz supply used in the USA
mcqs.why: At 50 Hz the current completes 50 full cycles each second, and since it reverses twice per cycle it reverses direction 100 times per second; all domestic appliances in Pakistan are designed for 50 Hz.

mcqs.q: The frequency of an alternating current is:
options: Its maximum value in a cycle
The number of complete cycles completed in one second, measured in hertz
mcqs.why: Frequency measures how rapidly the AC repeats its cycle: it is the number of complete cycles completed in one second, measured in hertz; amplitude and phase angle describe other properties.

mcqs.q: In a purely resistive AC circuit, the phase difference between voltage and current is:
options: 0 degrees, because they rise, fall and reverse together
mcqs.why: In a purely resistive circuit voltage and current reach their peaks and cross zero at the same instants, so the phase difference is 0 degrees; 90 degrees occurs only in purely inductive or capacitive circuits.

mcqs.q: An ordinary AC voltmeter is calibrated so that its scale reads directly:
options: The average value over a cycle
The RMS value of the alternating voltage
mcqs.why: AC voltmeters read the RMS value directly, the value producing the same heating effect as the equivalent DC; an oscilloscope shows the peak value, from which RMS must be calculated.

mcqs.q: The peak-to-peak voltage of a sine wave with peak value Vo is:
options: 2 Vo, from +Vo at the top to -Vo at the bottom
mcqs.why: Peak-to-peak voltage is measured from the top of the positive peak (+Vo) to the bottom of the negative peak (-Vo), a total swing of Vo - (-Vo) = 2 Vo.

mcqs.q: The power factor of a circuit is cos phi. In a purely resistive circuit phi = 0 degrees, so the power factor is:
mcqs.why: Power factor = cos phi = cos 0 degrees = 1 in a purely resistive circuit; this is the maximum value and means all the supplied power is usefully dissipated in the resistor.

mcqs.q: Reactance is the opposition to AC offered by inductance and capacitance. Unlike resistance, reactance:
options: Does not dissipate energy as heat; it stores and returns energy
mcqs.why: Inductive reactance XL = 2 pi f L and capacitive reactance XC = 1 / (2 pi f C) store and return energy rather than dissipating it as heat; total opposition including resistance is called impedance.

mcqs.q: At resonance in an RLC circuit, XL = XC, so the impedance is:
options: Minimum and equal to the resistance alone, with the current maximum and in phase with the voltage
Maximum and the current is minimum
mcqs.why: At resonance the two reactances cancel, impedance becomes minimum and equal to R alone, the current becomes maximum and is in phase with the voltage, so the circuit is called a resonant circuit.

mcqs.q: A transformer in a power distribution system is used to:
options: Step alternating voltage up or down, raising it for transmission and lowering it for safe domestic use
mcqs.why: A transformer steps AC voltage up for long-distance transmission, so current and line losses fall, and down again for safe domestic use; it works only on AC by mutual induction and does not convert AC to DC.

lessons.title: Reactance, Phase and Resonance
lessons.notes_html:
RMS Voltage and Its Significance

RMS voltage is the root mean square value of an alternating voltage, equal to Vo / sqrt(2) or about 0.707 times the peak voltage Vo. It is defined as that steady DC voltage which produces the same heating effect in a resistor as the AC voltage does. Its significance is that all ordinary AC voltmeters and ammeters are calibrated to read RMS values, and power calculations in AC circuits are based on RMS values. When we say the mains supply is 220 V, we are quoting its RMS value, not its peak value of about 311 V.

Peak Voltage, RMS Voltage and Average Voltage

Peak voltage Vo is the maximum value reached by the alternating voltage during a cycle. RMS voltage is the effective value, Vrms = 0.707 Vo, which gives the same heating effect as the equal DC voltage. Average voltage over a complete cycle is zero because the positive and negative halves cancel, but the average over a half cycle is 0.637 Vo. Thus the three values describe the same wave in different ways: peak for maximum stress, RMS for power and meter readings, and half-cycle average for rectifier calculations.

Alternating Current and Direct Current

Alternating current is an electric current whose magnitude changes continuously with time and whose direction reverses periodically, usually sinusoidally. Direct current flows steadily in one direction only and, ideally, has constant magnitude. AC can be stepped up or down by a transformer, which is why it is used for power transmission and distribution. DC is used in batteries, electronics and electroplating, where a fixed polarity is required.

Reactance: Capacitive and Inductive

Reactance is the opposition offered to alternating current by a capacitor or an inductor, measured in ohm. Inductive reactance XL = 2 pi f L is offered by a coil; it increases with frequency and inductance, and in it the current lags the voltage by 90 degrees. Capacitive reactance XC = 1 / (2 pi f C) is offered by a capacitor; it decreases as frequency and capacitance increase, and in it the current leads the voltage by 90 degrees. Neither type of reactance dissipates power as heat; both store energy temporarily and return it to the circuit.

Behaviour of Capacitors and Inductors in AC Circuits

A capacitor in an AC circuit continually charges and discharges as the voltage alternates, so current appears to pass although no charge crosses the dielectric. It offers capacitive reactance XC = 1 / (2 pi f C), blocks DC completely, and makes the current lead the voltage. An inductor opposes every change of current by a self-induced emf, offers inductive reactance XL = 2 pi f L, and makes the current lag behind the voltage. At high frequency the capacitor offers little opposition while the inductor offers a large opposition, and the reverse happens at low frequency.

Phase Relationship in Capacitive and Inductive Loads

In a purely capacitive load the current reaches its peak a quarter of a cycle before the voltage, so the current leads the voltage by 90 degrees. This happens because the capacitor must first be charged by the current before voltage builds up across its plates. In a purely inductive load the self-induced emf delays the rise of current, so the current lags the voltage by 90 degrees. In a practical load containing resistance as well, the phase difference lies between 0 and 90 degrees depending on which effect dominates.

Resonance in AC Circuits

Resonance in a series RLC circuit is the condition in which the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance, XL = XC, at a particular frequency fo = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C)). At this frequency the two reactances cancel, impedance is minimum and equal to R, current is maximum, and voltage and current are in phase. Resonance is used to tune radio and TV receivers to one selected station frequency. It is also used in filter circuits, induction heating and metal detectors.

The Role of Transformers in AC Circuits

A transformer transfers AC electrical energy from one circuit to another and changes the voltage level through mutual induction. It has a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on a common laminated iron core; alternating current in the primary produces a changing flux in the core, which induces an emf in the secondary. The voltage ratio equals the turns ratio, Vs / Vp = Ns / Np, so more secondary turns step the voltage up and fewer turns step it down. Transformers make long-distance AC transmission economical and provide the different voltages needed by electronic equipment.

The Series RLC Circuit: Impedance, Resonance and Phase Angle

In a series RLC circuit the same current flows through R, L and C, and the total impedance is Z = sqrt( R squared + (XL - XC) squared ). The phase angle is given by tan phi = (XL - XC) / R, so the circuit behaves inductively when XL is greater than XC and capacitively when XC is greater than XL. At resonance XL = XC, the impedance falls to its minimum value Z = R, the phase angle becomes zero, and the current reaches its maximum value. Away from resonance the impedance rises and the current decreases, which gives the circuit its frequency-selective character.

Operation and Applications of a Transformer

A transformer operates on mutual induction: AC in the primary coil sets up an alternating flux in the laminated core, and this changing flux induces an alternating emf in the secondary coil. The output voltage is fixed by the turns ratio Ns / Np, while in an ideal transformer the power out equals the power in, so stepping voltage up steps current down. It is applied in power stations and grid stations for transmission, in substations and pole transformers for distribution, and in chargers, adapters and electronic supplies for small voltages. Laminating the core and using soft iron reduce eddy-current and hysteresis losses in practical transformers.

mcqs.q: The RMS value of an alternating voltage with peak value Vo is:
mcqs.why: Vrms = Vo / sqrt(2) = 0.707 Vo; it is the steady DC voltage producing the same heating effect, and ordinary AC meters are calibrated to read RMS values.

mcqs.q: When we say the mains supply is 220 V, the peak value of that supply is about:
mcqs.why: 220 V is the RMS value; the peak value is Vo = Vrms x sqrt(2) = 220 x 1.414 = about 311 V, as stated in the lesson.

mcqs.q: For a sine wave, the average voltage over a complete cycle is zero, while the average over a half cycle is:
mcqs.why: The positive and negative halves cancel over a full cycle, giving zero average, but the average over a half cycle is 0.637 Vo, used in rectifier calculations.

mcqs.q: Inductive reactance XL = 2 pi f L increases with frequency and inductance, and in a purely inductive circuit the current:
options: Is in phase with the voltage
mcqs.why: An inductor's self-induced emf delays the rise of current, so in a purely inductive load the current lags the voltage by 90 degrees, while XL grows with both f and L.

mcqs.q: Capacitive reactance XC = 1 / (2 pi f C) decreases as frequency and capacitance increase, and in a purely capacitive circuit the current:
options: Is in phase with the voltage
mcqs.why: A capacitor must first be charged by the current before voltage builds up across its plates, so the current reaches its peak a quarter cycle earlier and leads the voltage by 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: A capacitor in an AC circuit blocks DC completely because:
options: At zero frequency XC = 1 / (2 pi f C) becomes infinite
Its reactance is zero for DC
mcqs.why: For DC, f = 0, so XC = 1 / (2 pi f C) is infinite and no current passes; in AC the capacitor continually charges and discharges so current appears to pass although no charge crosses the dielectric.

mcqs.q: At high frequency, the opposition offered by a capacitor and by an inductor are respectively:
options: Small for the capacitor and large for the inductor
mcqs.why: XC falls as frequency rises while XL = 2 pi f L rises with frequency, so at high frequency the capacitor offers little opposition and the inductor offers a large opposition, and the reverse at low frequency.

mcqs.q: The resonance frequency of a series RLC circuit is fo = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C)). Resonance is used in practice to:
options: Tune radio and TV receivers to one selected station frequency
Increase the resistance of a circuit
mcqs.why: At resonance XL = XC, impedance is minimum and equal to R, current is maximum and in phase with the voltage; this frequency selection is used in radio and TV tuning, filters, induction heating and metal detectors.

mcqs.q: For a series RLC circuit, the total impedance and phase angle are given by:
options: Z = sqrt( R^2 + (XL - XC)^2 ) and tan phi = (XL - XC) / R
Z = R + XL + XC and tan phi = R / (XL - XC)
mcqs.why: The same current flows through R, L and C in series, so Z = sqrt( R^2 + (XL - XC)^2 ) and tan phi = (XL - XC) / R; the circuit is inductive when XL > XC and capacitive when XC > XL.

mcqs.q: In an ideal transformer, stepping the voltage up by the turns ratio Ns / Np means the current is stepped down, because:
options: Energy is destroyed in the core
The power out ideally equals the power in
mcqs.why: A transformer works by mutual induction on a common laminated iron core, with Vs / Vp = Ns / Np; in an ideal transformer power out equals power in, so stepping voltage up steps current down.

lessons.title: Phasors, Impedance and Resonance in Depth
lessons.notes_html:
Phasors and AC Voltage

A phasor is a rotating vector whose length represents the peak value of a sinusoidal quantity and whose angle with a reference axis represents its phase. As the phasor rotates with angular velocity omega = 2 pi f, its projection on the vertical axis at any instant gives the instantaneous value of the voltage, V = Vo sin(omega t + phi). In a phasor diagram, voltages and currents of the same frequency are drawn as arrows with their correct phase differences, for example VR in phase with the current and VL 90 degrees ahead of it. Adding these arrows by the parallelogram or triangle rule gives the total supply voltage and the phase angle directly. Phasors thus convert difficult trigonometric additions of AC quantities into simple geometry, which is why they are used throughout AC circuit analysis.

Impedance and How It Differs from Resistance

Impedance Z is the total opposition offered to alternating current by the combined effect of resistance and reactance in a circuit. For a series RLC circuit, Z = sqrt( R squared + (XL - XC) squared ), and the current is I = V / Z, just as in Ohms law for DC. Resistance opposes both AC and DC and permanently converts electrical energy into heat, whereas impedance applies only to AC and includes reactive opposition that stores and returns energy without loss. Resistance is a scalar fixed by the material and dimensions, while impedance depends on frequency and carries an associated phase angle between voltage and current. Both impedance and resistance are measured in the same unit, the ohm.

Reactance of an Inductor and a Capacitor with Frequency

The inductive reactance is XL = 2 pi f L, so it is directly proportional to frequency and doubles whenever the frequency doubles. Physically, a faster-changing current induces a larger opposing emf in the coil, so the opposition grows with frequency and becomes infinite for very high frequency while vanishing for DC. The capacitive reactance is XC = 1 / (2 pi f C), so it is inversely proportional to frequency and falls as frequency rises. A capacitor charges and discharges more easily at high frequency, offering little opposition, but it blocks DC completely because at zero frequency XC becomes infinite. This opposite frequency behavior of L and C is the basis of filters and of the resonance condition XL = XC.

Resonance in RLC Circuits

Resonance occurs in an RLC circuit at the frequency fo = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C)) where the inductive reactance exactly equals the capacitive reactance, XL = XC. At this frequency the voltages across L and C are equal and opposite, so they cancel, and the supply voltage appears entirely across the resistor. The impedance becomes minimum, Z = R, the current becomes maximum, and the power factor becomes unity because voltage and current are in phase. The circuit then selects this one frequency strongly and rejects others, a property measured by the Q-factor and used in radio tuning. In parallel resonance the opposite behavior occurs: impedance is maximum and line current is minimum at resonance.

Series and Parallel Resonance Compared

In series resonance the R, L and C are in series, and at fo the impedance is minimum, the current is maximum, and the circuit is called an acceptor circuit. In parallel resonance the coil and capacitor are in parallel, and at resonance the total impedance is maximum, the line current is minimum, and the circuit is called a rejector circuit. In both cases resonance occurs when XL = XC and the power factor is unity at the resonant frequency. In series resonance the voltages across L and C can be many times the supply voltage (voltage magnification), while in parallel resonance the circulating branch currents can be many times the line current (current magnification). Series resonance is used for selecting a signal, and parallel resonance is used in tank circuits of oscillators and for rejecting an unwanted frequency.

Transient Response of an RLC Circuit

When an RLC circuit is first connected to an AC source, the current does not immediately settle into its steady sinusoidal value; a short-lived transient response is superimposed on the steady-state response. The inductor resists the sudden change of current and the capacitor initially behaves according to its uncharged or charged state, so currents and voltages may overshoot and oscillate at the natural frequency of the circuit. These transient oscillations decay exponentially with time because the resistance dissipates their energy as heat. After a few cycles the transient dies out and only the steady AC current at the supply frequency remains. The size and duration of the transient depend on the values of R, L, C and on the instant in the cycle at which the switch is closed.

Why AC Is Used for Long-Distance Power Transmission

AC is used for long-distance transmission because its voltage can be raised easily and cheaply by step-up transformers. Transmitting power P = V I at very high voltage means a very small current for the same power, and line loss I squared R falls sharply, so energy wastage and heating of the cables become very small. Thin, cheaper cables can then be used over hundreds of kilometers. At the receiving end, step-down transformers reduce the voltage to safe values for homes and factories. DC could not be transformed in this simple way when the power systems were developed, which is the main reason AC became the standard for transmission.

The Choke Coil

A choke coil is an inductor with a large inductance and very small resistance, used to control alternating current without wasting power. It offers a large reactance XL = 2 pi f L to AC and so limits the current, but unlike a resistor it does not dissipate energy as heat because the current and voltage are nearly 90 degrees out of phase in it. It is wound on a laminated iron core to obtain high inductance in a small size. Chokes are used in fluorescent tube circuits to limit current after starting, and in filter circuits to block AC ripple while allowing DC to pass. It cannot be used to control DC, because for DC it offers only its small ohmic resistance.

fo = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C))

mcqs.q: Impedance Z is the total opposition to AC from resistance and reactance together. For a series RLC circuit the current is:
options: I = V / Z, just as in Ohm's law for DC

options: Opposes both AC and DC and permanently converts electrical energy into heat, while impedance applies only to AC and includes reactive opposition that stores and returns energy
mcqs.why: Resistance is a scalar fixed by material and dimensions and dissipates energy as heat for both AC and DC; impedance depends on frequency, applies only to AC, and includes reactance, which stores and returns energy without loss.

mcqs.q: If the frequency supplied to an inductor is doubled, its inductive reactance XL = 2 pi f L:
options: Doubles, because XL is directly proportional to frequency
mcqs.why: XL = 2 pi f L is directly proportional to f, so doubling the frequency doubles XL; it becomes very large at high frequency and vanishes for DC, where f = 0.

mcqs.q: A capacitor blocks DC completely because at zero frequency its reactance XC = 1 / (2 pi f C) is:
mcqs.why: At f = 0, XC = 1 / (2 pi f C) becomes infinite, so a capacitor blocks DC; as frequency rises XC falls and the capacitor charges and discharges more easily.

mcqs.q: At series resonance, the voltages across L and C are equal and opposite and cancel, so the supply voltage appears entirely across:
options: The resistor, with impedance minimum at Z = R and current maximum
mcqs.why: At fo, XL = XC, the L and C voltages cancel, impedance is minimum and equal to R, current is maximum and the power factor is unity because voltage and current are in phase.

mcqs.q: Series resonance and parallel resonance differ in that at resonance:
options: Series gives maximum impedance, parallel gives minimum
Series impedance is minimum with maximum current (acceptor circuit), while parallel impedance is maximum with minimum line current (rejector circuit)
mcqs.why: In both cases resonance occurs when XL = XC with unity power factor, but a series circuit is an acceptor with minimum impedance and maximum current, while a parallel circuit is a rejector with maximum impedance and minimum line current.

mcqs.q: In series resonance the voltages across L and C can be many times the supply voltage. This effect is called:
mcqs.why: Series resonance gives voltage magnification, since VL and VC can each be many times the supply voltage although they cancel each other; parallel resonance instead gives current magnification of the branch currents.

mcqs.q: When an RLC circuit is first switched on, the transient oscillations die away because:
options: The resistance dissipates the transient energy as heat, so the oscillations decay exponentially and only the steady AC current remains
The inductor blocks all current permanently
The capacitor charges to the peak value and stays there
mcqs.why: The inductor resists sudden current change and the capacitor starts from its initial state, causing a short-lived transient; resistance dissipates its energy as heat, so it decays exponentially and after a few cycles only the steady-state current remains.

mcqs.q: A choke coil controls alternating current without wasting power because it has:
options: Large inductance and very small resistance, offering a large XL = 2 pi f L while dissipating almost no energy as heat
mcqs.why: A choke is an inductor of large inductance and very small resistance on a laminated iron core; its large reactance limits AC while, with current and voltage nearly 90 degrees out of phase, it dissipates almost no power, unlike a resistor. It cannot control DC, for which it offers only its small ohmic resistance.

lessons.title: Worked Examples
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example 1

A resistor (R) of 20 ohms is connected in series with a capacitor (C) of 10 microF in an AC circuit with a frequency of 50 Hz. Calculate the total impedance.

Step 1: Given: R = 20 ohm, C = 10 microF = 10 x10^-6 F, f = 50 Hz, impedance Z is required

Step 2: Formula: XC = 1 / (2 pi f C) and for a series RC circuit Z = sqrt( R squared + XC squared )

Step 3: Substitution: XC = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x 50 x 10 x10^-6) = 1 / (3.14 x10^-3)

Step 4: Calculation: XC = 318.3 ohm, so Z = sqrt( 20 squared + 318.3 squared ) = sqrt( 400 + 101321 ) = sqrt(101721)

Z = 318.9 ohm, approximately 319 ohm

Worked Example 2

For an inductor with an inductance (L) of 0.5 H and a frequency of 100 Hz, calculate the inductive reactance.

Step 1: Given: L = 0.5 H, f = 100 Hz, inductive reactance XL is required

Step 2: Formula: XL = 2 pi f L

Step 3: Substitution: XL = 2 x 3.1416 x 100 x 0.5

Step 4: Calculation: XL = 314.16 ohm

The inductive reactance is 314.16 ohms

Worked Example 3

In an RL circuit, the resistance (R) is 30 ohms, and the inductance (L) is 0.2 H. Calculate the total impedance at a frequency of 60 Hz.

Step 1: Given: R = 30 ohm, L = 0.2 H, f = 60 Hz, impedance Z is required

Step 2: Formula: XL = 2 pi f L and Z = sqrt( R squared + XL squared )

Step 3: Substitution: XL = 2 x 3.14 x 60 x 0.2 = 75.4 ohm, and Z = sqrt( 30 squared + 75.4 squared )

Step 4: Calculation: Z = sqrt( 900 + 5685 ) = sqrt(6585) = 81.1 ohm

The total impedance is 81.1 ohms

Worked Example 4

In an RC circuit, the resistance (R) is 50 ohms, and the capacitance (C) is 20 microF. Calculate the capacitive reactance.

Step 1: Given: R = 50 ohm, C = 20 microF = 20 x10^-6 F, and note that the frequency is not printed in the book question, while XC depends on frequency; the book answer of 31.83 ohms corresponds to f = 250 Hz, which is used here

Step 2: Formula: XC = 1 / (2 pi f C)

Step 3: Substitution: XC = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x 250 x 20 x10^-6) = 1 / (3.14 x10^-2)

Step 4: Calculation: XC = 31.83 ohm; in general XC falls as 1 / f, for example at 50 Hz the same capacitor would give XC = 159.2 ohm

The capacitive reactance is 31.83 ohms at 250 Hz

Worked Example 5

An AC circuit has a resistance of 40 ohms, an inductive reactance of 30 ohms, and a capacitive reactance of 20 ohms. Draw the impedance triangle and calculate the total impedance.

Step 1: Given: R = 40 ohm, XL = 30 ohm, XC = 20 ohm, total impedance Z is required

Step 2: Formula: Net reactance X = XL - XC, and Z = sqrt( R squared + X squared ); in the impedance triangle R is the base, X is the perpendicular and Z is the hypotenuse

Step 3: Substitution: X = 30 - 20 = 10 ohm, so Z = sqrt( 40 squared + 10 squared )

Step 4: Calculation: Z = sqrt( 1600 + 100 ) = sqrt(1700) = 41.2 ohm

The total impedance is 41.2 ohms

Worked Example 6

In a series RL circuit, the resistance (R) is 25 ohms, and the inductance (L) is 0.1 H. Calculate the phase angle and impedance at a frequency of 80 Hz.

Step 1: Given: R = 25 ohm, L = 0.1 H, f = 80 Hz, impedance Z and phase angle phi are required

Step 2: Formula: XL = 2 pi f L, Z = sqrt( R squared + XL squared ), and tan phi = XL / R

Step 3: Substitution: XL = 2 x 3.14 x 80 x 0.1 = 50.27 ohm, Z = sqrt( 25 squared + 50.27 squared ), tan phi = 50.27 / 25 = 2.01

Step 4: Calculation: Z = sqrt( 625 + 2527 ) = sqrt(3152) = 56.2 ohm, and phi = inverse tan of 2.01 = 63.6 degrees

Impedance is about 56.2 ohms and the current lags the voltage by a phase angle of about 63.6 degrees

Worked Example 7

In a parallel RC circuit, the resistance (R) is 60 ohms, and the capacitance (C) is 30 microF. Calculate the total current flowing through the circuit at a frequency of 120 Hz.

Step 1: Given: R = 60 ohm, C = 30 microF = 30 x10^-6 F, f = 120 Hz; note that the supply voltage is not printed in the book question and the book answer line prints only 60 V, so the supply is taken as V = 60 V, consistent with that value

Step 2: Formula: XC = 1 / (2 pi f C), resistor current IR = V / R, capacitor current IC = V / XC, and total current I = sqrt( IR squared + IC squared ) because the two branch currents are 90 degrees out of phase

Step 3: Substitution: XC = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x 120 x 30 x10^-6) = 44.2 ohm, IR = 60 / 60 = 1.0 A, IC = 60 / 44.2 = 1.36 A

Step 4: Calculation: I = sqrt( 1.0 squared + 1.36 squared ) = sqrt( 1 + 1.84 ) = sqrt(2.84) = 1.69 A

The total current is about 1.69 A for a 60 V supply, leading the voltage; without a stated supply voltage only XC = 44.2 ohms can be found uniquely

Worked Example 8

In an RLC circuit, the resistance (R) is 50 ohms, the inductance (L) is 0.1 H, and the capacitance (C) is 50 microF. Calculate the resonance frequency.

Step 1: Given: R = 50 ohm (not needed for fo), L = 0.1 H, C = 50 microF = 50 x10^-6 F, resonance frequency fo is required

Step 2: Formula: fo = 1 / (2 pi sqrt( L C ))

Step 3: Substitution: fo = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x sqrt( 0.1 x 50 x10^-6 )) = 1 / (6.28 x sqrt(5 x10^-6)) = 1 / (6.28 x 2.236 x10^-3)

Step 4: Calculation: fo = 1 / (1.405 x10^-2) = 71.2 Hz

The resonance frequency is about 71.2 Hz, at which the impedance is minimum and equal to 50 ohms

mcqs.q: A capacitor of 10 microF is used at a frequency of 50 Hz. Its capacitive reactance is:
That capacitor is in series with a resistor of 20 ohm at 50 Hz. The total impedance of the series RC circuit is about:
mcqs.why: Z = sqrt( R^2 + XC^2 ) = sqrt( 20^2 + 318.3^2 ) = sqrt( 400 + 101321 ) = sqrt(101721) = 318.9 ohm, approximately 319 ohm.

mcqs.q: An inductor of 0.5 H is used at a frequency of 100 Hz. Its inductive reactance is:
mcqs.why: XL = 2 pi f L = 2 x 3.1416 x 100 x 0.5 = 314.16 ohm, as calculated in the worked example.

mcqs.q: An inductor of 0.2 H is used at a frequency of 60 Hz. Its inductive reactance is:
mcqs.why: XL = 2 pi f L = 2 x 3.14 x 60 x 0.2 = 75.4 ohm, the value used in the RL worked example.

mcqs.q: That inductor is in series with a resistance of 30 ohm at 60 Hz. The total impedance is:
A capacitor of 20 microF is used at a frequency of 250 Hz. Its capacitive reactance is:
The same 20 microF capacitor used at 50 Hz instead of 250 Hz would have a capacitive reactance of:
mcqs.why: XC falls as 1 / f, so reducing the frequency from 250 Hz to 50 Hz (one fifth) multiplies XC by five: 31.83 x 5 = 159.2 ohm, the value noted in the lesson.

mcqs.q: An AC circuit has R = 40 ohm, XL = 30 ohm and XC = 20 ohm. The net reactance X = XL - XC is:
mcqs.why: In the impedance triangle the net reactance is X = XL - XC = 30 - 20 = 10 ohm, drawn as the perpendicular side with R as the base and Z as the hypotenuse.

mcqs.q: For that circuit (R = 40 ohm, net reactance 10 ohm), the total impedance is:
A series RL circuit has R = 25 ohm and L = 0.1 H at a frequency of 80 Hz. Its inductive reactance is:
mcqs.why: XL = 2 pi f L = 2 x 3.14 x 80 x 0.1 = 50.27 ohm, which is then combined with R = 25 ohm to find the impedance and phase angle.

mcqs.q: For that RL circuit, the impedance and phase angle are:
options: Z = 56.2 ohm, phi = 63.6 degrees, with the current lagging the voltage
mcqs.why: Z = sqrt( 25^2 + 50.27^2 ) = sqrt(3152) = 56.2 ohm and tan phi = XL / R = 50.27 / 25 = 2.01, so phi = 63.6 degrees and the current lags the voltage.

mcqs.q: In a parallel RC circuit, C = 30 microF at a frequency of 120 Hz. The capacitive reactance is:
mcqs.why: XC = 1 / (2 pi f C) = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x 120 x 30 x 10^-6) = 44.2 ohm, the first step of the parallel RC worked example.

mcqs.q: In that parallel RC circuit the supply is 60 V, R = 60 ohm and XC = 44.2 ohm. The branch currents are:
mcqs.why: Resistor current IR = V / R = 60 / 60 = 1.0 A and capacitor current IC = V / XC = 60 / 44.2 = 1.36 A, and the two branch currents are 90 degrees out of phase.

mcqs.q: The total current in that parallel RC circuit is:
mcqs.why: Because the branch currents are 90 degrees out of phase, I = sqrt( IR^2 + IC^2 ) = sqrt( 1.0^2 + 1.36^2 ) = sqrt(2.84) = 1.69 A, leading the voltage.

mcqs.q: An RLC circuit has L = 0.1 H and C = 50 microF (R = 50 ohm). Its resonance frequency is:
options: 71.2 Hz, at which the impedance is minimum and equal to 50 ohm
mcqs.why: fo = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C)) = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x sqrt(0.1 x 50 x 10^-6)) = 1 / (6.28 x 2.236 x 10^-3) = 71.2 Hz; R is not needed for fo, and at resonance Z is minimum and equal to R = 50 ohm.

lessons.title: Elasticity and the Classification of Solids
lessons.notes_html:
Elasticity, Ductility and the Yield Point

Elasticity is the property by which a body regains its original size and shape after the deforming force is removed. It is shown by materials such as steel and rubber within their elastic limit. Plasticity is the opposite behavior, in which the body keeps its new shape permanently. Rigidity and compressibility describe resistance to shape change and volume change, not recovery of shape.

Ductile substances can be stretched into wires and undergo large strains before they break, for example copper, gold and mild steel. Their stress-strain curve has a long plastic region in which the material keeps extending under load. Brittle substances such as glass break suddenly with almost no strain. Elastomers also stretch greatly, but the standard term in the book for substances drawn out with large strain is ductile.

The yield point is the point on the stress-strain curve beyond which strain increases rapidly even for a small increase in stress. Up to the elastic limit the material returns to its original length, but beyond the yield point it undergoes permanent plastic deformation. The fracture point comes later, where the material finally breaks. Hence the behavior described in the question identifies the yield point.

Only statement iii is wrong, because a longer rod twists more easily than a short rod for the same twisting couple; the angle of twist increases with length. Statement i is correct, since for the same mass and length a hollow shaft is stronger in torsion than a solid shaft. Statement ii is also correct by definition, as compressibility is 1 / B. Therefore the only wrong statement is III.

Moduli of Elasticity and Compressibility

Compressibility is defined as the reciprocal of the bulk modulus, compressibility = 1 / B. It measures how easily the volume of a material decreases under pressure, and its unit is per pascal (m squared per N). A material with a small bulk modulus, such as a gas, has a large compressibility. Solids have very large bulk modulus and therefore very small compressibility.

Compressibility = 1 / B

Bonding, Energy Bands and Magnetism in Solids

Metallic bonding confers good electrical and thermal conductivity on metals. In a metal the valence electrons form a free electron sea that is not attached to any one atom, and these delocalized electrons carry charge and heat through the solid. Covalent and ionic solids hold their electrons in fixed bonds or ions, so they are generally poor conductors. Hydrogen bonding occurs in materials such as water and does not give metallic conduction.

In a metallic crystal the delocalized, free electrons occupy the conduction band, which is partly filled or overlaps the valence band. Because there is no energy gap to cross, even a small applied voltage moves these electrons and produces a large current. In insulators the conduction band is empty and separated by a large forbidden gap. The presence of electrons in the conduction band at room temperature is what makes a metal a conductor.

Semiconductors have resistivity between that of conductors and insulators, roughly in the range 10^-5 to 10^2 ohm m. Their conductivity rises strongly with temperature and with doping, unlike that of metals. Examples are silicon and germanium, whose resistivity can be controlled over a wide range by adding impurities. They are therefore neither as conducting as metals nor as insulating as glass or rubber.

A ferromagnetic material contains small regions called domains, each magnetized in a different direction, so the unmagnetized material has no net magnetism. When it is placed in a strong magnetic field, the domains align in the direction of the field and the material becomes strongly magnetized. Hard ferromagnetic materials such as steel keep this alignment after the field is removed and become permanent magnets. Random orientation would give zero net magnetization, so option (a) is correct.

A ferromagnet is demagnetized by methods that throw its aligned domains back into random directions, such as heating it above the Curie point and hammering or jolting it. Passing it repeatedly through a decreasing alternating magnetic field, described in the option as spinning it in an external magnetic field, also removes the magnetization. Cooling or simply putting it in water does not destroy the domain alignment. Hence heating and hammering together with the alternating-field treatment is the correct set of methods.

mcqs.q: The property by which a body regains its original size and shape after the deforming force is removed is called:
mcqs.why: Elasticity is correct because it is defined as recovery of original size and shape once the deforming force is removed.

mcqs.q: Substances such as copper, gold and mild steel, which can be stretched into wires and undergo large strains before breaking, are called:
mcqs.why: Ductile substances is correct because they can be drawn into wires and show a long plastic region with large strain before fracture.

mcqs.q: On a stress-strain curve, the point beyond which strain increases rapidly even for a small increase in stress is the:
options: Breaking point of a brittle solid
mcqs.why: The yield point is correct because beyond it strain grows rapidly for little extra stress and permanent plastic deformation begins.

mcqs.q: The reciprocal of the bulk modulus B is called:
mcqs.why: Compressibility is correct because by definition compressibility = 1/B, with unit per pascal (m^2 per N).

mcqs.q: Which statement is WRONG? (i) A hollow shaft is stronger in torsion than a solid shaft of the same mass and length. (ii) Compressibility = 1/B. (iii) A longer rod is harder to twist than a short rod for the same couple.
mcqs.why: Statement (iii) only is wrong because the angle of twist increases with length, so a longer rod twists more easily, not harder.

mcqs.q: The good electrical and thermal conductivity of metals is conferred by:
mcqs.why: Metallic bonding is correct because the valence electrons form a free electron sea, not attached to any one atom, which carries charge and heat.

mcqs.q: In a metallic crystal, the delocalized free electrons occupy the:
mcqs.why: The conduction band is correct because in a metal it is partly filled or overlaps the valence band, so there is no gap for electrons to cross.

mcqs.q: The resistivity of semiconductors such as silicon and germanium lies roughly in the range:
mcqs.why: 10^-5 to 10^2 ohm m is correct because semiconductor resistivity lies between that of conductors and that of insulators such as glass.

mcqs.q: A ferromagnetic substance becomes strongly magnetized in a magnetic field because:
options: All its domains align in the direction of the field
All its domains align opposite to the field
Its domains are destroyed by the field
mcqs.why: Domain alignment with the field is correct because unmagnetized domains point in different directions and give no net magnetism until they align.

mcqs.q: A ferromagnet can be demagnetized by:
options: Cooling it and putting it in water
Heating it above the Curie point and hammering it
Rubbing it with a cloth only
Keeping it in a strong steady field
mcqs.why: Heating above the Curie point and hammering is correct because both throw the aligned domains back into random directions, removing the net magnetism.

lessons.title: Elastic Behaviour of Materials
lessons.notes_html:
Why Springs Are Made of Steel and Not of Copper

Springs are made of steel because steel has a much larger Youngs modulus and a higher elastic limit than copper. For the same load, a steel spring is deformed less and it returns completely to its original shape when the load is removed, even after repeated use. Copper is softer and more ductile, so a copper spring would soon take a permanent set and lose its spring action. Steel also resists fatigue better, which is essential for a spring working millions of times.

Breaking Force for Two Parallel Wires

When two identical wires are used in parallel, the load is shared between them and the total cross-sectional area becomes double. Breaking force equals breaking stress multiplied by area, and since breaking stress depends only on the material, doubling the area doubles the force needed to break the combination. Therefore the breaking force for two parallel wires of the same size is 2F. Each wire individually still breaks at force F, but together they support twice the load.

Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors

An intrinsic semiconductor is a chemically pure semiconductor, such as pure silicon or germanium, in which conduction is due only to electrons and holes produced in equal numbers by thermal energy. Its conductivity is low at room temperature and increases rapidly with temperature. An extrinsic semiconductor is one whose conductivity has been greatly increased by doping with a small amount of impurity, making it either n-type with electrons as majority carriers or p-type with holes as majority carriers. In an extrinsic semiconductor the numbers of electrons and holes are not equal, and its conductivity is controlled mainly by the amount of doping.

A Wire Replaced by One of Twice the Diameter

Doubling the diameter makes the cross-sectional area four times larger, since area is proportional to the square of diameter. (a) For a given load the extension is inversely proportional to area, from delta L = F L / (A Y), so the increase in length becomes one fourth of its previous value. (b) The maximum load a wire can bear equals breaking stress multiplied by area, so with four times the area the maximum bearable load becomes four times greater. Thus the thicker wire stretches less and is also stronger.

Sand Has No Definite Shape, Yet It Is a Solid

Each individual grain of sand is a solid crystal with its own definite shape, volume and strong intermolecular forces holding its particles in fixed positions. A heap of sand takes the shape of its container only because the heap consists of a very large number of tiny separate grains that can slide over one another. The flow is of separate solid pieces, not of the material of a single grain. Since every grain itself is rigid and keeps its volume, sand as a material is classified as a solid.

Importance of the Stress-Strain Curve

The stress-strain curve shows at a glance how a material behaves under load, from elastic stretching through yielding to fracture. From it we can read the elastic limit, yield point, ultimate tensile strength and breaking point, and the slope of its straight part gives Youngs modulus of the material. The shape of the curve tells whether the material is ductile, brittle or polymeric, so engineers can select the right material for a bridge, cable or machine part. The area under the curve also gives the energy absorbed per unit volume before fracture, which is a measure of toughness.

Why Liquids Do Not Possess Rigidity

Rigidity is the resistance to a change of shape under a shearing force, measured by the shear modulus. In a liquid the molecules are not held in fixed positions; the intermolecular forces are weak and the layers of liquid slide freely over one another when even a small shear is applied. A liquid therefore flows and takes the shape of its container instead of keeping its own shape. Since a liquid cannot maintain a shear strain, its modulus of rigidity is zero and it does not possess rigidity, although it does resist compression and has a bulk modulus.

Applications of the Curie Point

The Curie point is the temperature above which a ferromagnetic material loses its ferromagnetism and becomes paramagnetic, and it has several applications. It is used in temperature control devices and thermal switches, where a magnet releases a contact when the Curie temperature is reached, for example in electric rice cookers and fire alarms. Curie-point knowledge is essential in designing transformers, motors and magnetic recording media, which must operate well below the Curie temperature of their cores and coatings. It is also used in thermomagnetic generators and in medical hyperthermia treatment, where magnetic particles stop heating automatically at the Curie point, protecting healthy tissue.

Amorphous Materials and Their Uses

Amorphous materials are solids whose atoms have no long-range regular arrangement; they have only short-range order and no sharp melting point, softening gradually over a range of temperature. Common examples are glass, plastic, rubber and tar. Glass is used for windows, lenses, bottles and optical fibers, while plastics and rubber are used for pipes, insulation, tyres and household goods. Amorphous metallic alloys and amorphous silicon are used in transformer cores and solar cells because of their useful magnetic and electrical properties.

mcqs.q: Springs are made of steel rather than copper mainly because steel has:
options: A much larger Young's modulus and a higher elastic limit than copper
A smaller Young's modulus than copper
mcqs.why: Steel is correct because its larger Young's modulus and higher elastic limit mean less deformation and complete recovery even after repeated use.

mcqs.q: The breaking force for a single wire is F. The breaking force for two identical wires of the same size used in parallel is:
mcqs.why: 2F is correct because breaking force = breaking stress x area; the stress is unchanged but the total area doubles, so the force doubles.

mcqs.q: An intrinsic semiconductor is:
options: A chemically pure semiconductor such as pure silicon or germanium
Any semiconductor device such as a diode
mcqs.why: A chemically pure semiconductor is correct because in an intrinsic material conduction is only by electrons and holes produced in equal numbers by thermal energy.

mcqs.q: In an extrinsic semiconductor, the conductivity is controlled mainly by:
options: Thermal energy alone, with electrons and holes always equal
The size of the crystal only
The amount of doping, with electrons and holes not equal in number
mcqs.why: The amount of doping is correct because doping makes the material n-type or p-type and the numbers of electrons and holes are no longer equal.

mcqs.q: A wire is replaced by one of the same length and material but twice the diameter. Under a given load, its increase in length becomes:
options: One fourth of the previous value
mcqs.why: One fourth is correct: doubling the diameter makes the area four times larger, and extension delta L = FL/(AY) is inversely proportional to area.

mcqs.q: For the same wire of twice the diameter, the maximum load it can bear becomes:
mcqs.why: Four times greater is correct because maximum load = breaking stress x area, and doubling the diameter makes the area four times larger.

mcqs.q: Sand is classified as a solid even though a heap of sand takes the shape of its container, because:
options: Sand grains dissolve in the container
Sand has no intermolecular forces at all
A heap of sand is a single crystal
Each individual grain is a rigid solid crystal with definite shape and volume
mcqs.why: Each grain being a solid crystal is correct because the heap flows only as many tiny separate solid grains sliding over one another.

mcqs.q: On a stress-strain curve, the slope of the straight (elastic) part gives:
mcqs.why: Young's modulus is correct because the slope of the straight part is stress divided by strain, which is the definition of Young's modulus.

mcqs.q: Liquids do not possess rigidity because:
options: Their layers slide freely over one another, so their modulus of rigidity is zero
They have a very large bulk modulus
Their molecules are fixed in position
They cannot be compressed at all
mcqs.why: Zero rigidity is correct because weak intermolecular forces let liquid layers slide under even a small shear, so a liquid cannot maintain a shear strain.

mcqs.q: Amorphous materials such as glass, plastic, rubber and tar are solids which:
options: Have a perfectly regular long-range atomic arrangement
Have no long-range order and soften gradually over a temperature range instead of melting sharply
Always melt at one sharp temperature
mcqs.why: No long-range order is correct because amorphous solids have only short-range order and no sharp melting point, softening gradually on heating.

lessons.title: Elastic Moduli and the Force-Extension Graph
lessons.notes_html:
The Force-Extension Graph

A force-extension graph is plotted by loading a wire in steps, recording the extension for each load, and then unloading it to check recovery. For a ductile material the graph first rises as a straight line through the origin, where extension is proportional to force and Hooke law is obeyed; the slope of this part gives the stiffness of the wire. Next comes the elastic limit, after which the graph curves and the wire yields, extending greatly with little extra force in the plastic region. The force reaches a maximum at the ultimate tensile strength and then the wire necks and finally breaks at the fracture point. Brittle materials show only the straight part before sudden breaking, while polymeric materials show a long, curved, rubber-like extension; the area under the graph equals the work done in stretching the wire.

Relation Between Young's Modulus and Shear Modulus

Consider a cube of side L fixed at its base and sheared by a tangential force F on its top face, so the top face moves by a small distance x and the shear angle is theta = x / L. The shear stress is F / A and the shear strain is tan theta, approximately theta for small angles, so the shear modulus is G = (F / A) / theta. For an isotropic solid the three moduli are connected because a tensile stress can be resolved into shear components; the standard result is Y = 2 G (1 + sigma), where sigma is Poissons ratio. Equivalently G = Y / (2 (1 + sigma)), and combining with the bulk modulus gives Y = 3 B (1 - 2 sigma) and Y = 9 B G / (3 B + G). For most metals sigma is about 1/3, so Y is roughly 2.67 times G, showing that a material is harder to stretch than to shear. These relations allow any one modulus to be found when the other two are known.

Structure of Crystalline, Glassy, Amorphous and Polymeric Solids

Crystalline solids such as copper, quartz and common salt have atoms arranged in a perfectly regular, repeating three-dimensional pattern extending through the whole solid, so they have a sharp melting point and definite cleavage planes. Glassy and amorphous solids such as glass, tar and rubber have no long-range order; their atoms are arranged irregularly like a frozen liquid, so they soften gradually over a temperature range instead of melting sharply and are isotropic in their properties. Amorphous is the general class of non-crystalline solids, of which glass is the most familiar example. Polymeric solids such as polythene and nylon consist of very long chain molecules, often partly crystalline and partly amorphous, tangled together; they are light, flexible and can show very large elastic extensions. Thus the four types differ mainly in the degree and pattern of order in their internal structure.

mcqs.q: In the straight-line part of a force-extension graph through the origin:
options: Extension is proportional to force and Hooke's law is obeyed
The wire is necking before fracture
Extension stays constant as force increases
mcqs.why: Hooke's law is correct because in this first region extension is proportional to the applied force and the wire recovers on unloading.

mcqs.q: The slope of the straight part of a force-extension graph gives:
options: The work done in stretching the wire
mcqs.why: The stiffness of the wire is correct because stiffness is force per unit extension, which is exactly the slope of the straight part.

mcqs.q: The area under a force-extension graph equals:
options: The work done in stretching the wire
mcqs.why: The work done is correct because work is force multiplied by distance moved, which is the area enclosed under the force-extension curve.

mcqs.q: A brittle material on a force-extension graph shows:
options: A long plastic region before breaking
Only the straight part before sudden breaking
mcqs.why: Only the straight part is correct because brittle materials such as glass break suddenly with almost no strain and no plastic region.

mcqs.q: For an isotropic solid, Young's modulus Y and shear modulus G are related by (sigma = Poisson's ratio):
mcqs.why: Y = 2G(1 + sigma) is correct; equivalently G = Y/[2(1 + sigma)], which follows because a tensile stress can be resolved into shear components.

mcqs.q: The shear modulus of a cube sheared by a tangential force F on area A through a small shear angle theta is:
options: G = F x A x theta
mcqs.why: G = (F/A)/theta is correct because shear modulus is shear stress divided by shear strain, and for small angles the shear strain is approximately theta.

mcqs.q: For most metals Poisson's ratio sigma is about 1/3, so Young's modulus is approximately:
mcqs.why: 2.67 times G is correct: Y = 2G(1 + sigma) = 2G(1 + 1/3) = 2G x 4/3 = 2.67G, so a metal is harder to stretch than to shear.

mcqs.q: Crystalline solids such as copper, quartz and common salt are characterised by:
options: Softening gradually over a temperature range
A regular repeating three-dimensional pattern, a sharp melting point and definite cleavage planes
Being made only of long chain molecules
mcqs.why: A regular repeating pattern is correct because crystalline order extends through the whole solid, giving a sharp melting point and definite cleavage planes.

mcqs.q: Polymeric solids such as polythene and nylon consist of:
options: Very long chain molecules, often partly crystalline and partly amorphous, tangled together
Single atoms arranged in a perfect lattice
Free electrons in a conduction band
mcqs.why: Long chain molecules is correct because polymeric solids are built from tangled long chains, making them light, flexible and capable of very large elastic extensions.

mcqs.q: Which relation connects Young's modulus with the bulk modulus B and shear modulus G?
mcqs.why: Y = 9BG/(3B + G) is correct; together with Y = 3B(1 - 2 sigma) it lets any one modulus be found when the other two are known.

lessons.title: Energy Bands, Superconductivity and Magnetic Materials
lessons.notes_html:
Energy Bands in Solids

When a large number of atoms are brought together in a solid, their discrete energy levels split and merge into continuous ranges called energy bands, because the outer electrons are shared by neighboring atoms. The highest band completely filled at low temperature is the valence band, and the next band above it is the conduction band, in which electrons are free to move and carry current. Between them may lie a forbidden energy gap Eg, in which no electron states exist. In conductors the valence and conduction bands overlap or the conduction band is partly filled, so electrons move freely; in insulators the gap is large, about 5 eV or more; and in semiconductors the gap is small, about 1 eV. The size of this gap explains the electrical behavior of all solids.

Superconductivity and Its Applications

Superconductivity is the phenomenon in which certain materials, when cooled below a critical temperature Tc, lose all electrical resistance and also expel magnetic field from their interior (Meissner effect). Mercury becomes superconducting at 4.2 K, while some ceramic materials do so at much higher temperatures above 100 K. A current once started in a superconducting ring continues for years without any power supply, because there is no I squared R loss. Applications include very powerful electromagnets, MRI scanners in hospitals, magnetic levitation trains, highly sensitive magnetic detectors and lossless power cables. Superconducting magnets also make particle accelerators and future supercomputers with very fast, low-loss switches possible.

Superconductors for MRI, Maglevs and Supercomputers

In MRI (magnetic resonance imaging), superconducting coils cooled by liquid helium produce a strong, steady and uniform magnetic field that allows detailed images of soft tissues inside the body without harmful radiation. In Maglev trains, superconducting magnets lift the train several centimeters above the track and propel it, removing wheel friction so that speeds above 500 km per hour are reached quietly and smoothly in Japan and China. In supercomputers, superconducting Josephson junction switches change state in picoseconds and dissipate almost no heat, promising machines far faster and more energy-efficient than semiconductor computers. Superconductors are also proposed for compact powerful motors, fault-current limiters and energy storage rings. Their wider use is limited mainly by the cost and difficulty of keeping them at very low temperatures.

Hysteresis Loss

When a ferromagnetic material is taken through a complete cycle of magnetization, the graph of flux density B against magnetizing field H forms a closed loop called the hysteresis loop, and B lags behind H. The energy lost as heat in each cycle, called hysteresis loss, is proportional to the area of this loop. This loss arises because energy is spent in repeatedly turning the magnetic domains against internal friction, and it is not recovered when the field is removed. Soft magnetic materials such as soft iron have a narrow loop, small area and therefore small hysteresis loss, suiting them for transformer cores and electromagnets. Hard materials such as steel have a broad loop and large loss, but they retain strong magnetism and are used for permanent magnets.

The Hysteresis Loop: Field Strength and Magnetising Current

The magnetizing current in a coil wrapped around a ferromagnetic specimen produces the magnetic field strength H, which is proportional to that current, while the flux density B in the specimen is measured as the current is increased, decreased and reversed. Starting from an unmagnetized state, B rises steeply with H and then flattens at saturation, tracing the initial magnetization curve. When H is reduced to zero, B does not return to zero but keeps a residual value called remanence; a reversed field (coercive field) is then needed to bring B back to zero. Continuing the cycle in the opposite direction and back again completes a closed symmetric loop, the hysteresis loop. The shape of this loop thus synthesizes the whole history-dependent relationship between field strength and magnetizing current for that material.

Energy Bands and Soft and Hard Magnetic Materials

Energy bands arise when the energy levels of isolated atoms split into continuous allowed bands in a solid, separated by forbidden gaps; the valence band holds the outer bound electrons and the conduction band holds free electrons. On this basis solids are classified as conductors, with overlapping bands and no gap; insulators, with a wide forbidden gap of about 5 eV or more; and semiconductors, with a narrow gap of about 1 eV that a few electrons can cross at room temperature. Soft magnetic materials such as soft iron are easily magnetized and demagnetized, have high permeability, low coercivity and a narrow hysteresis loop with small loss, so they are used for transformer cores and electromagnets. Hard magnetic materials such as steel and alnico are difficult to magnetize but retain their magnetism strongly, with high remanence, high coercivity and a broad hysteresis loop. They are therefore used for permanent magnets in motors, meters and loudspeakers.

mcqs.q: In a solid, the valence band is:
options: The highest band completely filled at low temperature
The band in which electrons move freely and carry current
The forbidden gap between two bands
A band that contains no electrons at any temperature
mcqs.why: The highest completely filled band is correct because the valence band holds the outer bound electrons, and the conduction band lies above it.

mcqs.q: The forbidden energy gap Eg in an insulator is typically:
mcqs.why: About 5 eV or more is correct because the large gap keeps the conduction band empty, so insulators cannot conduct at room temperature.

mcqs.q: The forbidden energy gap in a semiconductor is small, about:
mcqs.why: About 1 eV is correct because this narrow gap lets a few electrons cross into the conduction band at room temperature, giving weak conduction.

mcqs.q: Superconductivity is the phenomenon in which a material cooled below its critical temperature Tc:
options: Stops conducting only at high currents
Loses all electrical resistance and expels magnetic field from its interior
mcqs.why: Zero resistance with the Meissner effect is correct because below Tc the material loses all resistance and expels magnetic field from its interior.

mcqs.q: Mercury becomes superconducting at a critical temperature of:
mcqs.why: 4.2 K is correct because mercury is the classic low-temperature superconductor, while some ceramics superconduct above 100 K.

mcqs.q: A current once started in a superconducting ring continues for years without a power supply because:
options: There is no I^2 R loss since the resistance is zero
The ring is connected to a battery
Magnetic domains keep pushing the current
mcqs.why: No I^2 R loss is correct because with zero resistance no electrical energy is converted to heat, so the current does not decay.

mcqs.q: In MRI scanners, superconducting coils are used because they produce:
options: A weak and rapidly changing magnetic field
A strong, steady and uniform magnetic field for imaging soft tissues without harmful radiation
mcqs.why: A strong steady uniform field is correct because MRI needs such a field, provided by superconducting coils cooled by liquid helium, to image soft tissues safely.

mcqs.q: Maglev trains using superconducting magnets can reach speeds of:
mcqs.why: Above 500 km per hour is correct because the magnets lift the train several centimetres above the track, removing wheel friction in Japan and China.

mcqs.q: The hysteresis loss in a ferromagnetic material taken through one magnetisation cycle is proportional to:
options: The area of the hysteresis loop
mcqs.why: The area of the loop is correct because energy is spent turning the domains against internal friction each cycle, and that lost energy equals the loop area.

mcqs.q: Soft magnetic materials such as soft iron are used for transformer cores because they have:
options: A broad hysteresis loop and large loss
A narrow hysteresis loop and therefore small hysteresis loss
mcqs.why: A narrow loop is correct because its small area means small hysteresis loss, and soft iron is easily magnetised and demagnetised, suiting transformer cores.

lessons.title: Worked Examples
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example 1

The lead in pencils is a graphite composition with a Youngs modulus of 1.0 x10^9 N/m squared. Calculate the change in length of the lead in an automatic pencil if you tap it straight into the pencil with a force of 4.0 N. The lead is 0.50 mm in diameter and 60 mm long.

Step 1: Given: Y = 1.0 x10^9 N/m squared, F = 4.0 N, diameter d = 0.50 mm so radius r = 0.25 x10^-3 m, length L = 60 mm = 0.060 m, change in length delta L is required

Step 2: Formula: Y = (F / A) / (delta L / L), so delta L = F L / (A Y), with A = pi r squared
