Step 3: Substitution: A = 3.14 x (0.25 x10^-3) squared = 1.96 x10^-7 m squared, and delta L = (4.0 x 0.060) / (1.96 x10^-7 x 1.0 x10^9)

Step 4: Calculation: delta L = 0.24 / 196 = 1.22 x10^-3 m

The lead shortens by about 1.2 mm (the book answer is given as 1.0 mm approximately)

Worked Example 2

A wire of 2.2 m long and 2.25 mm in diameter, when stretched by a weight of 8.8 kg, its length has been increased by 0.25 mm. Find the stress, strain, and Youngs modulus of the material of the wire. Given g = 9.8 m/s squared.

Step 1: Given: L = 2.2 m, d = 2.25 mm so r = 1.125 x10^-3 m, mass = 8.8 kg so F = m g = 8.8 x 9.8 = 86.24 N, delta L = 0.25 mm = 0.25 x10^-3 m

Step 2: Formula: A = pi r squared, stress = F / A, strain = delta L / L, Y = stress / strain

Step 3: Substitution: A = 3.14 x (1.125 x10^-3) squared = 3.98 x10^-6 m squared, stress = 86.24 / 3.98 x10^-6, strain = 0.25 x10^-3 / 2.2

Step 4: Calculation: stress = 2.2 x10^7 N/m squared, strain = 1.14 x10^-4, Y = 2.2 x10^7 / 1.14 x10^-4 = 1.9 x10^11 N/m squared, approximately 2 x10^11 N/m squared

Stress is 2.2 x10^7 N/m squared, strain is 1.14 x10^-4, and Youngs modulus is about 2 x10^11 N/m squared

Worked Example 3

A farmer making juice fills a glass bottle to the brim and caps it tightly. The juice expands more than the glass when it warms up, in such a way that the volume increases by 0.2 percent (i.e., delta V / V0 = 2 x10^-3) relative to the space available. Calculate the normal force exerted by the juice per square centimeter, if its bulk modulus is 1.8 x10^9 N/m squared. Assuming that the bottle does not break.

Step 1: Given: volume strain delta V / V0 = 2 x10^-3, bulk modulus B = 1.8 x10^9 N/m squared, pressure and force per cm squared are required

Step 2: Formula: B = pressure / volume strain, so pressure P = B x (delta V / V0), and force per unit area is the pressure itself

Step 3: Substitution: P = 1.8 x10^9 x 2 x10^-3

Step 4: Calculation: P = 3.6 x10^6 N/m squared; converting to one square centimeter, force = 3.6 x10^6 x 10^-4 = 360 N per cm squared

The juice exerts a normal force of 360 N on each square centimeter of the bottle

Worked Example 4

The elastic limit of copper is 1.5 x10^8 N/m squared. It is to be stretched by a load of 10 kg. Find the diameter of the wire if the elastic limit is not to be exceeded.

Step 1: Given: elastic limit (maximum stress) = 1.5 x10^8 N/m squared, mass = 10 kg so F = 10 x 9.8 = 98 N, diameter d is required

Step 2: Formula: stress = F / A, so A = F / stress, and d = sqrt( 4 A / pi )

Step 3: Substitution: A = 98 / 1.5 x10^8 = 6.53 x10^-7 m squared, d = sqrt( 4 x 6.53 x10^-7 / 3.14 )

Step 4: Calculation: d = sqrt( 8.32 x10^-7 ) = 9.12 x10^-4 m

The diameter of the wire must be at least 0.912 mm

Worked Example 5

What would be the greatest length of a steel wire which is fixed at one end, and can it be hanged freely without breaking? The breaking stress of steel is 7.8 x10^8 N/m squared, and the density of steel is 7800 kg/m cubed.

Step 1: Given: breaking stress = 7.8 x10^8 N/m squared, density rho = 7800 kg/m cubed, g = 9.8 m/s squared, greatest length L is required

Step 2: Formula: The wire breaks under its own weight when stress = weight / area = (A L rho g) / A = L rho g, so L = breaking stress / (rho g)

Step 3: Substitution: L = 7.8 x10^8 / (7800 x 9.8)

Step 4: Calculation: L = 7.8 x10^8 / 76440 = 1.02 x10^4 m

The greatest length is 1.02 x10^4 m, about 10.2 km

Worked Example 6

A mild steel wire of radius 0.55 mm and length 3.5 m is stretched by a force of 52 N. Calculate: (a) Longitudinal stress, (b) Longitudinal strain, and (c) Elongation produced in the wire if Youngs modulus is 2.1 x10^11 N/m squared.

Step 1: Given: r = 0.55 mm = 0.55 x10^-3 m, L = 3.5 m, F = 52 N, Y = 2.1 x10^11 N/m squared

Step 2: Formula: A = pi r squared, stress = F / A, strain = stress / Y, elongation delta L = strain x L

Step 3: Substitution: A = 3.14 x (0.55 x10^-3) squared = 9.50 x10^-7 m squared, stress = 52 / 9.50 x10^-7, strain = stress / 2.1 x10^11

Step 4: Calculation: (a) stress = 5.47 x10^7 N/m squared, (b) strain = 5.47 x10^7 / 2.1 x10^11 = 2.6 x10^-4, (c) delta L = 2.6 x10^-4 x 3.5 = 9.1 x10^-4 m

Longitudinal stress is 5.47 x10^7 N/m squared, longitudinal strain is 2.6 x10^-4, and elongation is 0.91 mm

Worked Example 7

Calculate the change in volume of a lead block of volume 1.3 m cubed subjected to a pressure of 12 atm. Also, calculate the compressibility of lead. Given the bulk modulus as B = 80 x10^9 N/m squared.

Step 1: Given: V = 1.3 m cubed, pressure P = 12 atm = 12 x 1.013 x10^5 = 1.216 x10^6 N/m squared, B = 80 x10^9 N/m squared

Step 2: Formula: B = P / (delta V / V), so delta V = P V / B, and compressibility = 1 / B

Step 3: Substitution: delta V = (1.216 x10^6 x 1.3) / 80 x10^9, compressibility = 1 / (80 x10^9)

Step 4: Calculation: delta V = 1.58 x10^6 / 8.0 x10^10 = 1.97 x10^-5 m cubed, compressibility = 1.25 x10^-11 per pascal

The volume decreases by 1.97 x10^-5 m cubed and the compressibility of lead is 1.25 x10^-11 m squared per N

Worked Example 8

The thickness of a metal plate is 0.35 inches. It is drilled to have a hole of radius 0.08 inches on the plate. If the shear strength is 4 x10^4 lbs/in squared, determine the force needed to make that hole.

Step 1: Given: plate thickness t = 0.35 in, hole radius r = 0.08 in, shear strength = 4 x10^4 lbs/in squared, force F is required

Step 2: Formula: The sheared area is the surface area of the cylinder cut out, A = circumference x thickness = 2 pi r t, and F = shear strength x A

Step 3: Substitution: A = 2 x 3.14 x 0.08 x 0.35 = 0.176 in squared, F = 4 x10^4 x 0.176

Step 4: Calculation: F = 7.04 x10^3 lbs

The sheared area is 0.176 in squared and the force needed is about 7 x10^3 lbs

mcqs.q: Pencil lead has Young's modulus 1.0 x 10^9 N/m^2. A force of 4.0 N acts on lead 0.50 mm in diameter and 60 mm long. The change in length is about:
A 2.2 m wire of diameter 2.25 mm is stretched by a weight of 8.8 kg (g = 9.8 m/s^2). The stress in the wire is:
For the same wire (length 2.2 m, extension 0.25 mm), the strain is:
mcqs.why: 1.14 x 10^-4 is correct: strain = delta L/L = (0.25 x 10^-3)/2.2 = 1.14 x 10^-4, a pure ratio with no unit.

mcqs.q: Using stress 2.2 x 10^7 N/m^2 and strain 1.14 x 10^-4 for that wire, Young's modulus is about:
mcqs.why: 2 x 10^11 N/m^2 is correct: Y = stress/strain = (2.2 x 10^7)/(1.14 x 10^-4) = 1.9 x 10^11 N/m^2, approximately 2 x 10^11 N/m^2.

mcqs.q: Juice in a capped bottle has volume strain delta V/V0 = 2 x 10^-3 and bulk modulus 1.8 x 10^9 N/m^2. The pressure produced is:
mcqs.why: 3.6 x 10^6 N/m^2 is correct: P = B x (delta V/V0) = 1.8 x 10^9 x 2 x 10^-3 = 3.6 x 10^6 N/m^2.

mcqs.q: The normal force exerted by that juice on each square centimetre of the bottle (pressure 3.6 x 10^6 N/m^2) is:
mcqs.why: 360 N per cm^2 is correct: force = P x A = 3.6 x 10^6 x 10^-4 (since 1 cm^2 = 10^-4 m^2) = 360 N.

mcqs.q: The elastic limit of copper is 1.5 x 10^8 N/m^2. For a load of 10 kg (98 N), the wire diameter must be at least:
The breaking stress of steel is 7.8 x 10^8 N/m^2 and its density is 7800 kg/m^3 (g = 9.8 m/s^2). The greatest length of steel wire that can hang freely without breaking under its own weight is:
mcqs.why: 1.02 x 10^4 m is correct: stress = L rho g, so L = breaking stress/(rho g) = (7.8 x 10^8)/(7800 x 9.8) = (7.8 x 10^8)/76440 = 1.02 x 10^4 m, about 10.2 km.

mcqs.q: A mild steel wire of radius 0.55 mm is stretched by a force of 52 N. Its longitudinal stress is:
For that mild steel wire (stress 5.47 x 10^7 N/m^2, Y = 2.1 x 10^11 N/m^2), the longitudinal strain is:
The elongation of that 3.5 m mild steel wire (strain 2.6 x 10^-4) is:
mcqs.why: 0.91 mm is correct: delta L = strain x L = 2.6 x 10^-4 x 3.5 = 9.1 x 10^-4 m = 0.91 mm.

mcqs.q: A lead block of volume 1.3 m^3 is subjected to a pressure of 12 atm (= 1.216 x 10^6 N/m^2), with B = 80 x 10^9 N/m^2. The change in volume is:
The compressibility of that lead (bulk modulus B = 80 x 10^9 N/m^2) is:
mcqs.why: 1.25 x 10^-11 per pascal is correct: compressibility = 1/B = 1/(80 x 10^9) = 1.25 x 10^-11 m^2 per N.

mcqs.q: A plate 0.35 in thick is drilled with a hole of radius 0.08 in. The sheared area is:
mcqs.why: 0.176 in^2 is correct: the sheared area is the cylinder surface A = 2 pi r t = 2 x 3.14 x 0.08 x 0.35 = 0.176 in^2.

mcqs.q: With shear strength 4 x 10^4 lbs/in^2 and sheared area 0.176 in^2, the force needed to make that hole is:
mcqs.why: 7.04 x 10^3 lbs is correct: F = shear strength x A = 4 x 10^4 x 0.176 = 7.04 x 10^3 lbs, about 7 x 10^3 lbs.

lessons.title: Semiconductors, Doping and Devices
lessons.notes_html:
Pure and Doped Semiconductors

A semiconductor element such as silicon or germanium has four valence electrons in its outermost shell. These four electrons form covalent bonds with four neighboring atoms in the crystal. Having exactly four valence electrons gives the element conductivity between that of a conductor and an insulator. Elements with one valence electron are typically metals, not semiconductors.

A pure semiconductor with no added impurity is called an intrinsic semiconductor. In it, the numbers of conduction electrons and holes are exactly equal, because every electron freed by thermal energy leaves one hole behind. A semiconductor deliberately doped with an impurity is called extrinsic. Transistor and diode are devices made from semiconductors, not names for the pure material itself.

An acceptor atom is a trivalent atom, such as boron, aluminium or gallium, having three valence electrons. When it replaces a silicon atom it can accept one extra electron, thereby creating a hole and producing a p-type semiconductor. A penta-valent atom such as phosphorus is a donor atom, which gives an electron instead. Minority and majority carrier describe the charge carriers, not the impurity atom.

Silicon should be doped with boron to obtain a p-type semiconductor, because boron is trivalent and creates holes by accepting electrons. The holes become the majority charge carriers in the doped material. Arsenic is penta-valent and would give an n-type semiconductor with electrons as majority carriers. Germanium is itself a tetravalent semiconductor and would not dope silicon in this way.

The voltage gain of an emitter follower (common-collector) circuit is low in the sense that it is slightly less than one, about 0.99, so the output voltage almost exactly follows the input voltage. There is no voltage amplification, but there is appreciable current and power gain. Its high input impedance and low output impedance make it useful as a buffer stage between circuits. Hence among the given choices its voltage gain is described as low.

Rectifiers, LEDs and Amplifier Circuits

In a full-wave rectifier both half cycles of the input AC are converted into output pulses in the same direction. Because two output pulses are produced for every one input cycle, the output ripple frequency is twice the input line frequency. For a 50 Hz input, the full-wave output has a ripple frequency of 100 Hz. A half-wave rectifier, by contrast, gives an output frequency equal to the input frequency.

An LED is constructed from a direct band gap semiconductor such as gallium arsenide (GaAs) or its related compounds. In these materials electrons falling from the conduction band to the valence band release their energy directly as photons of light. Ordinary silicon and germanium are indirect band gap materials and release most of the energy as heat, so they cannot make an efficient LED. Changing the compound changes the band gap and hence the color of the emitted light.

A half-wave rectifier passes only one half cycle of the input and blocks the other half, so one output pulse is produced per input cycle. The repetition rate of the output pulses is therefore equal to the line (input) frequency. For a 50 Hz supply the half-wave output pulses repeat 50 times per second. This also means its ripple is larger and harder to filter than that of a full-wave rectifier.

The common-emitter circuit is the conventional, most widely used transistor amplifier configuration. It provides both voltage gain and current gain, giving the largest power gain of the three configurations, with a phase reversal of 180 degrees between input and output. The common-collector circuit is the emitter follower, used as a buffer, and the common-base circuit is used mainly at high frequencies. For general-purpose amplification the common-emitter connection is the standard choice.

Applying negative feedback to an op-amp greatly increases its bandwidth, because the gain-bandwidth product remains constant while the closed-loop gain is reduced. Negative feedback also makes the gain stable and accurately set by the external resistors, reduces distortion and improves input and output impedances. The most direct measurable improvement listed in the options is the increased bandwidth. This trade of excess gain for wider bandwidth and stability is the main reason negative feedback is used in practical amplifiers.

mcqs.q: A semiconductor element such as silicon or germanium has how many valence electrons in its outermost shell?
mcqs.why: Four is correct because silicon and germanium have four valence electrons forming covalent bonds with four neighbouring atoms.

mcqs.q: A pure semiconductor with no added impurity is called:
mcqs.why: Intrinsic is correct because a pure semiconductor is intrinsic, with electrons and holes produced in equal numbers by thermal energy.

mcqs.q: An acceptor atom is a:
mcqs.why: Trivalent atom is correct because acceptors such as boron, aluminium and gallium have three valence electrons and create holes in a p-type material.

mcqs.q: To obtain a p-type semiconductor, silicon should be doped with:
mcqs.why: Boron is correct because it is trivalent, accepts an electron and creates holes, which become the majority carriers in p-type silicon.

mcqs.q: The voltage gain of an emitter follower (common-collector) circuit is:
options: Slightly less than one, about 0.99, so it is described as low
mcqs.why: About 0.99 is correct because the output almost exactly follows the input; there is no voltage amplification, though there is current and power gain.

mcqs.q: For a 50 Hz input, the output ripple frequency of a full-wave rectifier is:
mcqs.why: 100 Hz is correct because a full-wave rectifier gives two output pulses per input cycle, so the ripple frequency is twice the 50 Hz line frequency.

mcqs.q: An LED is constructed from a direct band gap semiconductor such as:
mcqs.why: Gallium arsenide is correct because in direct band gap materials electrons falling to the valence band release their energy directly as photons of light.

mcqs.q: A half-wave rectifier supplied at 50 Hz produces output pulses repeating at:
mcqs.why: 50 times per second is correct because a half-wave rectifier passes only one half cycle, giving one output pulse per input cycle, equal to the line frequency.

mcqs.q: The conventional, most widely used transistor amplifier configuration is the:
mcqs.why: Common-emitter is correct because it gives both voltage and current gain, the largest power gain, and a 180 degree phase reversal between input and output.

mcqs.q: Applying negative feedback to an op-amp greatly increases its:
mcqs.why: Bandwidth is correct because the gain-bandwidth product stays constant while closed-loop gain falls, and feedback also makes the gain stable and reduces distortion.

lessons.title: The P-N Junction, the Transistor and the Op-Amp
lessons.notes_html:
The P-N Junction and How Holes and Electrons Are Produced

A p-n junction is formed when a p-type and an n-type semiconductor are joined in a single crystal, and the device so formed is called a junction diode. In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor, thermal energy breaks some covalent bonds; each freed electron leaves behind a vacant position called a hole, so electrons and holes are produced in equal pairs. In n-type material, penta-valent donor atoms provide extra free electrons, while in p-type material trivalent acceptor atoms create extra holes. At the junction, electrons and holes diffuse across and recombine, forming a thin depletion region with a barrier potential of about 0.7 V for silicon.

PNP and NPN Transistors

A transistor is a three-layer semiconductor device with emitter, base and collector, used for amplification and switching. In a p-n-p transistor a thin n-type base layer is sandwiched between p-type emitter and collector, and the majority carriers through the device are holes flowing from emitter to collector. In an n-p-n transistor a thin p-type base is sandwiched between n-type emitter and collector, and the majority carriers are electrons. The two types work with opposite supply polarities and opposite directions of conventional current, and their circuit symbols differ in the direction of the arrow on the emitter.

Common-Base and Common-Collector Configurations

In the common-base configuration the base is common to the input and output circuits; the signal is applied to the emitter and taken from the collector. It gives voltage gain but a current gain slightly less than one, has low input and high output impedance, and is suited to high-frequency work. In the common-collector configuration the collector is common; the signal is applied to the base and taken from the emitter, and the circuit is called the emitter follower. It gives a current gain but a voltage gain of just under one, with high input impedance and low output impedance, so it is used as a buffer. The third configuration, common-emitter, is the one most used for general amplification.

Operation of a Transistor

A transistor operates with its emitter-base junction forward biased and its collector-base junction reverse biased, so charge carriers injected by the emitter cross the thin base to the collector. A small base current IB controls a much larger collector current IC, with IC = beta IB, and the total emitter current is IE = IB + IC. When a weak AC signal is applied to the base, it produces large variations of collector current through a load resistor, giving amplification. By driving the transistor fully on (saturation) or fully off (cut-off), the same device also operates as an electronic switch.

Transistor as a Switch and as an Amplifier

As a switch, a transistor is used in its cut-off state (no base current, transistor OFF) or its saturation state (large base current, transistor fully ON), for example to turn a relay, lamp or motor on and off from a small control signal. As a common-emitter amplifier, the transistor is biased in the active region and a small input signal at the base produces a large amplified output across the collector resistor. The output is 180 degrees out of phase with the input in this configuration. Voltage gain, current gain and power gain are all appreciable, which is why the common-emitter amplifier is the conventional amplifier circuit.

Effect of Negative Feedback on the Gain of an Operational Amplifier

Negative feedback returns a part of the output signal to the inverting input, so it opposes the input and reduces the overall gain of the amplifier. The closed-loop gain then depends almost entirely on the external feedback and input resistors, for an inverting amplifier gain = -Rf / R1, and not on the op-amps own very large but uncertain open-loop gain. In exchange for reduced gain, the amplifier gains stability, wider bandwidth, lower distortion and better control of input and output impedances. Understanding this trade-off, gain exchanged for accuracy and stability, is the key effect of negative feedback on an operational amplifier.

Inverting and Non-Inverting Amplifiers

In the inverting amplifier the input signal is applied through resistor R1 to the inverting (-) terminal of the op-amp, the non-inverting (+) terminal is grounded, and feedback resistor Rf connects the output back to the inverting input; the gain is -Rf / R1 and the output is inverted. In the non-inverting amplifier the signal is applied directly to the (+) terminal, while a voltage divider of R1 and Rf feeds part of the output back to the (-) terminal; the gain is 1 + Rf / R1 and the output is in phase with the input. Both circuits use negative feedback to set a precise, stable gain. The inverting circuit also serves as a summing amplifier when several inputs are connected to the same node.

Gain of the Inverting Amplifier: Virtual Earth Derivation

In an ideal op-amp with negative feedback, the two input terminals are at almost the same potential; since the non-inverting terminal is grounded, the inverting terminal is a virtual earth, at 0 V but drawing no current. The input current through R1 is therefore I = Vi / R1, and because the op-amp takes no input current, this same current must flow through the feedback resistor Rf. The voltage drop across Rf is I Rf, and the output end of Rf is at Vo = - I Rf, the negative sign appearing because the output must drive the current in the opposite sense. Substituting I gives Vo = - (Rf / R1) Vi, so the gain is Av = Vo / Vi = -Rf / R1. The gain is thus set only by the ratio of the two external resistors.

Properties of an Ideal Operational Amplifier

An ideal operational amplifier has infinite open-loop voltage gain, so even a microvolt of difference between its inputs would saturate a real device, and feedback is used to control it. It has infinite input impedance, drawing no input current, and zero output impedance, so it can drive any load without loss of signal. Its bandwidth is infinite, its common-mode rejection ratio is infinite, and its output responds instantly with zero noise and zero offset. Real op-amps only approach these values, but the ideal properties make circuit design simple through rules such as the virtual earth approximation.

mcqs.q: A p-n junction formed in a single crystal, used as a device, is called a:
mcqs.why: Junction diode is correct because joining p-type and n-type material in one crystal forms a p-n junction, which is the junction diode.

mcqs.q: In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor, electrons and holes are produced when:
options: Thermal energy breaks covalent bonds, each freed electron leaving one hole
The crystal is cooled to zero kelvin
mcqs.why: Thermal breaking of bonds is correct because each electron freed by thermal energy leaves a vacant position, a hole, so electrons and holes appear in equal pairs.

mcqs.q: The barrier potential formed at a silicon p-n junction is about:
mcqs.why: 0.7 V is correct because diffusion and recombination at a silicon junction create a depletion region with a barrier potential of about 0.7 V.

mcqs.q: In a p-n-p transistor, the majority carriers flowing through the device are:
options: Holes flowing from emitter to collector
mcqs.why: Holes from emitter to collector is correct because in a p-n-p device a thin n-type base lies between p-type emitter and collector, so holes are the majority carriers.

mcqs.q: In an n-p-n transistor, the base layer is:
options: A thin p-type layer sandwiched between n-type emitter and collector
A thin n-type layer between p-type regions
mcqs.why: A thin p-type base is correct because the n-p-n transistor has n-type emitter and collector with a thin p-type base between them, and electrons are the majority carriers.

mcqs.q: The common-base configuration gives:
options: Voltage gain but current gain slightly less than one, suiting high-frequency work
Current gain greater than one and no voltage gain
Voltage gain of exactly one only
mcqs.why: Current gain slightly less than one is correct because in common-base the signal enters at the emitter and leaves at the collector, with low input and high output impedance.

mcqs.q: The common-collector circuit is called the emitter follower because:
options: Its collector follows the base exactly
It amplifies voltage by a large factor
Its output at the emitter follows the input, with voltage gain just under one
mcqs.why: Emitter follower is correct because the signal is applied to the base and taken from the emitter with voltage gain just under one, high input and low output impedance, suiting it as a buffer.

mcqs.q: For normal transistor operation, the junctions must be biased so that:
options: The emitter-base junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction is reverse biased
The emitter-base junction is reverse biased and the collector-base junction is forward biased
mcqs.why: Emitter-base forward and collector-base reverse is correct because carriers injected by the emitter then cross the thin base to the collector, giving amplification.

mcqs.q: The three transistor currents are related by:
mcqs.why: IE = IB + IC is correct because the emitter current splits into the small base current and the larger collector current, with IC = beta IB.

mcqs.q: When a transistor is used as a switch, its two working states are:
options: Forward bias and reverse bias of a diode
mcqs.why: Cut-off and saturation is correct because with no base current the transistor is OFF, and with large base current it is fully ON, like an electronic switch.

mcqs.q: In a common-emitter amplifier, the output signal is:
options: 90 degrees out of phase with the input
Unrelated in phase to the input
180 degrees out of phase with the input
mcqs.why: 180 degrees out of phase is correct because the common-emitter amplifier inverts the signal while providing voltage, current and power gain.

mcqs.q: Negative feedback in an op-amp amplifier makes the closed-loop gain:
options: Depend only on the op-amp's uncertain open-loop gain
Depend almost entirely on the external feedback and input resistors
mcqs.why: Depend on the external resistors is correct because feedback reduces gain but makes it stable and accurate, set by Rf and R1, with wider bandwidth and lower distortion.

mcqs.q: An inverting op-amp amplifier has Rf = 100 kilo-ohms and R1 = 10 kilo-ohms. Its voltage gain is:
mcqs.why: -10 is correct: gain = -Rf/R1 = -(100 kilo-ohms)/(10 kilo-ohms) = -10, and the negative sign shows the output is inverted.

mcqs.q: The voltage gain of a non-inverting op-amp amplifier is:
mcqs.why: 1 + Rf/R1 is correct because the signal is applied to the (+) terminal and a divider of R1 and Rf feeds part of the output back to the (-) terminal, keeping the output in phase.

mcqs.q: An ideal operational amplifier has:
options: Finite gain, finite input impedance and large output impedance
Infinite open-loop gain, infinite input impedance and zero output impedance
Large input current drawn from the source
mcqs.why: Infinite gain, infinite input impedance and zero output impedance is correct, together with infinite bandwidth and infinite CMRR, which makes rules such as virtual earth work.

lessons.title: Diodes, Rectification and Special Devices
lessons.notes_html:
Intrinsic and Doped Semiconductors: N-Type and P-Type

An intrinsic semiconductor is a completely pure semiconductor such as silicon or germanium, in which the numbers of free electrons and holes are equal and conduction is purely due to thermally broken covalent bonds. A doped, or extrinsic, semiconductor is one to which a controlled small amount of impurity (about 1 atom in 10 million) has been added to greatly increase its conductivity. An N-type semiconductor is produced by doping with a penta-valent donor impurity such as phosphorus, arsenic or antimony; four of its valence electrons bond with silicon atoms and the fifth becomes a free electron, so electrons are the majority carriers. A P-type semiconductor is produced by doping with a trivalent acceptor impurity such as boron, aluminium or gallium; it creates a vacancy or hole for each impurity atom, so holes are the majority carriers. In both types the crystal remains electrically neutral overall, because the numbers of protons and electrons in the material are still balanced.

The P-N Junction: Forward and Reverse Biasing

A P-N junction is the boundary formed within a single crystal where p-type material meets n-type material, and it forms the junction diode. At the junction, electrons from the n-side and holes from the p-side diffuse across and recombine, leaving a depletion region containing fixed ions and a barrier potential of about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium. In forward biasing the positive terminal of the battery is connected to the p-side and the negative to the n-side; the barrier is lowered, the depletion region narrows, and a large current flows once the applied voltage exceeds the barrier potential. In reverse biasing the connections are reversed; the barrier is raised, the depletion region widens, and only a tiny leakage current of minority carriers flows. If the reverse voltage reaches the breakdown value, a large reverse current suddenly flows and may destroy an ordinary diode.

I-V Characteristic Curves of a P-N Junction

The I-V characteristic of a P-N junction is a graph of the current through the diode against the voltage applied across it. In the forward direction the current remains almost zero until the knee voltage (about 0.3 V for germanium and 0.7 V for silicon) is reached, after which the current rises very steeply for small increases of voltage. In the reverse direction only a very small, almost constant leakage current flows as the reverse voltage increases, showing the diode blocking current. At a sufficiently large reverse voltage, breakdown occurs and the reverse current increases sharply, either by the zener or the avalanche mechanism. The curve therefore shows clearly that a diode conducts in one direction only, which is the basis of rectification.

Rectification: Half-Wave and Full-Wave

Rectification is the process of converting alternating current into direct current, and a junction diode is used for it because it conducts in one direction only. In half-wave rectification a single diode passes only the half cycles of one polarity and blocks the other half, so the output is pulsating DC with gaps and a ripple frequency equal to the supply frequency. In full-wave rectification, either two diodes with a center-tapped transformer or a four-diode bridge are used, so both half cycles are passed in the same direction through the load. The full-wave output is smoother, has double the ripple frequency and is easier to filter into steady DC with a capacitor. Rectifiers form the first stage of almost every DC power supply used in electronic equipment.

LED, Photodiode and Photovoltaic Cell

An LED (light emitting diode) is a forward-biased p-n junction made of gallium arsenide type material which emits light when electrons recombine with holes, the color depending on the band gap of the material. It is used in indicator lamps, displays, remote controls (infrared), lighting and optical communication because it is small, fast and long-lasting. A photodiode is a junction diode operated in reverse bias whose reverse current increases when light falls on the junction and creates extra electron-hole pairs; it is used in light sensors, optical receivers, alarms and remote-control receivers. A photovoltaic cell (solar cell) is a large-area p-n junction that converts light energy directly into electrical energy without any external supply, generating a voltage when photons create electron-hole pairs that are separated by the junction field. Solar cells are used in calculators, satellites, street lighting and solar power plants.

Transistor as a Switch and as an Amplifier

As a switch, the transistor is operated between cut-off, where zero base current makes it behave like an open switch, and saturation, where sufficient base current makes it behave like a closed switch with a very small voltage across it. A small control signal at the base can thus switch a much larger current in the collector circuit, as in relay drivers, logic circuits and motor controls. As a common-emitter amplifier, the emitter is common to input and output, the base-emitter junction is forward biased and the collector junction reverse biased, and the transistor works in the active region. A small change of base current then produces a beta times larger change of collector current, giving voltage, current and power gain with a 180 degrees phase shift. This dual ability, switching and amplification, makes the transistor the fundamental building block of modern electronics.

Properties of an Ideal Operational Amplifier

An ideal op-amp is assumed to have infinite open-loop gain, infinite input impedance, zero output impedance and infinite bandwidth. Because of the infinite gain, in a feedback circuit the difference between its two input terminals is effectively zero, and because of the infinite input impedance it draws no current from the signal source or the feedback network. It rejects any signal common to both inputs completely (infinite CMRR), responds without delay or slew-rate limit, and has no offset voltage, drift or noise. Although no real device is ideal, practical op-amps come close enough that circuits designed with the ideal rules, such as the virtual earth method, work accurately. These properties are what make the op-amp a universal building block for amplifiers, filters, oscillators and analog computing circuits.

mcqs.q: In a doped (extrinsic) semiconductor, the amount of impurity added is about:
mcqs.why: About 1 atom in 10 million is correct because only a controlled small amount of impurity is added, yet it greatly increases the conductivity.

mcqs.q: An N-type semiconductor is produced by doping silicon with:
options: A trivalent acceptor such as boron
A penta-valent donor such as phosphorus, arsenic or antimony
mcqs.why: A penta-valent donor is correct because four of its valence electrons bond with silicon atoms and the fifth becomes a free electron, the majority carrier.

mcqs.q: In a P-type semiconductor, the majority charge carriers are:
mcqs.why: Holes is correct because each trivalent acceptor atom creates a vacancy or hole, so holes become the majority carriers in p-type material.

mcqs.q: Even after doping, the semiconductor crystal remains:
mcqs.why: Electrically neutral overall is correct because the numbers of protons and electrons in the material are still balanced in both n-type and p-type crystals.

mcqs.q: The barrier potential of a germanium p-n junction is about:
mcqs.why: 0.3 V is correct because the germanium barrier (and knee voltage) is about 0.3 V, compared with about 0.7 V for silicon.

mcqs.q: In forward biasing of a p-n junction:
options: The positive terminal goes to the p-side, the barrier is lowered and the depletion region narrows
The positive terminal goes to the n-side and the depletion region widens
The barrier is raised and only leakage current flows
mcqs.why: Barrier lowered and depletion region narrowed is correct because forward bias opposes the barrier, so a large current flows once the applied voltage exceeds the barrier potential.

mcqs.q: In reverse biasing of a p-n junction:
options: The depletion region narrows and a large current flows
The depletion region widens and only a tiny leakage current of minority carriers flows
mcqs.why: Depletion region widened with tiny leakage is correct because reverse bias raises the barrier, so only a small minority-carrier leakage current flows until breakdown.

mcqs.q: On the forward I-V characteristic of a silicon diode, the current:
options: Stays almost zero until the knee voltage of about 0.7 V, then rises very steeply
mcqs.why: Knee at about 0.7 V is correct because below the knee almost no current flows, and above it the current rises steeply for small increases of voltage.

mcqs.q: At a sufficiently large reverse voltage, a p-n junction undergoes breakdown, in which:
options: The reverse current suddenly increases sharply, by the zener or avalanche mechanism
The diode becomes an insulator forever
mcqs.why: Reverse current increasing sharply is correct because breakdown, by the zener or avalanche mechanism, lets a large reverse current flow and may destroy an ordinary diode.

mcqs.q: In half-wave rectification, the ripple frequency of the output is:
mcqs.why: Equal to the supply frequency is correct because a single diode passes only one half cycle per input cycle, so the output pulses repeat at the supply frequency.

mcqs.q: Full-wave rectification can be obtained using:
options: A single resistor and capacitor only
Two diodes with a centre-tapped transformer, or a four-diode bridge
mcqs.why: Two diodes with a centre tap or a four-diode bridge is correct because both half cycles are then passed in the same direction, giving double the ripple frequency and a smoother output.

mcqs.q: An LED emits light when it is:
options: Reverse biased and kept in darkness
Connected to no supply at all
Forward biased, with electrons recombining with holes, the colour depending on the band gap
mcqs.why: Forward biased recombination is correct because an LED is a forward-biased p-n junction of gallium arsenide type material that emits light on electron-hole recombination.

mcqs.q: A photodiode is operated in reverse bias, and its reverse current:
options: Decreases when light falls on it
Increases when light falls on the junction and creates extra electron-hole pairs
mcqs.why: Increases with light is correct because light creates extra electron-hole pairs at the junction, increasing the reverse current, which is used in light sensors and optical receivers.

mcqs.q: A photovoltaic (solar) cell converts:
options: Light energy directly into electrical energy without any external supply
Electrical energy into light without a supply
mcqs.why: Light directly into electrical energy is correct because photons create electron-hole pairs separated by the junction field, generating a voltage in calculators, satellites and solar plants.

mcqs.q: As a switch, a transistor in the cut-off state behaves like:
options: A closed switch with large current
An open switch, because zero base current means no collector current
mcqs.why: An open switch is correct because in cut-off there is no base current, while in saturation sufficient base current makes it behave like a closed switch.

lessons.title: Worked Examples
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example 1

A Ge diode has a voltage drop of 0.4 V when 12 mA flow through it. If the same 470 Ohm is used, what battery voltage is needed?

Step 1: Given: Diode voltage drop Vd = 0.4 V (book prints 04 V), current I = 12 mA = 0.012 A, series resistor R = 470 ohm, battery voltage V is required

Step 2: Formula: The battery voltage equals the diode drop plus the drop across the series resistor, V = Vd + I R

Step 3: Substitution: V = 0.4 + (0.012 x 470) = 0.4 + 5.64

Step 4: Calculation: V = 6.04 V

A battery voltage of 6.04 V is needed

Worked Example 2

A semiconductor diode laser has a peak emission wavelength of 1.55 micro m. Find its band gap in eV.

Step 1: Given: Wavelength lambda = 1.55 micro m = 1.55 x10^-6 m = 1550 nm, band gap Eg is required; use h c = 1240 eV nm

Step 2: Formula: Eg = h c / lambda

Step 3: Substitution: Eg = 1240 / 1550

Step 4: Calculation: Eg = 0.80 eV

The band gap is 0.8 eV

Worked Example 3

Calculate the current through 48 ohm resistor in the circuit shown in Fig. (i). Assume the diodes to be of silicon and forward resistance of each diode is 1 ohm.

Step 1: Given: Supply 10 V, load resistor 48 ohm, silicon diodes with barrier voltage 0.7 V each and forward resistance 1 ohm each; in Fig. (i) the conducting path contains two diodes in series with the 48 ohm resistor, as redrawn in the book Fig. (ii)

Step 2: Formula: Net voltage across the resistive path = supply voltage minus the two diode barrier drops, and current I = net voltage / total resistance

Step 3: Substitution: Net voltage = 10 - 0.7 - 0.7 = 8.6 V, total resistance = 48 + 1 + 1 = 50 ohm, I = 8.6 / 50

Step 4: Calculation: I = 0.172 A = 172 mA

The current through the 48 ohm resistor is 172 mA, with 8.6 V across the resistive combination of 50 ohms

Worked Example 4

Find the voltage VA in the circuit shown in Fig.(i). Use simplified model.

Step 1: Given: Supply 20 V, a silicon diode (barrier 0.7 V) and a germanium diode (barrier 0.3 V) connected in parallel between the supply and point A, with a 3 kilo-ohm resistor from A to ground; VA is required, using the simplified (barrier voltage) model of Fig. (ii)

Step 2: Formula: The diode with the smaller barrier voltage conducts first and clamps the node, so VA = supply voltage minus the smallest barrier drop that turns on

Step 3: Substitution: The Ge diode needs only 0.3 V, so it conducts and VA = 20 - 0.3; the Si diode then has only 0.3 V across it, less than its 0.7 V barrier, so it stays off

Step 4: Calculation: VA = 20 - 0.3 = 19.7 V

The voltage at point A is 19.7 V

Worked Example 5

In a common base connection, IE = 1 mA, IC = 0.95 mA. Calculate the value of IB.

Step 1: Given: Emitter current IE = 1 mA, collector current IC = 0.95 mA, base current IB is required

Step 2: Formula: IE = IB + IC, so IB = IE - IC

Step 3: Substitution: IB = 1 - 0.95

Step 4: Calculation: IB = 0.05 mA

The base current is 0.05 mA (50 micro A)

Worked Example 6

Find the value of beta if (i) alpha = 0.9 (ii) alpha = 0.98 (iii) alpha = 0.99.

Step 1: Given: alpha values 0.9, 0.98 and 0.99, beta is required in each case

Step 2: Formula: beta = alpha / (1 - alpha)

Step 3: Substitution: (i) beta = 0.9 / (1 - 0.9) = 0.9 / 0.1, (ii) beta = 0.98 / (1 - 0.98) = 0.98 / 0.02, (iii) beta = 0.99 / (1 - 0.99) = 0.99 / 0.01

Step 4: Calculation: (i) beta = 9, (ii) beta = 49, (iii) beta = 99

Beta is 9, 49 and 99 respectively, showing that beta rises very rapidly as alpha approaches 1

Worked Example 7

Calculate IE in a transistor for which beta = 50 and IB = 20 micro A.

Step 1: Given: beta = 50, IB = 20 micro A = 0.02 mA, emitter current IE is required

Step 2: Formula: IC = beta IB, and IE = IB + IC = (beta + 1) IB

Step 3: Substitution: IC = 50 x 20 micro A = 1000 micro A = 1.00 mA, IE = 0.02 mA + 1.00 mA

Step 4: Calculation: IE = 1.02 mA

The emitter current is 1.02 mA

Worked Example 8

Find the alpha rating of the transistor shown in Fig. Hence determine the value of IC using both alpha and beta rating of the transistor.

Step 1: Given: From the figure, IB = 240 micro A = 0.24 mA, IE = 12 mA, beta = 49, alpha and IC are required

Step 2: Formula: alpha = beta / (beta + 1), and IC = beta IB; also IC = alpha IE

Step 3: Substitution: alpha = 49 / (49 + 1) = 49 / 50, IC = 49 x 0.24 mA, check by IC = 0.98 x 12 mA

Step 4: Calculation: alpha = 0.98, IC = 11.76 mA by both methods (49 x 0.24 = 11.76 and 0.98 x 12 = 11.76)

The alpha rating is 0.98 and the collector current is 11.76 mA

mcqs.q: A Ge diode has a voltage drop of 0.4 V when 12 mA flows through it, with a series resistor of 470 ohms. The battery voltage needed is:
mcqs.why: 6.04 V is correct: V = Vd + IR = 0.4 + (0.012 x 470) = 0.4 + 5.64 = 6.04 V, the diode drop plus the resistor drop.

mcqs.q: In that Ge diode circuit, the voltage drop across the 470 ohm resistor alone is:
mcqs.why: 5.64 V is correct: the resistor drop is IR = 0.012 A x 470 ohms = 5.64 V, which added to the 0.4 V diode drop gives the 6.04 V battery voltage.

mcqs.q: A semiconductor diode laser has peak emission wavelength 1.55 micro m. Its band gap is:
mcqs.why: 0.80 eV is correct: Eg = hc/lambda = 1240 eV nm / 1550 nm = 0.80 eV, using the wavelength converted to 1550 nm.

mcqs.q: The wavelength 1.55 micro m used in that laser example is equal to:
mcqs.why: 1550 nm is correct because 1 micro m = 1000 nm, so 1.55 micro m = 1.55 x 1000 = 1550 nm, the value used in Eg = 1240/1550.

mcqs.q: A 10 V supply drives two silicon diodes (0.7 V barrier each) in series with a 48 ohm resistor. The net voltage across the resistive path is:
mcqs.why: 8.6 V is correct: net voltage = supply minus the two diode barrier drops = 10 - 0.7 - 0.7 = 8.6 V.

mcqs.q: Each of those diodes has forward resistance 1 ohm, in series with the 48 ohm resistor. The total resistance of the path is:
mcqs.why: 50 ohms is correct: total resistance = 48 + 1 + 1 = 50 ohms, the load resistor plus the forward resistance of each diode.

mcqs.q: The current through the 48 ohm resistor in that circuit (net voltage 8.6 V, total resistance 50 ohms) is:
mcqs.why: 172 mA is correct: I = net voltage / total resistance = 8.6/50 = 0.172 A = 172 mA.

mcqs.q: A silicon diode (0.7 V) and a germanium diode (0.3 V) are in parallel between a 20 V supply and point A. Using the simplified model, VA is:
mcqs.why: 19.7 V is correct: the Ge diode conducts first, so VA = 20 - 0.3 = 19.7 V, and the Si diode then has only 0.3 V across it and stays off.

mcqs.q: In that parallel-diode circuit, the silicon diode stays OFF because:
options: It has only 0.3 V across it, less than its 0.7 V barrier voltage
It is reverse biased by the battery
Its resistance is infinite at all voltages
The germanium diode blocks all current
mcqs.why: Only 0.3 V across it is correct because the conducting Ge diode clamps the node, leaving the Si diode below its 0.7 V barrier, so it cannot turn on.

mcqs.q: In a common-base connection, IE = 1 mA and IC = 0.95 mA. The base current IB is:
mcqs.why: 0.05 mA is correct: IB = IE - IC = 1 - 0.95 = 0.05 mA, which is 50 micro A.

mcqs.q: If alpha = 0.9 for a transistor, the value of beta is:
mcqs.why: 9 is correct: beta = alpha/(1 - alpha) = 0.9/(1 - 0.9) = 0.9/0.1 = 9.

mcqs.q: If alpha = 0.98 for a transistor, the value of beta is:
mcqs.why: 49 is correct: beta = alpha/(1 - alpha) = 0.98/(1 - 0.98) = 0.98/0.02 = 49, showing how fast beta rises as alpha approaches 1.

mcqs.q: If alpha = 0.99 for a transistor, the value of beta is:
For a transistor with beta = 50 and IB = 20 micro A, the emitter current IE is:
mcqs.why: 1.02 mA is correct: IC = beta IB = 50 x 20 micro A = 1000 micro A = 1.00 mA, and IE = IB + IC = 0.02 + 1.00 = 1.02 mA.

mcqs.q: A transistor has IB = 240 micro A, IE = 12 mA and beta = 49. Its alpha rating and collector current are:
mcqs.why: Alpha = 0.98 and IC = 11.76 mA is correct: alpha = beta/(beta+1) = 49/50 = 0.98, and IC = beta IB = 49 x 0.24 = 11.76 mA, checked by alpha x IE = 0.98 x 12 = 11.76 mA.

lessons.title: Signal Levels and Logic Gates
lessons.notes_html:
Binary Levels and Truth Tables

The low state, logic 0, is typically represented by 0 volts (ground level) in digital circuits. The high state, logic 1, is typically represented by +5 volts in TTL circuits. Voltages near the low level are read as 0 and voltages near the high level are read as 1, with a threshold in between. This two-level system is the basis of all binary digital electronics.

In binary representation the digit 0 corresponds to the low state of the signal, the lower voltage level. The digit 1 correspondingly represents the high state, the higher voltage level such as +5 V. Digital circuits process information entirely in these two states, 0 and 1. A truth table is written using these binary values for all inputs and outputs.

A truth table lists every possible combination of inputs of a logic gate or circuit together with the resulting output for that combination. It therefore completely defines and allows analysis of the logical behavior of the circuit. For a gate with n inputs there are 2 to the power n rows in the table. It is not used to measure voltage, resistance or power, which are analog quantities.

OR, AND, NOT and XOR Gates

The OR gate produces an output of 1 whenever at least one of its inputs is 1, and its output is 0 only when all inputs are 0. Its Boolean expression is F = A + B. The AND gate needs all inputs to be 1 for an output of 1, and the XOR gate gives 1 only when the inputs are different. Hence the gate described is the OR gate.

In the simple OR demonstration circuit the two switches are in parallel with the battery and lamp, so closing either switch completes the circuit. The lamp therefore turns ON when switch A or switch B or both are closed. It remains OFF only when both switches are open. This is exactly the truth table of a 2-input OR gate.

In the AND demonstration circuit the two switches are in series with the battery and the lamp, so the circuit is completed only when both switches are closed. When both switches are closed the current flows and the lamp is ON. If either switch is open the lamp stays OFF, in agreement with the AND truth table in which the output is 1 only for the input combination 1, 1.

An OR gate gives output 0 only in the single case where all of its inputs are 0, and this rule holds for any number of inputs. For a 3-input OR gate the combination 0, 0, 0 therefore produces output 0. Every other combination, having at least one input equal to 1, produces output 1. The output is perfectly defined, so options (c) and (d) do not apply.

A NOT gate, or inverter, always produces the opposite of its single input. With input 1 (high) its output is 0 (low), and with input 0 its output is 1. Its Boolean expression is F = NOT A, written with a bar over the A. This inversion action makes the NOT gate one of the three basic gates of digital electronics.

An XOR (exclusive OR) gate gives output 1 only when its two inputs are different, that is for 0, 1 and 1, 0. When both inputs are 1 the inputs are the same, so the output is 0, which distinguishes XOR from the ordinary OR gate. Its Boolean expression is F = A XOR B, the sum of the two unlike product terms. XOR gates are widely used in adders and in parity checking circuits.

The XOR function F = A (NOT B) + (NOT A) B is built from a combination of AND gates and an OR gate, with NOT gates providing the complemented inputs. Two AND gates form the two product terms for the unlike input combinations, and an OR gate combines their outputs into the final XOR output. Among the given choices the AND plus OR combination (together with NOT for the complements) is therefore the standard equivalent of an XOR gate. XOR can alternatively be built entirely from NAND gates, but that combination is not among the choices in its simple form.

OR: F = A + B ; AND: F = A . B ; NOT: F = NOT A

mcqs.q: The voltage level typically associated with the low state (logic 0) in digital electronics is:
mcqs.why: 0 volts is correct because the low state, logic 0, is typically represented by 0 volts (ground level), while logic 1 is about +5 V in TTL circuits.

mcqs.q: In TTL digital circuits, the high state (logic 1) is typically represented by:
mcqs.why: +5 volts is correct because TTL circuits use about +5 V for the high state and 0 V for the low state, with a threshold in between.

mcqs.q: In binary representation, the digit 0 in digital electronics corresponds to:
mcqs.why: The low state is correct because binary 0 is the lower voltage level and binary 1 is the high state such as +5 V.

mcqs.q: The primary purpose of a truth table in digital electronics is to:
options: Analyse the output states for every combination of inputs
mcqs.why: Analysing outputs for all input combinations is correct because a truth table lists every input combination with its resulting output and completely defines the circuit's logical behaviour.

mcqs.q: Which logic gate produces an output of 1 when at least one of its inputs is 1, with Boolean expression F = A + B?
mcqs.why: The OR gate is correct because its output is 1 whenever at least one input is 1 and 0 only when all inputs are 0, written F = A + B.

mcqs.q: In the 2-input OR demonstration circuit, the switches are in parallel with the battery and lamp. If either switch is closed, the lamp is:
mcqs.why: ON is correct because closing either parallel switch completes the circuit, so the lamp lights when switch A or B or both are closed.

mcqs.q: In the 2-input AND demonstration circuit, the switches are in series. The lamp is ON only when:
options: One switch is open and one closed
mcqs.why: Both switches closed is correct because the series circuit is completed only then, matching the AND truth table where output is 1 only for inputs 1, 1.

mcqs.q: In a 3-input OR gate, if all three inputs are 0, the output will be:
mcqs.why: 0 is correct because an OR gate gives output 0 only in the single case where all its inputs are 0, for any number of inputs.

mcqs.q: If the input to a NOT gate is 1 (high), its output will be:
mcqs.why: 0 is correct because a NOT gate (inverter) always produces the opposite of its single input, so input 1 gives output 0 and input 0 gives output 1.

mcqs.q: In a 2-input XOR gate, when both inputs are 1, the output will be:
mcqs.why: 0 is correct because XOR gives 1 only when its inputs are different (0,1 or 1,0); when both inputs are 1 they are the same, so the output is 0.

lessons.title: Working with Logic Gates
lessons.notes_html:
Significance of Signal Levels

Signal levels allow information to be represented by just two well-separated voltage ranges, so a digital circuit is almost unaffected by small noise and distortion. The low level, logic 0, is typically 0 V, and the high level, logic 1, is typically +5 V in TTL circuits. A threshold level separates the two ranges: voltages below it are read as 0 and voltages above it as 1, which gives the circuit its noise margin and reliable operation. The difference between the high and low levels is called the voltage swing, and a larger swing improves noise immunity.

Binary Representation and the High and Low States

Digital electronics uses the binary system, in which every signal is represented by one of two digits, 0 or 1, called bits. The binary 1 is represented physically by the high state, a higher voltage such as +5 V, corresponding to a closed (ON) switch condition, and the binary 0 is represented by the low state, about 0 V, corresponding to an open (OFF) condition. Combinations of bits in logic gates follow the rules of Boolean algebra, with the output for every input combination given by a truth table. Because only two states are involved, digital systems are simple, reliable and form the basis of computers and modern communication.

Three Logic Gates: Symbols and Operation

The AND gate has a D-shaped symbol with two or more inputs and one output F = A . B; its output is 1 only when all inputs are 1, like two switches in series lighting a lamp only when both are closed. The OR gate has a curved-input, pointed-output symbol and gives F = A + B; its output is 1 when at least one input is 1, like switches in parallel. The NOT gate is a triangle with a small circle at its output and gives F = NOT A; it inverts its single input, producing 1 for input 0 and 0 for input 1. The complete operation of each gate is summarized by its truth table.

A Combination of Gates That Behaves Like XOR

An XOR output is 1 only when the inputs differ, F = A (NOT B) + (NOT A) B, and this expression shows the required combination directly. Take inputs A and B, pass each through a NOT gate to obtain NOT A and NOT B, then feed A with NOT B into one AND gate and NOT A with B into a second AND gate. Finally combine the outputs of the two AND gates in an OR gate; the result is 1 for input combinations 0,1 and 1,0 and 0 for 0,0 and 1,1. This AND-OR-NOT combination therefore has exactly the truth table of a single XOR gate.

A Circuit Model of the 2-Input AND Gate

Connect a battery, two switches A and B and a lamp all in series in a single loop; this series arrangement is the electrical model of a 2-input AND gate, with the switches as inputs and the lamp glow as output 1. When both switches are open, or when only one of them is closed, the loop is broken, no current flows and the lamp remains OFF, corresponding to outputs 0 for inputs 0,0, 0,1 and 1,0. Only when both switches are closed is the circuit completed, current flows through the lamp and it is illuminated, corresponding to output 1 for input 1,1. The lamp is therefore illuminated under exactly one condition: both inputs high. This simple experiment demonstrates the AND truth table and the idea that an AND gate acts as a logical decision element requiring all conditions to be satisfied together.

Truth Table for a 3-Input OR Gate

A 3-input OR gate has three inputs A, B, C and one output F = A + B + C, so its truth table has 2 to the power 3 = 8 rows, one for every combination of inputs. The rows are: 0 0 0 gives 0; 0 0 1 gives 1; 0 1 0 gives 1; 0 1 1 gives 1; 1 0 0 gives 1; 1 0 1 gives 1; 1 1 0 gives 1; and 1 1 1 gives 1. The table shows that the output is 0 in only the first row, where every input is 0. In all seven remaining rows at least one input is 1, so the output is 1, which is exactly the OR rule extended to three inputs. The truth table thus represents the complete input-output relationship of the gate in a compact form that can be checked against any real circuit.

ABCF = A + B + C

1101
1111

mcqs.q: Signal levels give digital circuits reliable operation because:
options: Information is represented by two well-separated voltage ranges, with a threshold between them, giving a noise margin
They use a continuous range of voltages
They remove the need for a power supply
Small noise always changes the logic state
mcqs.why: Two well-separated ranges is correct because voltages below the threshold are read as 0 and above it as 1, so small noise and distortion hardly affect the circuit.

mcqs.q: The voltage swing of a digital signal is:
options: The difference between the high and low levels, a larger swing improving noise immunity
mcqs.why: The difference between high and low levels is correct because that difference is the voltage swing, and a larger swing improves the noise immunity of the circuit.

mcqs.q: Binary 1 is represented physically by:
options: The low state, about 0 V, an open switch
The high state, a higher voltage such as +5 V, corresponding to a closed (ON) switch
mcqs.why: The high state is correct because binary 1 is the higher voltage such as +5 V (closed switch) and binary 0 is the low state of about 0 V (open switch).

mcqs.q: The AND gate, with Boolean expression F = A . B, has a symbol that is:
options: A triangle with a small circle at its output
Curved at the input and pointed at the output
D-shaped, with output 1 only when all inputs are 1
mcqs.why: D-shaped is correct because the AND gate has that symbol and its output is 1 only when all inputs are 1, like two switches in series lighting a lamp.

mcqs.q: The OR gate, with Boolean expression F = A + B, has a symbol that is:
options: Curved at the input and pointed at the output, giving output 1 when at least one input is 1
mcqs.why: Curved input and pointed output is correct because that is the OR gate symbol, and it gives F = A + B, output 1 when at least one input is 1, like switches in parallel.

mcqs.q: The NOT gate symbol is:
options: A triangle with a small circle at its output, inverting its single input
A curved shape with a pointed output
mcqs.why: A triangle with a small circle is correct because the NOT gate inverts its single input, F = NOT A, producing 1 for input 0 and 0 for input 1.

mcqs.q: A combination of gates that behaves like an XOR gate, F = A(NOT B) + (NOT A)B, is built by:
options: Connecting two OR gates in series only
Using NOT gates for the complements, two AND gates for the product terms, and an OR gate to combine them
mcqs.why: NOT plus two ANDs plus an OR is correct because the two AND gates form A(NOT B) and (NOT A)B for the unlike combinations and the OR gate combines them into the XOR output.

mcqs.q: In the circuit model of a 2-input AND gate (battery, two switches and a lamp in series), the lamp is illuminated under exactly one condition:
options: When at least one switch is closed
When exactly one switch is closed
mcqs.why: Both switches closed is correct because only then is the series loop completed and current flows, giving output 1 for input 1,1 and 0 for the other three combinations.

mcqs.q: The truth table of a 3-input OR gate has how many rows?
mcqs.why: 8 rows is correct because a gate with n inputs has 2^n rows in its truth table, and for n = 3 that is 2^3 = 8 combinations.

mcqs.q: In the truth table of a 3-input OR gate, the number of rows in which the output is 1 is:
mcqs.why: 7 is correct because the output is 0 only in the first row (0,0,0); in all seven remaining rows at least one input is 1, so the output is 1.

lessons.title: Special and General Relativity
lessons.notes_html:
Einstein's Theories and the Equivalence Principle

The General Theory of Relativity, published by Einstein in 1915, gave a completely new understanding of gravity. Instead of a mysterious force acting at a distance, gravity is described as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy, and objects move along the natural curved paths in this spacetime. The theory correctly explained the extra precession of Mercurys orbit and predicted the bending of light by the Sun. The speed of light and mass-energy equivalence belong mainly to the earlier Special Theory of 1905.

The equivalence principle of general relativity states that inertial mass and gravitational mass are equivalent, so no local experiment can distinguish between being at rest in a gravitational field and accelerating in empty space. This is why a person in a freely falling lift feels weightless, and why all bodies fall with the same acceleration in a gravitational field. It is the foundation on which Einstein built the geometric theory of gravity. The equivalence of matter and energy, E = m c squared, belongs to special relativity, not to this principle.

The equivalence principle states that the effects of gravity and of acceleration are indistinguishable for an observer inside a closed system. An observer in a windowless spaceship accelerating at 9.8 m/s squared in empty space feels the same weight and sees dropped objects fall exactly as on the surface of the Earth. Conversely, in a freely falling lift the observer feels weightless, as if gravity had been switched off. This deep connection between acceleration and gravity led Einstein to describe gravity as spacetime curvature.

Relativistic Effects at High Speed

The relativistic mass is m = m0 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared). For v = 0.9c, sqrt(1 - 0.81) = sqrt(0.19) = 0.436, so m = 1 / 0.436 = 2.3 kg. The mass increases with speed but stays finite for any speed less than c, becoming infinite only in the limit v = c, which no material object can reach. Hence the moving mass is about 2.3 kg.

Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime produced by accelerating masses, and they are a prediction of the general theory of relativity, not of special relativity, which deals only with inertial frames and ignores gravity. Time dilation, length contraction and relativistic mass increase are all direct consequences of Einsteins two postulates of special relativity. Gravitational waves were detected directly for the first time in 2015 by the LIGO observatories. Therefore gravitational waves are the phenomenon not predicted by special relativity.

As an object moves faster, its relativistic mass m = m0 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared) grows, and the energy needed to accelerate it further grows with it. At v = c the mass and the required energy would become infinite, which is impossible, so no material object can reach or exceed the speed of light. Length contraction to zero and time stopping are also limiting descriptions at v = c, but the direct barrier stated in the theory is the infinite mass and energy requirement. Only massless particles such as photons always travel exactly at c.

The Galilean transformation adds velocities simply, u = u prime + v, which would make the speed of light different for observers moving at different speeds. Experiments such as Michelson-Morley showed that the speed of light is the same, c, for all inertial observers, so the Galilean rule contradicts a fundamental fact of nature. At speeds much less than c the error is negligible and the Galilean transformation works well, but near c it must be replaced by the Lorentz transformation. Time dilation is one of the effects the Galilean view misses, but the root failure is the violation of the constancy of the speed of light.

m = m0 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2)

Gravity, Light Bending and Black Holes

Light bends near a massive object because the mass curves the spacetime around it and light follows the straightest possible path through this curved spacetime; the observed effect, including the formation of multiple or distorted images, is called gravitational lensing. It is not refraction, because there is no change of medium, and it is not reflection or diffraction. The bending of starlight by the Sun, first measured during the eclipse of 1919, was the first famous confirmation of general relativity. Astronomers now use gravitational lensing as a natural telescope to study distant galaxies.

A black hole has such immense gravity that within its event horizon the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light, so no light or signal can ever come out of it. Since we see objects only by the light they emit or reflect, the black hole itself remains invisible and can only be detected by its effects on nearby matter and stars. Hot gas spiraling into it glows brightly in X-rays, revealing its presence. The first image of a black holes shadow, of M87, was obtained in 2019 by the Event Horizon Telescope from the light of this surrounding matter.

An inertial frame is one that is either at rest or moving with constant velocity in a straight line, so that Newtons laws hold in it without fictitious forces. A train moving smoothly at constant speed is therefore an everyday example of an inertial frame, and a ball dropped inside it falls straight down relative to the train. An accelerating car, a spinning platform and a plane in turbulence are all non-inertial frames because their velocity is changing. Inside these frames objects appear to be pushed by unexplained pseudo-forces.

options: As a mysterious force acting at a distance
As the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy
As the bending of light by refraction in a medium
As the equivalence of matter and energy

mcqs.why: The lesson states that general relativity describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy, with objects moving along the natural curved paths in that spacetime, not as a force acting at a distance.

mcqs.why: The lesson says the effects of gravity and acceleration are indistinguishable in a closed system, so the observer accelerating at 9.8 m/s^2 feels the same weight and sees objects fall exactly as on Earth.

lessons.title: Frames, Transformations and the Speed Limit
lessons.notes_html:
Lorentz Transformation Reduces to the Galilean Transformation at Low Speeds

The Lorentz transformations are x prime = (x - v t) / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared) and t prime = (t - v x / c squared) / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared). When v is much less than c, v squared / c squared is negligible compared with 1, so the square root factor becomes 1 (gamma becomes 1). Also the term v x / c squared in the time equation becomes negligible, so t prime = t. The equations then reduce to x prime = x - v t and t prime = t, which are exactly the Galilean transformations. This shows that Newtonian mechanics is the low-speed limiting case of relativity.

Kinetic Energy of a Particle Moving at the Speed of Light

The relativistic kinetic energy is K.E. = (m - m0) c squared, with m = m0 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared). If v were equal to c, the denominator would become zero and the relativistic mass m would become infinite. The kinetic energy required would therefore also be infinite, which can never be supplied by any finite source. Hence no material particle can ever be accelerated to the velocity of light, and the question of its kinetic energy at c has no finite answer.

Special and General Relativity in Simple Terms

Special relativity (1905) deals with objects moving at constant velocity in inertial frames and with the constancy of the speed of light, and it leads to time dilation, length contraction and E = m c squared. It does not include gravity or acceleration. General relativity (1915) extends the ideas to all frames, including accelerating ones, and explains gravity as the curvature of spacetime produced by mass and energy. In simple words, special relativity tells how space and time behave at very high speeds, while general relativity tells how mass shapes space and time to produce gravity.

Inertial and Non-Inertial Frames of Reference

An inertial frame is at rest or moves with constant velocity in a straight line; in it a body with no net force stays at rest or moves uniformly, and Newtons laws hold in their simple form. A non-inertial frame is accelerating, decelerating or rotating; in it Newtons laws do not hold directly and fictitious (pseudo) forces, such as the backward push felt in an accelerating car, must be introduced. A uniformly moving train is inertial, while a braking train, a turning car and a rotating merry-go-round are non-inertial. Einsteins special relativity applies to inertial frames, while general relativity covers both kinds of frames.

Why No Object Can Move at the Speed of Light

According to relativity the mass of a moving object is m = m0 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared), which increases without limit as v approaches c. Accelerating the object further therefore demands more and more energy, and reaching c would require infinite energy and would give it infinite mass and zero contracted length, all of which are impossible. Every experiment with particles in accelerators confirms that they approach c ever more closely but never reach it, however much energy is supplied. Only massless particles, such as photons, travel at exactly the speed of light.

Limitation of the Galilean Transformation and the Lorentz Solution

The Galilean equations x prime = x - v t and t prime = t assume that time is absolute and that velocities simply add, so they predict that a moving observer would measure a different speed of light, contradicting the Michelson-Morley experiment and Einsteins postulate that c is the same for all inertial observers. Lorentz solved this by introducing the factor gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared) and making time itself relative, t prime = (t - v x / c squared) / gamma denominator form. In the Lorentz transformation, space and time measurements adjust together in exactly the way needed to keep the speed of light equal to c in every inertial frame. For v much less than c the Lorentz equations reduce to the Galilean ones, so everyday mechanics is preserved.
