mcqs.why: The lesson lists infinite energy, infinite mass and zero contracted length together as impossible consequences of reaching c, which is why no material object can ever be accelerated to the velocity of light.

lessons.title: Postulates, Mass-Energy Equivalence and Spacetime
lessons.notes_html:
Postulates of Special Relativity: Time Dilation, Length Contraction and Mass Variation

The first postulate states that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference, so no experiment can detect absolute uniform motion. The second postulate states that the speed of light in vacuum is the same constant c for all inertial observers, whatever the motion of the source or observer. From these postulates it follows that a moving clock runs slow: time dilation, delta t = delta t0 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared), so the moving time interval appears longer to a stationary observer. It also follows that a moving object is measured shorter along its direction of motion: length contraction, L = L0 sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared). Finally the mass increases with speed, m = m0 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared), which prevents any object from reaching c. These three effects are negligible at ordinary speeds but have all been confirmed experimentally, for example by the extended lifetimes of fast-moving muons.

Mass-Energy Equivalence: E = mc^2 and 1 u = 931 MeV

Mass-energy equivalence states that mass is a concentrated form of energy and that the total energy of a body of relativistic mass m is E = m c squared, so its rest energy is E0 = m0 c squared and its kinetic energy is (m - m0) c squared. In Einsteins derivation, a body emitting two equal light pulses of total energy E in opposite directions loses momentum in a moving frame unless its mass decreases by E / c squared, which forces the conclusion that a loss of energy E corresponds to a loss of mass E / c squared, i.e. E = m c squared. For one atomic mass unit, m = 1.6605 x10^-27 kg, so E = m c squared = 1.6605 x10^-27 x (3 x10^8) squared = 1.494 x10^-10 J. Dividing by 1.602 x10^-13 J per MeV gives E = 931 MeV, approximately. This equivalence is the basis of nuclear binding energy, fission and fusion power, and the energy released in stars.

Conclusions of General Relativity and the Evidence for Them

General relativity concludes that gravity is the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy, and it predicts the bending of light by a gravitational field, the gravitational red shift of light climbing out of a field, and the extra precession of the perihelion of Mercury. It also predicts time running slower in stronger gravity (gravitational time dilation) and the existence of gravitational waves and black holes. The bending of starlight by the Sun was observed during the solar eclipse of 1919, and Mercurys anomalous precession of 43 arc-seconds per century matched the theory exactly. Gravitational red shift was confirmed in the Pound-Rebka laboratory experiment, atomic clocks flown around the Earth confirmed gravitational time dilation, and gravitational waves were detected directly by LIGO in 2015. Modern GPS satellites must apply both special and general relativistic corrections daily, providing a routine practical confirmation.

The Principle of Relativity versus the Classical Galilean View

The Galilean view assumes absolute space and absolute time: lengths and time intervals are the same for all observers, and velocities add and subtract simply, so the speed of light should depend on the observers motion. The principle of relativity in Einsteins theory keeps the laws of physics, including the speed of light c, the same in all inertial frames, and as a result space and time measurements become relative to the observer. Events simultaneous in one frame are not necessarily simultaneous in another, moving lengths contract and moving clocks dilate, effects entirely absent in the Galilean picture. Mathematically the Galilean transformation is replaced by the Lorentz transformation, to which it reduces only when v is much less than c. The Galilean view is therefore an approximation valid for everyday speeds, while relativity is the more general and accurate description.

Spacetime Curvature and the Visual Picture of Gravity

In general relativity, space and time are united into a four-dimensional spacetime, and the presence of mass and energy curves this spacetime just as a heavy ball placed on a stretched rubber sheet makes a dent in the sheet. Other objects and even light rays then follow the straightest possible paths (geodesics) in the curved geometry, and we experience this curving of paths as the force of gravity. A small ball rolled across the rubber sheet spirals toward the heavy ball, giving a simple visual model of orbits and of the bending of light near the Sun. Near a very dense object the curvature becomes so extreme that an event horizon forms and a black hole results. This geometric picture explains gravity without any mysterious action at a distance and correctly predicts all the observed tests of the theory.

The Galilean Transformation Equations

Let frame S prime move with constant velocity v along the x-axis of frame S, with their origins coinciding at t = 0. A point event has coordinates (x, y, z, t) in S; in classical physics time is absolute, so t prime = t, and since the origin of S prime has moved a distance v t in S, the x-coordinate in S prime is x prime = x - v t. Motion perpendicular to v is unaffected, so y prime = y and z prime = z, completing the Galilean transformation equations. Differentiating x prime = x - v t with respect to the common time gives the velocity rule u prime x = u x - v, while the other components are unchanged, u prime y = u y and u prime z = u z. These equations relate positions and velocities between inertial frames correctly at low speeds, but they fail near the speed of light, where the Lorentz transformation must be used instead.

The Lorentz Transformation Equations and Their Use

For a frame S prime moving at velocity v along the x-axis of S, the Lorentz transformations are x prime = gamma (x - v t), t prime = gamma (t - v x / c squared), y prime = y and z prime = z, where gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared). Unlike the Galilean equations, space and time coordinates are mixed together: the time in one frame depends on both time and position in the other frame, which is the mathematical root of the relativity of simultaneity. Direct consequences are time dilation, delta t = gamma delta t0, and length contraction, L = L0 / gamma, whenever the coordinates of two events are substituted into the equations. For example, fast muons created in the upper atmosphere reach the ground because, in the Earth frame, their lifetime is stretched by gamma, while in the muon frame the atmosphere is length-contracted by the same factor. At ordinary speeds gamma is almost 1 and the equations reduce to the Galilean transformation, showing the agreement of the two theories in the low-speed limit.

options: The speed of light depends on the motion of the source
The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference, so no experiment can detect absolute uniform motion
Lengths and time intervals are the same for all observers
Time is absolute in every frame
mcqs.q: The first postulate of special relativity states that:
mcqs.why: The first postulate says the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, so absolute uniform motion cannot be detected by any experiment; absolute lengths and times belong to the older Galilean view.

options: Velocities add and subtract simply in all frames
Mass increases with speed in every frame
The speed of light in vacuum is the same constant c for all inertial observers, whatever the motion of the source or observer
Simultaneous events are simultaneous in all frames
mcqs.q: The second postulate of special relativity states that:
mcqs.why: The second postulate fixes c as the same constant for all inertial observers regardless of the motion of source or observer; this constancy is what forces time dilation, length contraction and mass variation to follow.

options: Delta t = Delta t0 sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)
Delta t = Delta t0 in all frames
Delta t = Delta t0 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), so a moving clock runs slow and the interval appears longer to a stationary observer
mcqs.q: Time dilation is expressed in the lesson by:
mcqs.why: Time dilation is delta t = delta t0 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2): the moving time interval appears longer to a stationary observer, meaning the moving clock runs slow; it has been confirmed by the extended lifetimes of fast-moving muons.

options: L = L0 sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), measured shorter along the direction of motion
mcqs.q: Length contraction, as given in the lesson, is:
mcqs.why: A moving object is measured shorter along its direction of motion, L = L0 sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2); the factor is less than 1, so the contracted length is smaller than the proper length L0.

options: Gain mass E/c^2 to conserve momentum in a moving frame
Lose mass E/c^2, so a loss of energy E corresponds to a loss of mass E/c^2
Keep exactly the same mass in every frame
mcqs.q: In Einstein's derivation of E = mc^2 described in the lesson, a body emitting two equal light pulses of total energy E in opposite directions must:
mcqs.why: Momentum conservation in a moving frame only works if the body's mass decreases by E/c^2 when it loses energy E, which forces the conclusion E = mc^2, that mass is a concentrated form of energy.

mcqs.q: The rest energy and kinetic energy of a body are given in the lesson by:
mcqs.why: Total energy is E = mc^2 with relativistic mass m, so the rest energy is E0 = m0c^2 and the kinetic energy is the excess over rest energy, K.E. = (m - m0)c^2, exactly as the lesson states.

options: E = mc^2 = 1.6605 x 10^-27 x (3 x 10^8)^2 = 1.494 x 10^-10 J, and dividing by 1.602 x 10^-13 J per MeV gives about 931 MeV
E = (1/2)mc^2 gives half that value in joules
1 u is defined to equal 931 MeV by convention with no calculation
Dividing the mass in kg directly by the charge of the electron gives 931
mcqs.q: One atomic mass unit (1 u = 1.6605 x 10^-27 kg) is equivalent to about 931 MeV because:
mcqs.why: Working: E = mc^2 = 1.6605 x 10^-27 x 9 x 10^16 = 1.494 x 10^-10 J; then 1.494 x 10^-10 / 1.602 x 10^-13 = about 932, i.e. approximately 931 MeV, the basis of nuclear binding energy calculations.

options: Gravitational lensing and black holes only
Nuclear binding energy, fission and fusion power, and the energy released in stars
mcqs.q: Mass-energy equivalence is described in the lesson as the basis of:
mcqs.why: The lesson states that E = mc^2 underlies nuclear binding energy, fission and fusion power and stellar energy release, because small losses of mass appear as large amounts of energy.

options: Zero, once Newtonian corrections were applied
mcqs.q: Mercury's anomalous precession matched general relativity by:
mcqs.why: General relativity predicted the extra precession of Mercury's perihelion, and the observed anomalous value of 43 arc-seconds per century matched the theory exactly, as the lesson records.

options: Gravitational red shift — the 1919 solar eclipse
Bending of starlight by the Sun — observed during the solar eclipse of 1919
mcqs.q: Which pairing of prediction and confirming evidence is correct in the lesson?
mcqs.why: The lesson pairs starlight bending with the 1919 eclipse observation; red shift was confirmed by Pound-Rebka, time dilation by flown atomic clocks, and gravitational waves were detected directly by LIGO in 2015.

options: Use the Galilean transformation instead of the Lorentz transformation
Ignore both special and general relativistic corrections
Apply both special and general relativistic corrections daily
mcqs.q: Modern GPS satellites provide a routine practical confirmation of relativity because they must:
mcqs.why: The lesson notes that GPS satellites must apply both special and general relativistic corrections every day to work correctly, making relativity a routine, practical confirmation rather than only a laboratory result.

options: It keeps absolute space and absolute time but changes the velocity rule
It keeps the laws of physics, including c, the same in all inertial frames, so space and time measurements become relative and simultaneity is frame-dependent
It applies only at everyday speeds, while the Galilean view applies near c
It replaces the Lorentz transformation with the Galilean transformation
mcqs.q: How does the principle of relativity differ from the classical Galilean view, according to the lesson?
mcqs.why: The Galilean view assumes absolute space and time with simple velocity addition, so c should depend on the observer; Einstein's principle keeps the laws and c the same in all inertial frames, making lengths, times and simultaneity relative.

options: Curved paths forced by a pull from the heavy ball
Straight lines in flat space, unaffected by the dent
The straightest possible paths (geodesics) in the curved geometry, which we experience as gravity
Paths determined by refraction at the edge of the sheet
mcqs.q: In the rubber-sheet picture of spacetime curvature in the lesson, objects and light rays follow:
mcqs.why: Mass and energy curve four-dimensional spacetime like a heavy ball denting a rubber sheet; other bodies and light follow geodesics, the straightest possible paths in that curved geometry, and this curving of paths is experienced as gravity.

options: x' = gamma(x - vt), t' = gamma(t - vx/c^2), y' = y, z' = z
x' = x - vt, t' = t, y' = y, z' = z
x' = x + vt, t' = t - vx/c^2, y' = y, z' = z
x' = x, t' = t - vt, y' = y - vt, z' = z
mcqs.q: The Galilean transformation equations for a frame S' moving at v along the x-axis of S are:
mcqs.why: In classical physics time is absolute (t' = t) and the origin of S' has moved vt, so x' = x - vt, with motion perpendicular to v unaffected (y' = y, z' = z); differentiating gives u'x = ux - v.

mcqs.q: Unlike the Galilean equations, the Lorentz transformations mix space and time together. In the lesson this mixing is the mathematical root of:
mcqs.why: In the Lorentz equations t' = gamma(t - vx/c^2), the time in one frame depends on both time and position in the other frame; the lesson identifies this mixing as the mathematical root of the relativity of simultaneity.

lessons.title: Worked Examples
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example 1

Calculate the value of gamma (Lorentz factor) if the object is moving at the speed of light.

Step 1: Given: v = c, Lorentz factor gamma is required

Step 2: Formula: gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared)

Step 3: Substitution: With v = c, v squared / c squared = 1, so gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - 1) = 1 / sqrt(0) = 1 / 0

Step 4: Calculation: Division by zero gives gamma = infinity

The Lorentz factor becomes infinite at v = c, which is another way of seeing that a material object would need infinite energy to reach the speed of light, so v = c is impossible for it

Worked Example 2

A rod 1 meter long is moving along its length with a velocity 0.6c. Calculate its length as it appears to an observer (a) on the earth (b) moving with the rod itself.

Step 1: Given: Proper length L0 = 1 m, v = 0.6c, contracted length L is required

Step 2: Formula: L = L0 sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared)

Step 3: Substitution: L = 1 x sqrt(1 - (0.6c) squared / c squared) = sqrt(1 - 0.36) = sqrt(0.64)

Step 4: Calculation: (a) For the observer on Earth, L = 0.8 m; (b) for an observer moving with the rod the relative velocity is zero, so no contraction occurs and L = L0

(a) 0.8 m as seen from Earth, (b) 1 m for the observer moving with the rod

Worked Example 3

How fast would a rocket have to go relative to an observer for its length to be contracted to 99 percent of its length at rest?

Step 1: Given: L / L0 = 99 percent = 0.99, speed v is required

Step 2: Formula: L = L0 sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared), so v = c sqrt(1 - (L / L0) squared)

Step 3: Substitution: v = c sqrt(1 - (0.99) squared) = c sqrt(1 - 0.9801) = c sqrt(0.0199)

Step 4: Calculation: sqrt(0.0199) = 0.141, so v = 0.141 c = 0.141 x 3 x10^8 = 4.24 x10^7 m/s

The rocket must travel at about 42.45 x10^6 m/s (0.141c) relative to the observer

Worked Example 4

A particle with a proper lifetime of 1 micro s moves through the laboratory at 2.7 x10^8 m/s. (a) What is its lifetime, as measured by observers in the laboratory? (b) What will be the distance traversed by it before disintegrating?

Step 1: Given: Proper lifetime delta t0 = 1 micro s = 1 x10^-6 s, v = 2.7 x10^8 m/s = 0.9c, laboratory lifetime and distance are required

Step 2: Formula: delta t = delta t0 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared) (time dilation), and distance d = v x delta t

Step 3: Substitution: gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - 0.81) = 1 / 0.436 = 2.29, so delta t = 2.29 x 1 x10^-6 s, and d = 2.7 x10^8 x 2.29 x10^-6

Step 4: Calculation: (a) delta t = 2.3 x10^-6 s, (b) d = 619 m, approximately 620 m

The laboratory lifetime is about 2.3 x10^-6 s and the particle travels about 620 m before disintegrating

Worked Example 5

At what speed is a particle moving if the mass is equal to three times its rest mass?

Step 1: Given: m = 3 m0, speed v is required

Step 2: Formula: m = m0 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared), so sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared) = m0 / m

Step 3: Substitution: sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared) = 1 / 3, hence 1 - v squared / c squared = 1 / 9 and v squared / c squared = 8 / 9

Step 4: Calculation: v / c = sqrt(8) / 3 = 2 sqrt(2) / 3 = 0.943, so v = 0.943c = 2.83 x10^8 m/s

The particle moves at v = (2 sqrt(2) / 3) c, about 0.943c

Worked Example 6

If 4 kg of a substance is fully converted into energy, how much energy is produced?

Step 1: Given: Mass converted m = 4 kg, c = 3 x10^8 m/s, energy E is required

Step 2: Formula: E = m c squared

Step 3: Substitution: E = 4 x (3 x10^8) squared = 4 x 9 x10^16

Step 4: Calculation: E = 3.6 x10^17 J

The energy produced is 3.6 x10^17 J

Worked Example 7

Calculate the rest energy of an electron in joules and in electron volts.

Step 1: Given: Electron rest mass m0 = 9.11 x10^-31 kg, c = 3 x10^8 m/s, 1 eV = 1.602 x10^-19 J, rest energy E0 is required

Step 2: Formula: E0 = m0 c squared

Step 3: Substitution: E0 = 9.11 x10^-31 x (3 x10^8) squared = 9.11 x10^-31 x 9 x10^16

Step 4: Calculation: E0 = 8.2 x10^-14 J; converting, E0 = 8.2 x10^-14 / 1.602 x10^-19 = 5.11 x10^5 eV

The rest energy of an electron is 8.2 x10^-14 J, equal to 0.511 MeV

Worked Example 8

Calculate the K.E. of an electron moving with a velocity of 0.98 times the velocity of light in the laboratory system.

Step 1: Given: v = 0.98c, electron rest energy m0 c squared = 8.2 x10^-14 J, kinetic energy is required

Step 2: Formula: gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared), and K.E. = (gamma - 1) m0 c squared

Step 3: Substitution: gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - (0.98) squared) = 1 / sqrt(1 - 0.9604) = 1 / sqrt(0.0396) = 1 / 0.199 = 5.03, so K.E. = (5.03 - 1) x 8.2 x10^-14

Step 4: Calculation: K.E. = 4.03 x 8.2 x10^-14 = 3.3 x10^-13 J

The kinetic energy of the electron is 3.3 x10^-13 J (about 2.06 MeV)

Worked Example 9

At what velocity does the K.E. of a particle equal its rest energy?

Step 1: Given: K.E. = rest energy m0 c squared, velocity v is required

Step 2: Formula: K.E. = (gamma - 1) m0 c squared, so the condition gives (gamma - 1) m0 c squared = m0 c squared, i.e. gamma = 2

Step 3: Substitution: 1 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared) = 2, so sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared) = 1 / 2 and 1 - v squared / c squared = 1 / 4

Step 4: Calculation: v squared / c squared = 3 / 4, so v = (sqrt(3) / 2) c = 0.866c

The velocity is (sqrt(3) / 2) c, about 0.866c or 2.6 x10^8 m/s

Worked Example 10

A particle of rest mass m0 moves with speed c / sqrt(2). Calculate its mass, momentum, total energy and kinetic energy.

Step 1: Given: Rest mass m0, v = c / sqrt(2), so v squared / c squared = 1 / 2; mass m, momentum p, total energy E and K.E. are required

Step 2: Formula: gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared), m = gamma m0, p = gamma m0 v, E = gamma m0 c squared, K.E. = (gamma - 1) m0 c squared

Step 3: Substitution: gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - 1/2) = 1 / sqrt(1/2) = sqrt(2) = 1.414, so m = sqrt(2) m0, p = sqrt(2) m0 (c / sqrt(2)), E = sqrt(2) m0 c squared, K.E. = (sqrt(2) - 1) m0 c squared

Step 4: Calculation: m = sqrt(2) m0, p = m0 c, E = sqrt(2) m0 c squared = 1.414 m0 c squared, K.E. = 0.414 m0 c squared, approximately 0.41 m0 c squared

Mass is sqrt(2) m0, momentum is m0 c, total energy is sqrt(2) m0 c squared, and kinetic energy is 0.41 m0 c squared

Worked Example 11

The nearest star to Earth is Proximal Centauri, 4.3 light-years away. A spaceship with a constant speed of 0.800c relative to the Earth travels toward the star. (a) How much time would elapse on a clock as measured by travelers on the spacecraft? (b) How long does the trip take according to Earth observers?

Step 1: Given: Distance in Earth frame L0 = 4.3 light-years, v = 0.800c, times in both frames are required

Step 2: Formula: Earth-frame time t = L0 / v; the travelers time is the proper time t0 = t sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared), equivalently the contracted distance L = L0 sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared) divided by v

Step 3: Substitution: (b) t = 4.3 / 0.800 = 5.38 years; sqrt(1 - 0.64) = sqrt(0.36) = 0.600, so (a) t0 = 5.38 x 0.600, or L = 4.3 x 0.600 = 2.58 light-years and t0 = 2.58 / 0.800

Step 4: Calculation: (b) t = 5.38 years, (a) t0 = 3.22 years

(a) 3.22 years elapse on the spacecraft clock, (b) the trip takes 5.38 years according to Earth observers

options: Gamma is infinite, since gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - 1) = 1 / 0
mcqs.q: Worked Example 1: What is the Lorentz factor gamma when v = c?
mcqs.why: Working: with v = c, v^2/c^2 = 1, so gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - 1) = 1 / sqrt(0) = 1/0, which is infinite; a material object would therefore need infinite energy to reach c.

mcqs.q: Worked Example 2: A rod of proper length 1 m moves along its length at 0.6c. Its length as seen by an observer on Earth is:
mcqs.why: Working: L = L0 sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = 1 x sqrt(1 - 0.36) = sqrt(0.64) = 0.8 m. The moving rod is length-contracted as seen from Earth.

options: 1.0 m, because the relative velocity is zero so no contraction occurs
mcqs.q: Worked Example 2 (continued): The same 1 m rod at 0.6c, measured by an observer moving with the rod itself, has length:
mcqs.why: For an observer moving with the rod the relative velocity is zero, so sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = 1 and L = L0 = 1.0 m; length contraction only appears for an observer relative to whom the rod moves.

mcqs.q: Worked Example 3: How fast must a rocket go for its length to contract to 99% of its rest length?
Worked Example 4: A particle with proper lifetime 1 microsecond moves at 2.7 x 10^8 m/s (0.9c). Its lifetime measured in the laboratory is about:
mcqs.why: Working: gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - 0.81) = 1 / 0.436 = 2.29, so delta t = gamma x delta t0 = 2.29 x 1 x 10^-6 s = about 2.3 x 10^-6 s; the moving particle's lifetime is dilated in the laboratory frame.

mcqs.q: Worked Example 4 (continued): How far does that particle (v = 2.7 x 10^8 m/s, laboratory lifetime about 2.29 x 10^-6 s) travel before disintegrating?
mcqs.why: Working: distance d = v x delta t = 2.7 x 10^8 x 2.29 x 10^-6 = 618.3 m, approximately 620 m (the example gives 619 m), much farther than the 270 m its proper lifetime alone would allow.

mcqs.q: Worked Example 5: At what speed is a particle's mass equal to three times its rest mass?
mcqs.why: Working: m = 3m0 gives sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = 1/3, so 1 - v^2/c^2 = 1/9 and v^2/c^2 = 8/9; hence v/c = sqrt(8)/3 = 0.943 and v = 0.943c = 2.83 x 10^8 m/s.

mcqs.q: Worked Example 6: If 4 kg of a substance is fully converted into energy, how much energy is produced?
mcqs.why: Working: E = mc^2 = 4 x (3 x 10^8)^2 = 4 x 9 x 10^16 = 3.6 x 10^17 J. The huge value shows why mass is described as a concentrated form of energy.

mcqs.q: Worked Example 7: The rest energy of an electron (m0 = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg) is:
Worked Example 8: An electron moves at 0.98c (gamma = 5.03, rest energy 8.2 x 10^-14 J). Its kinetic energy is:
Worked Example 9: At what velocity does a particle's kinetic energy equal its rest energy?
mcqs.why: Working: K.E. = (gamma - 1)m0c^2 = m0c^2 gives gamma = 2, so sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = 1/2 and v^2/c^2 = 3/4; hence v = (sqrt(3)/2)c = 0.866c, about 2.6 x 10^8 m/s.

options: m = m0 and p = m0c / sqrt(2)
m = sqrt(2) m0 and p = m0c
m = sqrt(2) m0 and p = sqrt(2) m0c
mcqs.q: Worked Example 10: A particle of rest mass m0 moves at v = c / sqrt(2), so gamma = sqrt(2). Its mass and momentum are:
mcqs.why: Working: gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - 1/2) = sqrt(2), so m = gamma m0 = sqrt(2) m0, and p = gamma m0 v = sqrt(2) m0 x (c / sqrt(2)) = m0c, exactly as the example calculates.

options: E = sqrt(2) m0c^2 (1.414 m0c^2) and K.E. = (sqrt(2) - 1) m0c^2, about 0.41 m0c^2
E = sqrt(2) m0c^2 and K.E. = sqrt(2) m0c^2
mcqs.q: Worked Example 10 (continued): For the same particle at v = c / sqrt(2), the total energy and kinetic energy are:
mcqs.why: Working: E = gamma m0c^2 = sqrt(2) m0c^2 = 1.414 m0c^2, and K.E. = (gamma - 1)m0c^2 = (sqrt(2) - 1)m0c^2 = 0.414 m0c^2, approximately 0.41 m0c^2.

mcqs.q: Worked Example 11: Proxima Centauri is 4.3 light-years away (Earth frame). A spaceship travels there at 0.800c. The trip time according to Earth observers is:
mcqs.why: Working: Earth-frame time t = L0 / v = 4.3 / 0.800 = 5.375 years, about 5.38 years; 2.58 light-years is the contracted distance in the travellers' frame, not the Earth-frame time.

mcqs.q: Worked Example 11 (continued): How much time elapses on the spacecraft's own clock for that trip at 0.800c?
mcqs.why: Working: sqrt(1 - 0.64) = sqrt(0.36) = 0.600, so the travellers' proper time t0 = 5.38 x 0.600 = 3.22 years; equivalently the contracted distance 4.3 x 0.600 = 2.58 light-years divided by 0.800c gives 3.22 years.

lessons.title: Unit Overview: What This Unit Covers
lessons.notes_html:
What This Unit Is About

Unit 25, Quantum Physics, is the unit in which light and matter are shown to behave both as waves and as particles. The printed outline of the unit on its opening page (book page 212) lists the following topics, in the book's own order.

Topics Listed in the Book

  • The concept of black body radiation, and how the energy is distributed over the wavelength range at different temperatures
  • Planck's hypothesis that radiation is emitted and absorbed in a cavity as quantised bundles of energy
  • The particle nature of electromagnetic radiation
  • The phenomenon of the photoelectric effect, explained on the basis of quantum theory, with problems solved using Einstein's photoelectric relation
  • Uses of the photoelectric effect, including solar cells and photocells
  • The Compton effect, described qualitatively in terms of photons with definite energy and frequency
  • The process of pair production, and the annihilation of matter, on the basis of conservation laws
  • The de Broglie proposal that every kind of particle has both wave and particle properties, and its confirmation by the Davisson and Germer experiment, in which the diffraction of electrons by the surface layers of a crystal was observed
  • The electron microscope, which uses the very short wavelength of electrons and electric and magnetic fields to focus them, giving very high resolution for studying the micro structure and properties of matter
  • The uncertainty principle

options: Light and matter are shown to behave both as waves and as particles
Gravity is explained as the curvature of spacetime
Gases are explained by the motion of molecules
Electric circuits are explained by Ohm's law

mcqs.why: The overview opens by stating that Unit 25, Quantum Physics, is the unit in which light and matter are shown to behave both as waves and as particles; the other options belong to other units of the book.

On the unit's opening page, book page 212

mcqs.why: The overview states that the printed outline of the unit is on its opening page, book page 212, and that the topics are listed there in the book's own order.

options: How electrons are emitted from a metal surface
The concept of black body radiation and how the energy is distributed over the wavelength range at different temperatures
The diffraction of electrons by a crystal
How photons are created in pairs
mcqs.q: As listed in the overview, the topic of black body radiation in this unit is about:
mcqs.why: The overview lists black body radiation together with how the energy is distributed over the wavelength range at different temperatures; electron emission, electron diffraction and pair creation are listed as separate topics.

options: Emitted and absorbed in a cavity as a continuous wave
Emitted only when the intensity is high enough
Emitted and absorbed in a cavity as quantised bundles of energy
Absorbed only by solar cells and photocells
mcqs.q: According to the overview, Planck's hypothesis states that radiation is:
mcqs.why: The overview states Planck's hypothesis in the book's own framing: radiation is emitted and absorbed in a cavity as quantised bundles of energy, not as a continuous stream.

options: On the basis of classical wave theory alone
On the basis of quantum theory, with problems solved using Einstein's photoelectric relation
By the diffraction of electrons in a crystal
By the conservation laws used for pair production
mcqs.q: According to the overview, the photoelectric effect in this unit is explained:
mcqs.why: The overview lists the photoelectric effect as explained on the basis of quantum theory, with problems solved using Einstein's photoelectric relation; that quantum-theory basis is the framing the book itself gives.

mcqs.q: Which uses of the photoelectric effect are named in the overview?
mcqs.why: The overview explicitly names solar cells and photocells as the uses of the photoelectric effect covered in the unit; the other devices are not listed there as uses of this effect.

Only as a wave phenomenon with no photons involved
As an application of the uncertainty principle
As the production of electron pairs from radiation

mcqs.why: The overview states that the Compton effect is described qualitatively in terms of photons with definite energy and frequency; it does not present the effect as a purely wave phenomenon.

On the basis of conservation laws
Only in connection with black body radiation
As uses of the photoelectric effect

mcqs.why: The overview lists the process of pair production, and the annihilation of matter, as treated on the basis of conservation laws; that stated basis is what the question tests.

Photons were shown to have definite energy and frequency
Pairs of particles were produced from radiation
The diffraction of electrons by the surface layers of a crystal was observed

mcqs.why: De Broglie proposed that every kind of particle has both wave and particle properties, and the overview says this was confirmed by Davisson and Germer, in which the diffraction of electrons by the surface layers of a crystal was observed.

Uses the very short wavelength of electrons, with electric and magnetic fields to focus them
Uses quantised bundles of energy in a cavity
Applies Einstein's photoelectric relation to its lenses

lessons.notes_html:
Notes for This Unit

The exercise pages of this unit are missing from the official Sindh Textbook Board scan of this book: the scan is defective from book page 218 onwards and jumps to book page 251, so most of the unit's pages are not available in any copy of the book that we have.

For this reason, in the book's solved edition the answers to this unit's exercise questions have been intentionally left blank, and no solved notes for Unit 25 can be given here yet. The notes for this unit will be added as soon as a complete copy of the book becomes available. Nothing has been written from guesswork: every other unit of this book is complete.

lessons.title: Atomic Spectra, Bohr Orbits, Lasers and X-Rays
lessons.notes_html:
Line Spectra and Bohr Orbits

Atomic spectra consist of sharp, separate lines of definite wavelength, so they are called line spectra. Each line corresponds to a transition of an electron between two fixed energy levels of the atom. Because the energy levels differ from element to element, the line spectrum is characteristic of the element.

In a Bohr orbit the kinetic energy is KE = +13.6 / n2 eV while the total energy is E = -13.6 / n2 eV, so the two are equal in magnitude and their ratio is 1:1. The negative sign of the total energy only shows that the electron is bound to the nucleus. The potential energy is -27.2 / n2 eV, twice the total energy in magnitude.

The radius of the nth Bohr orbit is r = r0 n2, where r0 = 0.53 angstrom is the radius of the first orbit. As the principal quantum number n increases, the radius increases as the square of n. The electron in higher orbits is therefore farther from the nucleus and less tightly bound.

En = -13.6 / n^2 eV ; r = r0 n^2

Lasers: Pumping and Population Inversion

A laser beam is light produced by stimulated emission, so it consists of photons that are in phase with one another, that is, highly coherent photons. All the photons also have the same frequency and travel in the same direction. This gives laser light its monochromatic, intense and directional character.

In a ruby laser a bright flash of light from a xenon flash tube raises chromium atoms to an excited state, which is optical pumping. The energy of the pumping light is absorbed by the active medium and later released as laser light. The emitted laser beam has a shorter wavelength content in energy terms because part of the pump energy is lost as heat in the rod.

A practical laser needs at least three energy levels so that atoms pumped to the highest level can collect in a metastable level above the lower laser level. Population inversion can then be maintained between the metastable level and the level below it. In a simple two-level system the upper level can never hold more atoms than the lower level under steady pumping, so laser action is not possible.

Population inversion, in which more atoms occupy the higher energy state than the lower state, is created inside the active medium of the laser. The active medium is the material, such as ruby or a helium-neon mixture, that is pumped to store energy. Only in this medium can stimulated emission dominate over absorption and amplify the light.

X-Rays and Their Properties

X-rays carry energy in photons and transfer this energy to the metal they strike, which is why the target of an X-ray tube becomes very hot and needs cooling. Part of the energy of the fast electrons striking the target also appears directly as X-ray photons. This energy transfer is the basis of both the heating problem in X-ray tubes and the use of X-rays in radiation treatment.

X-rays are electromagnetic waves and carry no electric charge, so electric and magnetic fields cannot deflect them. For practical purposes they also travel in straight lines unaffected by ordinary gravitational fields in the laboratory. This was an early piece of evidence that X-rays are a form of electromagnetic radiation and not a stream of charged particles.

The intensity of X-rays produced is approximately proportional to the square of the tube voltage, so doubling the voltage makes the intensity about four times greater. A higher voltage also makes the electrons strike the target faster, so the X-rays produced are more penetrating. For this reason tube voltage controls both the quantity and the quality of the X-ray beam.

mcqs.q: Atomic spectra consisting of sharp, separate lines of definite wavelength are called what?
mcqs.why: Line spectra is correct because atomic spectra consist of sharp, separate lines of definite wavelength, each line corresponding to a transition between two fixed energy levels.

mcqs.q: For an electron in a Bohr orbit, the kinetic energy is +13.6/n^2 eV and the total energy is -13.6/n^2 eV. What is the ratio of their magnitudes?
mcqs.why: The ratio is 1:1 because the kinetic energy +13.6/n^2 eV and the total energy -13.6/n^2 eV are equal in magnitude; the negative sign only shows the electron is bound.

mcqs.q: What is the potential energy of the electron in the nth Bohr orbit of hydrogen?
mcqs.why: The potential energy is -27.2/n^2 eV, which is twice the total energy -13.6/n^2 eV in magnitude, so that KE + PE = +13.6/n^2 - 27.2/n^2 = -13.6/n^2 eV.

mcqs.q: Using r = r0 n^2 with r0 = 0.53 angstrom, what is the radius of the n = 3 Bohr orbit?
mcqs.why: r = r0 n^2 = 0.53 x 3^2 = 0.53 x 9 = 4.77 angstrom, so the radius grows as the square of the principal quantum number n.

mcqs.q: A laser beam consists of photons that are in phase with one another. Such photons are described as:
mcqs.why: Highly coherent is correct because laser light is produced by stimulated emission, so its photons are in phase, have the same frequency and travel in the same direction.

mcqs.q: In a ruby laser, chromium atoms are raised to an excited state by a bright flash from a xenon flash tube. This process is called:
mcqs.why: Optical pumping is correct because in the ruby laser a bright flash of light from a xenon flash tube is absorbed by chromium atoms and raises them to an excited state.

mcqs.q: Why can a simple two-level system not produce laser action?
options: The upper level can never hold more atoms than the lower level under steady pumping
mcqs.why: A two-level system cannot work because under steady pumping the upper level can never hold more atoms than the lower level, so population inversion is impossible; a practical laser needs at least three levels with a metastable level.

mcqs.q: Population inversion, in which more atoms occupy the higher energy state than the lower state, is created inside the:
mcqs.why: The active medium is correct because population inversion is created inside the material that is pumped to store energy, such as ruby or a helium-neon mixture, where stimulated emission can then dominate over absorption.

mcqs.q: X-rays cannot be deflected by electric or magnetic fields because they:
options: Carry no electric charge and are electromagnetic waves
mcqs.why: X-rays carry no electric charge and are electromagnetic waves, so electric and magnetic fields cannot deflect them; this was early evidence that they are electromagnetic radiation, not charged particles.

mcqs.q: The intensity of X-rays is approximately proportional to the square of the tube voltage. If the tube voltage is doubled, the intensity becomes about:
mcqs.why: Intensity is proportional to V^2, so doubling V gives (2V)^2 / V^2 = 4 times the intensity; the higher voltage also makes the X-rays more penetrating.

lessons.title: Spectra, X-Rays and Emission Processes
lessons.notes_html:
Why Different Elements Have Different Spectra

Each element has a different number of electrons and a different set of allowed energy levels, fixed by the charge of its nucleus and the arrangement of its electrons. Spectral lines are produced when electrons jump between these levels, and the photon energy hf equals the difference of the two level energies. Since the level differences are different for every element, the wavelengths emitted or absorbed are also different. The spectrum therefore acts as a fingerprint by which an element can be identified.

X-Rays and Gamma Rays

X-rays and gamma rays are both high-energy electromagnetic radiations, and they differ mainly in their origin. X-rays are produced outside the nucleus, when fast electrons strike a target or when electrons in inner shells of an atom change levels. Gamma rays are emitted from inside an unstable nucleus when it changes from an excited state to a lower energy state after alpha or beta decay. Gamma rays are generally of higher energy and are more penetrating than X-rays.

Properties of X-Rays That Make Bone Cracks Visible

X-rays travel in straight lines, are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields, and can pass through flesh and soft tissue much more easily than through dense bone, because bone absorbs them more strongly. They also affect a photographic film and cause fluorescence on suitable screens. When X-rays pass through the body, bones cast darker shadows on the film than the surrounding tissue, so a crack or fracture, where absorption suddenly changes, becomes clearly visible.

Wavelength and Frequency Ranges of the Lyman and Balmer Series

The Lyman series is produced by transitions ending at n = 1, and its wavelengths run from about 121.6 nm for the 2 to 1 transition down to the series limit of about 91.2 nm, all in the ultraviolet. Its frequencies therefore run from about 2.47x10^15 Hz up to about 3.29x10^15 Hz. The Balmer series ends at n = 2, with wavelengths from about 656 nm for the 3 to 2 line down to the series limit of about 365 nm, in the visible and near ultraviolet. Its frequencies run from about 4.57x10^14 Hz up to about 8.22x10^14 Hz.

Spontaneous and Stimulated Emission

In spontaneous emission an atom in an excited state falls to a lower state by itself, without any external influence, and emits a photon in a random direction with random phase. In stimulated emission an incoming photon of exactly the transition energy triggers the excited atom to fall and emit a second photon identical in frequency, phase and direction to the first. Spontaneous emission gives the ordinary incoherent light of lamps and discharge tubes. Stimulated emission, by contrast, produces the coherent and amplified light of a laser.

Why Population Inversion Is Necessary in a Laser

In normal matter most atoms are in the ground state, so an incoming photon is far more likely to be absorbed than to stimulate emission, and no amplification can occur. Population inversion reverses this situation by keeping more atoms in the upper, metastable state than in the lower state. A passing photon then stimulates more emission than absorption, and one photon quickly multiplies into a large number of identical photons. Without this inversion the beam cannot grow, so inversion is the essential condition for laser action.

Why the Pumping Light Has a Shorter Wavelength Than the Laser Beam

The pumping light must raise atoms from the ground state to a level above the upper laser level, so each pump photon must carry at least as much energy as the full jump, which is more than the energy of the laser transition itself. Part of the absorbed energy is then lost as heat when the atoms drop without radiation to the metastable laser level. Since photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength, the more energetic pump light has the shorter wavelength. The laser light, corresponding to the smaller remaining jump, therefore always has the longer wavelength.

mcqs.q: Why does each element have a different spectrum that acts as its fingerprint?
options: Each element has a different set of allowed energy levels, so the level differences and emitted wavelengths differ
All elements have identical energy levels
Spectra depend only on the container
mcqs.why: Each element has a different number of electrons and a different set of allowed energy levels fixed by its nuclear charge, and since hf equals the difference of two level energies, the wavelengths differ for every element.

mcqs.q: How do X-rays and gamma rays differ mainly in origin?
options: X-rays come from inside the nucleus, gamma rays from outside it
Both are produced only by fast electrons
X-rays are produced outside the nucleus, gamma rays are emitted from inside an unstable nucleus
Neither has any difference in origin
mcqs.why: X-rays are produced outside the nucleus when fast electrons strike a target or inner-shell electrons change levels, while gamma rays are emitted from inside an unstable nucleus falling to a lower energy state after alpha or beta decay.

mcqs.q: Compared with X-rays, gamma rays are generally:
options: Lower in energy and less penetrating
Higher in energy and more penetrating
mcqs.why: Gamma rays are generally of higher energy and are more penetrating than X-rays, although both are high-energy electromagnetic radiations differing mainly in origin.

mcqs.q: Which property makes cracks in bones visible on an X-ray film?
options: Bone transmits X-rays more easily than flesh
Bone absorbs X-rays more strongly than soft tissue, so bones cast darker shadows and a crack shows as a sudden change in absorption
mcqs.why: Bone absorbs X-rays more strongly than flesh and soft tissue, so bones cast darker shadows on the film; where a crack changes the absorption suddenly, the fracture becomes clearly visible.

mcqs.q: The Lyman series, from transitions ending at n = 1, has wavelengths running approximately from:
options: 121.6 nm down to 91.2 nm, all in the ultraviolet
mcqs.why: The Lyman series runs from about 121.6 nm for the 2 to 1 transition down to the series limit of about 91.2 nm, all in the ultraviolet, with frequencies from about 2.47x10^15 Hz to 3.29x10^15 Hz.

mcqs.q: The Balmer series, from transitions ending at n = 2, has wavelengths running approximately from:
options: 656 nm for the 3 to 2 line down to about 365 nm at the series limit
mcqs.why: The Balmer series runs from about 656 nm for the 3 to 2 line down to the series limit of about 365 nm, in the visible and near ultraviolet, with frequencies from about 4.57x10^14 Hz to 8.22x10^14 Hz.

mcqs.q: In spontaneous emission, an excited atom falls to a lower state:
options: Only when triggered by an incoming photon
By itself, emitting a photon in a random direction with random phase
mcqs.why: In spontaneous emission the atom falls by itself without external influence and emits a photon in a random direction with random phase, which is why ordinary lamps give incoherent light.

mcqs.q: In stimulated emission, the second photon emitted is:
options: Identical in frequency, phase and direction to the incoming photon
mcqs.why: Stimulated emission is triggered by an incoming photon of exactly the transition energy, and the emitted second photon is identical in frequency, phase and direction, producing coherent amplified laser light.

mcqs.q: Why is population inversion essential for laser action?
options: It makes atoms fall spontaneously faster
Without it a photon is more likely to be absorbed than to stimulate emission, so no amplification can occur
It removes the need for pumping
mcqs.why: In normal matter most atoms are in the ground state, so absorption beats stimulated emission; inversion keeps more atoms in the upper metastable state so a passing photon stimulates more emission than absorption and the beam grows.

mcqs.q: Why does pumping light always have a shorter wavelength than the laser beam in an optically pumped laser?
options: Pump photons are less energetic than laser photons
The laser light gains energy as heat
Pump photons must carry more energy than the laser transition, and part is lost as heat, so the more energetic pump light has the shorter wavelength
Wavelength is unrelated to photon energy
mcqs.why: Each pump photon must supply at least the full jump to a level above the upper laser level, and part of that energy is lost as heat on dropping to the metastable level; since photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength, the pump light has the shorter wavelength.

lessons.title: The Bohr Model, X-Ray Production and Lasers in Detail
lessons.notes_html:
Postulates of the Bohr Model and the Hydrogen Spectrum Series

Bohr postulated that the electron moves in certain stable circular orbits without radiating energy, that its angular momentum is quantised as mvr = nh / (2 pi), and that a photon is emitted or absorbed only in a jump between orbits, with hf equal to the energy difference. These postulates explain the hydrogen series directly: jumps ending at n = 1 give the Lyman series, at n = 2 the Balmer series, and at n = 3, 4 and 5 the Paschen, Brackett and Pfund series, all from the one formula for En. The model contradicts classical physics because classical theory requires an orbiting, and therefore accelerating, electron to radiate continuously and spiral into the nucleus, which Bohr simply forbade for the allowed orbits. For the energy, the Coulomb force supplies the centripetal force, mv2 / r = e2 / (4 pi epsilon0 r2), and combining this with quantised angular momentum gives KE = +13.6 / n2 eV and PE = -27.2 / n2 eV. Adding them, En = KE + PE = -13.6 / n2 eV, which clearly shows that En is proportional to 1 / n2 and becomes zero at n equal to infinity.

How X-Rays Are Produced: Cooling Fins of the X-Ray Tube

X-rays are produced in an evacuated tube when a beam of fast electrons, accelerated through a high voltage from a heated cathode, is suddenly stopped on striking a metal target such as tungsten set in the anode. Most of the kinetic energy of the electrons becomes heat, but a small fraction is converted into X-ray photons by sudden deceleration and by ejecting inner-shell electrons of the target atoms. The shortest wavelength produced is fixed by the tube voltage through eV = hc / lambda min. Because about 99 percent of the energy appears as heat, the anode would melt without cooling. Cooling fins increase the surface area of the anode and help it lose this heat quickly, often together with oil circulation and a rotating anode, so the tube can work safely for long periods.

X-Rays and the Study of Crystal Structure

The wavelength of X-rays, about 10^-10 m, is of the same order as the spacing between atoms in a crystal, so a crystal acts as a natural three-dimensional diffraction grating for them. The regular planes of atoms reflect the X-rays, and the reflected beams reinforce only at angles satisfying the Bragg condition, giving a diffraction pattern from which the arrangement and spacing of atoms can be calculated. The main properties of X-rays are that they travel in straight lines at the speed of light, are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields, and penetrate matter to a degree depending on its density. They affect photographic film, cause fluorescence, and ionise gases through which they pass. They are also harmful to living cells in large doses, so their use needs proper shielding.

What Is a Laser? Why a Two-Level System Cannot Work

A laser is a device that produces an intense, coherent beam of light by stimulated emission of radiation, the name being short for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. Laser light is monochromatic, highly coherent, highly directional with very little spreading, and very intense compared with ordinary light sources. These properties come from photons that are identical in frequency, phase and direction. A two-level system cannot be used for laser production, because pumping can at best make the two populations equal: as soon as atoms are raised, stimulated emission by the pump light itself sends them down again. Population inversion, the condition needed for net amplification, is therefore impossible in a steady two-level system, and at least three levels with a metastable state are required.

Pumping and Its Methods: Optical Pumping

Pumping is the process by which atoms of the active medium are raised from the ground state to an excited state so that population inversion can be created and maintained. The main methods are optical pumping by a bright light source, electrical pumping by a gas discharge, chemical pumping using the energy of a chemical reaction, and pumping by direct electric current in semiconductor lasers. In optical pumping, used in the ruby laser, a powerful flash tube surrounds the ruby rod and its intense flash is absorbed by chromium atoms in the rod. The atoms rise to a broad upper band, drop quickly without radiation to a metastable level, and collect there. When the metastable level holds more atoms than the lower level, population inversion is achieved and laser action can begin.

Principle, Construction and Working of the Helium-Neon Laser

The principle of the laser is stimulated emission in a medium that has been pumped into population inversion, placed between two mirrors forming an optical resonator so that the light is amplified by repeated passes. A helium-neon laser consists of a long discharge tube filled with helium and neon in the ratio of about 10 to 1, with a fully reflecting mirror at one end and a partly transparent mirror at the other, and electrodes connected to a high voltage supply. An electric discharge excites the helium atoms, which collide with neon atoms and transfer energy to them because their excited levels nearly coincide, producing population inversion in neon. Neon atoms then emit red laser light of wavelength 632.8 nm by stimulated emission. The mirrors reflect the light back and forth for further amplification, and a small part escapes through the partial mirror as the laser beam.

Properties of Lasers and Their Uses in Medicine, Defence and Communication

Laser light is monochromatic, coherent, highly directional and very intense, and it can be focused to an extremely small spot of very high energy density. It can also be produced in very short pulses and travels without appreciable spreading over long distances. In medicine lasers are used in eye surgery, in removing tumours, in dentistry and as a bloodless scalpel that cuts and seals tissue at the same time. In defence they are used for range finding, target marking, guidance of weapons and measurement of distances. In communication they carry information through optical fibres, where their high frequency allows a very large number of signals to be sent at the same time.

Wave Number and the Rydberg Formula

The wave number of radiation is the number of waves contained in unit length, equal to 1 / lambda, and it is directly proportional to the frequency and energy of the photon. In the Bohr model the energy of level n is En = -RH hc / n2, where RH is the Rydberg constant for hydrogen. When an electron jumps from a higher level n to a lower level p, the photon emitted has energy hf = RH hc (1 / p2 - 1 / n2). Dividing both sides by hc and using f / c = 1 / lambda gives 1 / lambda = RH (1 / p2 - 1 / n2), with RH = 1.097x10^7 per metre. Setting p = 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 in this one expression gives the Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett and Pfund series respectively.

Deriving the Bohr Radius and the Radii of Quantised Orbits

For an electron of mass m and charge -e moving in a circle of radius r around the proton, the Coulomb attraction provides the centripetal force, so mv2 / r = e2 / (4 pi epsilon0 r2). Bohr quantisation of angular momentum gives mvr = nh / (2 pi), from which v = nh / (2 pi m r). Substituting this value of v in the force equation and simplifying removes v and leaves r = epsilon0 n2 h2 / (pi m e2). For the first orbit, n = 1, this gives the Bohr radius r0 = 5.29x10^-11 m = 0.53 angstrom. The general relation is therefore r n = r0 n2, showing that the allowed radii increase as the square of the principal quantum number, as 1, 4, 9, 16 and so on.

mcqs.q: According to Bohr's postulate, the angular momentum of the electron in an allowed orbit is quantised as:
mcqs.why: Bohr postulated mvr = nh/(2 pi), together with stable non-radiating orbits and photon emission or absorption only in jumps between orbits with hf equal to the energy difference.

mcqs.q: Transitions ending at n = 1, n = 2 and n = 3 give, respectively, the:
mcqs.why: Jumps ending at n = 1 give the Lyman series, at n = 2 the Balmer series, and at n = 3, 4 and 5 the Paschen, Brackett and Pfund series, all from the one formula for En.

mcqs.q: The total energies of hydrogen levels n = 1, n = 2 and n = 3 are respectively:
mcqs.why: En = -13.6/n^2 eV gives E1 = -13.6/1 = -13.6 eV, E2 = -13.6/4 = -3.4 eV and E3 = -13.6/9 = -1.51 eV, so En is proportional to 1/n^2 and becomes zero at n = infinity.

mcqs.q: How does the Bohr model contradict classical physics?
options: Classical theory requires an accelerating orbiting electron to radiate continuously and spiral into the nucleus, which Bohr forbade for allowed orbits
mcqs.why: Classical physics requires an orbiting, therefore accelerating, electron to radiate continuously and spiral into the nucleus; Bohr simply postulated that electrons in allowed orbits do not radiate.

mcqs.q: In X-ray production, about what fraction of the electrons' kinetic energy appears as heat in the target?
mcqs.why: About 99 percent of the kinetic energy becomes heat and only a small fraction becomes X-ray photons, so without cooling the anode would melt during long operation.

mcqs.q: The shortest wavelength produced by an X-ray tube is fixed by the tube voltage V through:
mcqs.why: The relation is eV = hc/lambda(min): the full kinetic energy eV of the fastest electron sets the maximum photon energy hc/lambda(min) and hence the shortest wavelength.

mcqs.q: What is the purpose of cooling fins on the anode of an X-ray tube?
options: To increase the surface area so the anode loses heat quickly
mcqs.why: Cooling fins increase the surface area of the anode and help it lose heat quickly, often together with oil circulation and a rotating anode, so the tube can work safely for long periods.

mcqs.q: Why can X-rays be used to study crystal structure?
options: They are deflected by crystal atoms
Their wavelength, about 10^-10 m, is of the same order as the spacing between atoms in a crystal, so the crystal acts as a diffraction grating
mcqs.why: X-rays have wavelength about 10^-10 m, the same order as interatomic spacing, so a crystal acts as a natural three-dimensional diffraction grating and the Bragg diffraction pattern reveals the arrangement and spacing of atoms.

mcqs.q: The word LASER is short for:
options: Light Absorption by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Light Amplification by Spontaneous Emission of Radiation
Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Light Attenuation by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
mcqs.why: LASER stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation, because the device produces an intense coherent beam by stimulated emission.

mcqs.q: Which set correctly lists methods of pumping?
options: Optical, electrical, chemical and direct-current pumping in semiconductor lasers
mcqs.why: Pumping raises atoms of the active medium to an excited state, and the main methods are optical pumping by bright light, electrical pumping by gas discharge, chemical pumping, and direct electric current in semiconductor lasers.

mcqs.q: In the helium-neon laser, the helium and neon are mixed in the ratio of about:
mcqs.why: The helium-neon tube is filled with helium and neon in the ratio of about 10 to 1; discharge-excited helium atoms collide with neon atoms and transfer energy to them, producing population inversion in neon.

mcqs.q: Neon atoms in a helium-neon laser emit red laser light of wavelength:
mcqs.why: Neon atoms emit red laser light of wavelength 632.8 nm by stimulated emission; the mirrors reflect the light back and forth for amplification and a small part escapes through the partial mirror as the beam.

mcqs.q: The wave number of radiation is defined as:
options: 1/lambda, the number of waves in unit length
mcqs.why: Wave number equals 1/lambda, the number of waves contained in unit length, and it is directly proportional to the frequency and energy of the photon.

mcqs.q: In the Rydberg formula 1/lambda = RH (1/p^2 - 1/n^2), the Rydberg constant RH for hydrogen is:
mcqs.why: RH = 1.097x10^7 per metre; the formula follows from hf = RH hc (1/p^2 - 1/n^2) on dividing by hc, and p = 1 to 5 gives the Lyman through Pfund series.

mcqs.q: The Bohr radius, the radius of the first orbit of hydrogen, is:
mcqs.why: Combining mv^2/r = e^2/(4 pi epsilon0 r^2) with mvr = nh/(2 pi) gives r = epsilon0 n^2 h^2/(pi m e^2), and for n = 1 this is r0 = 5.29x10^-11 m = 0.53 angstrom, with radii growing as 1, 4, 9, 16.

lessons.title: Worked Examples
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example 1

In the Bohr model, how many times larger is the radius of the fifth Bohr orbit compared to that of the first Bohr orbit?

Step 1: Given: orbit numbers n = 5 and n = 1, radius of first orbit r1 = r0

Step 2: Formula: the radius of the nth orbit is r n = r0 multiplied by n2

Step 3: Substitution: r5 = r0 x 25 and r1 = r0 x 1

Step 4: Calculation: ratio r5 / r1 = 25 / 1 = 25

The fifth Bohr orbit has 25 times the radius of the first orbit.

Worked Example 2

What is the energy of a photon that, when absorbed by a hydrogen atom, could cause an electronic transition from (a) the n = 3 state to the n = 5 state and (b) the n = 5 state to the n = 8 state?

Step 1: Given: ground state energy of hydrogen E1 = -13.6 eV, and the energy of level n is En = -13.6 / n2 eV

Step 2: Formula: photon energy needed = E higher - E lower = 13.6 x (1 / n lower2 - 1 / n higher2) eV

Step 3: Substitution for part (a): E = 13.6 x (1 / 9 - 1 / 25) = 13.6 x 0.0711

Step 4: Calculation for part (a): E = 0.97 eV

Step 5: Substitution for part (b): E = 13.6 x (1 / 25 - 1 / 64) = 13.6 x 0.0244

Step 6: Calculation and Result: E = 0.33 eV, so photons of about 0.97 eV and 0.33 eV respectively can produce the two transitions, and both lie in the infrared region.

Worked Example 3

A hydrogen atom is in its first excited state (n = 2). Calculate (a) the kinetic energy of the electron, (b) the potential energy of the system, and (c) the total energy of the system.

Step 1: Given: level n = 2, and for hydrogen the total energy is En = -13.6 / n2 eV

Step 2: Formula: total energy E2 = -13.6 / 4, kinetic energy KE = -E total, and potential energy PE = 2 x E total

Step 3: Substitution: E2 = -13.6 / 4 = -3.4 eV

Step 4: Calculation: KE = -(-3.4) = +3.4 eV, and PE = 2 x (-3.4) = -6.8 eV

Step 5: Check: KE + PE = 3.4 - 6.8 = -3.4 eV, which equals the total energy

For n = 2 the kinetic energy is 3.4 eV, the potential energy is -6.8 eV and the total energy is -3.4 eV.

Worked Example 4

Calculate the energy of an electron in the n = 2 orbit of a hydrogen atom according to the Bohr model.

Step 1: Given: orbit number n = 2, ground state energy of hydrogen E1 = -13.6 eV = -2.176x10^-18 J, and 1 eV = 1.602x10^-19 J

Step 2: Formula: energy of the nth orbit, En = E1 / n2

Step 3: Substitution: E2 = -13.6 / 4 eV = -3.40 eV

Step 4: Calculation in joule: E2 = -3.40 x 1.602x10^-19 = -5.447x10^-19 J

The energy of the electron in the n = 2 orbit is -5.447x10^-19 J, the negative sign showing that the electron is bound to the nucleus.

Worked Example 5

Calculate the speed of the electron if it orbits in (a) the smallest allowed orbit and (b) the second smallest orbit? (c) If the electron moves to larger orbits, does its speed increase, decrease, or stay the same?

Step 1: Given: the speed in the first Bohr orbit is v1 = 2.19x10^6 m/s, and speed varies as v n = v1 / n

Step 2: Formula: v n = (2.19x10^6 / n) m/s for the nth orbit of hydrogen

Step 3: Substitution for part (a): for the smallest orbit n = 1, v1 = 2.19x10^6 / 1 = 2.19x10^6 m/s

Step 4: Substitution for part (b): for the second orbit n = 2, v2 = 2.19x10^6 / 2 = 1.09x10^6 m/s

Step 5: Reasoning for part (c): speed is inversely proportional to n, so as n increases for larger orbits the speed falls

The speeds are 2.19x10^6 m/s in the first orbit and 1.09x10^6 m/s in the second orbit, and the speed decreases as the electron moves to larger orbits.

Worked Example 6

What are the (a) energy, (b) magnitude of the momentum, and (c) wavelength of the photon emitted when a hydrogen atom undergoes a transition from a state with n = 3 to a state with n = 1?

Step 1: Given: initial level ni = 3, final level nf = 1, E1 = -13.6 eV, h = 6.63x10^-34 J s, c = 3x10^8 m/s

Step 2: Formula: photon energy E = 13.6 x (1 / nf2 - 1 / ni2) eV, momentum p = E / c, and wavelength lambda = hc / E

Step 3: Substitution: E = 13.6 x (1 / 1 - 1 / 9) = 13.6 x 8 / 9

Step 4: Calculation of energy: E = 12.1 eV = 12.1 x 1.602x10^-19 = 1.938x10^-18 J

Step 5: Calculation of momentum: p = 1.938x10^-18 / 3x10^8 = 6.45x10^-27 N s

Step 6: Calculation of wavelength: lambda = (6.63x10^-34 x 3x10^8) / 1.938x10^-18 = 1.026x10^-7 m = 102.6 nm

The emitted photon has energy 12.1 eV, momentum 6.45x10^-27 N s and wavelength about 102 nm, in the Lyman series.

Worked Example 7

What is the energy of the photon emitted by hydrogen atom when the hydrogen atom changes directly from the n = 5 state to the n = 2 state?

Step 1: Given: initial level ni = 5, final level nf = 2, E1 = -13.6 eV

Step 2: Formula: photon energy E = 13.6 x (1 / nf2 - 1 / ni2) eV

Step 3: Substitution: E = 13.6 x (1 / 4 - 1 / 25) = 13.6 x (0.25 - 0.04)

Step 4: Calculation: E = 13.6 x 0.21 = 2.856 eV

The photon emitted in the direct 5 to 2 transition has an energy of about 2.85 eV and belongs to the Balmer series.

Worked Example 8

How much work must be done to pull apart the electron and the proton that make up the hydrogen atom if the atom is initially in (a) its ground state and (b) the state with n = 3?

Step 1: Given: the total energy of the atom in level n is En = -13.6 / n2 eV, and to free the electron its total energy must be raised to zero

Step 2: Formula: work required W = 0 - En = +13.6 / n2 eV, which is the ionisation energy from that level

Step 3: Substitution for part (a): for the ground state n = 1, W = 13.6 / 1 = 13.6 eV

Step 4: Substitution for part (b): for n = 3, W = 13.6 / 9 = 1.51 eV

Work of 13.6 eV is needed from the ground state, but only 1.51 eV from the n = 3 state, because the electron is already less tightly bound there.

Worked Example 9

(a) What is the wavelength of light for the least energetic photon emitted in the Balmer series of the hydrogen atom spectrum lines? (b) What is the wavelength of the series limit?

Step 1: Given: the Balmer series ends at nf = 2; the least energetic photon comes from the smallest jump, ni = 3 to nf = 2, and the series limit comes from ni = infinity to nf = 2

Step 2: Formula: E = 13.6 x (1 / nf2 - 1 / ni2) eV and lambda = hc / E, with hc = 1240 eV nm

Step 3: Substitution for part (a): E = 13.6 x (1 / 4 - 1 / 9) = 13.6 x 0.1389 = 1.89 eV

Step 4: Calculation for part (a): lambda = 1240 / 1.89 = 656 nm, about 659 nm as printed in the book

Step 5: Substitution for part (b): at the limit E = 13.6 x (1 / 4 - 0) = 3.40 eV

Step 6: Calculation for part (b): lambda = 1240 / 3.40 = 365 nm, about 366 nm

The least energetic Balmer photon has wavelength about 659 nm (red light) and the Balmer series limit is about 366 nm.

Worked Example 10

A laser emits light with a wavelength of 632.8 nm and has a power output of 55 mW. Calculate the energy of one photon emitted by this laser.

Step 1: Given: wavelength lambda = 632.8 nm = 632.8x10^-9 m, h = 6.63x10^-34 J s, c = 3x10^8 m/s, E = ?

Step 2: Formula: energy of one photon, E = hc / lambda; the power output is not needed for the energy of a single photon

Step 3: Substitution: E = (6.63x10^-34 x 3x10^8) / 632.8x10^-9

Step 4: Calculation: numerator = 1.989x10^-25, so E = 1.989x10^-25 / 6.328x10^-7 = 3.14x10^-19 J

Each photon of the helium-neon laser light carries an energy of 3.14x10^-19 J, about 1.96 eV.

Worked Example 11

Calculate the wavelength of X-rays if the energy of one photon emitted by the X-ray machine is 1.9878x10^-15 joules.

Step 1: Given: photon energy E = 1.9878x10^-15 J, h = 6.63x10^-34 J s, c = 3x10^8 m/s, lambda = ?

Step 2: Formula: E = hc / lambda, rearranged as lambda = hc / E

Step 3: Substitution: lambda = (6.63x10^-34 x 3x10^8) / 1.9878x10^-15

Step 4: Calculation: numerator = 1.989x10^-25, so lambda = 1.989x10^-25 / 1.9878x10^-15 = 1.0x10^-10 m

The wavelength of the X-rays is 1.0x10^-10 m, that is 0.1 nm, typical of X-rays used in diffraction and medical work.

mcqs.q: How many times larger is the radius of the fifth Bohr orbit than that of the first orbit?
mcqs.why: r(n) = r0 n^2, so r5/r1 = 25/1 = 25; the fifth Bohr orbit has 25 times the radius of the first orbit.

mcqs.q: What photon energy is needed to raise hydrogen from n = 3 to n = 5?
mcqs.why: E = 13.6 x (1/9 - 1/25) = 13.6 x 0.0711 = 0.97 eV, so a photon of about 0.97 eV in the infrared can produce the n = 3 to n = 5 transition.

mcqs.q: What photon energy is needed to raise hydrogen from n = 5 to n = 8?
mcqs.why: E = 13.6 x (1/25 - 1/64) = 13.6 x 0.0244 = 0.33 eV, so a photon of about 0.33 eV can produce the n = 5 to n = 8 transition.

mcqs.q: For hydrogen in the first excited state n = 2, the kinetic and potential energies are respectively:
mcqs.why: E2 = -13.6/4 = -3.4 eV; KE = -E(total) = +3.4 eV and PE = 2 x E(total) = -6.8 eV, and the check KE + PE = 3.4 - 6.8 = -3.4 eV confirms the total energy.

mcqs.q: The energy of an electron in the n = 2 orbit of hydrogen, expressed in joules, is:
mcqs.why: E2 = -13.6/4 = -3.40 eV, and converting with 1 eV = 1.602x10^-19 J gives E2 = -3.40 x 1.602x10^-19 = -5.447x10^-19 J, the negative sign showing the electron is bound.

mcqs.q: The speed of the electron in the second Bohr orbit, given v1 = 2.19x10^6 m/s and v(n) = v1/n, is:
options: 1.09x10^6 m/s, and speed decreases in larger orbits
mcqs.why: v2 = 2.19x10^6 / 2 = 1.09x10^6 m/s; since speed is inversely proportional to n, the speed decreases as the electron moves to larger orbits.

mcqs.q: What is the energy of the photon emitted when hydrogen falls from n = 3 to n = 1?
mcqs.why: E = 13.6 x (1/1 - 1/9) = 13.6 x 8/9 = 12.1 eV = 1.938x10^-18 J, so the n = 3 to n = 1 transition emits a photon of 12.1 eV in the Lyman series.

mcqs.q: For the n = 3 to n = 1 photon of energy 1.938x10^-18 J, the magnitude of its momentum p = E/c is:
mcqs.why: p = E/c = 1.938x10^-18 / 3x10^8 = 6.45x10^-27 N s, which is the momentum magnitude of the photon emitted in the n = 3 to n = 1 transition.

mcqs.q: The wavelength of the photon emitted in the n = 3 to n = 1 transition is about:
mcqs.why: lambda = hc/E = (6.63x10^-34 x 3x10^8) / 1.938x10^-18 = 1.026x10^-7 m = 102.6 nm, about 102 nm, in the Lyman series.

mcqs.q: What is the energy of the photon emitted when hydrogen changes directly from n = 5 to n = 2?
mcqs.why: E = 13.6 x (1/4 - 1/25) = 13.6 x 0.21 = 2.856 eV, about 2.85 eV, and this direct 5 to 2 transition belongs to the Balmer series.

mcqs.q: How much work is needed to free the electron from hydrogen in its ground state and from n = 3, respectively?
mcqs.why: W = 0 - En = +13.6/n^2 eV, so from the ground state W = 13.6/1 = 13.6 eV and from n = 3, W = 13.6/9 = 1.51 eV, because the electron is less tightly bound at n = 3.

mcqs.q: The least energetic photon in the Balmer series comes from n = 3 to n = 2. Its wavelength is about:
options: 656 nm (about 659 nm as printed in the book)
mcqs.why: E = 13.6 x (1/4 - 1/9) = 1.89 eV and lambda = hc/E = 1240/1.89 = 656 nm, about 659 nm as printed in the book, which is red light.

mcqs.q: The wavelength of the Balmer series limit, from n = infinity to n = 2, is about:
mcqs.why: At the limit E = 13.6 x (1/4 - 0) = 3.40 eV and lambda = 1240/3.40 = 365 nm, about 366 nm, which is the Balmer series limit.

mcqs.q: A helium-neon laser emits light of wavelength 632.8 nm. The energy of one photon, E = hc/lambda, is:
mcqs.why: E = (6.63x10^-34 x 3x10^8) / 632.8x10^-9 = 1.989x10^-25 / 6.328x10^-7 = 3.14x10^-19 J, about 1.96 eV; the 55 mW power output is not needed for one photon.

mcqs.q: If an X-ray photon has energy 1.9878x10^-15 J, its wavelength lambda = hc/E is:
mcqs.why: lambda = (6.63x10^-34 x 3x10^8) / 1.9878x10^-15 = 1.989x10^-25 / 1.9878x10^-15 = 1.0x10^-10 m = 0.1 nm, typical of X-rays used in diffraction and medical work.

lessons.title: Radioactivity, Half-Life and Binding Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Balancing Nuclear Reactions

Balancing the reaction, the mass numbers give 9 + 4 = 12 + A, so A = 1, and the atomic numbers give 4 + 2 = 6 + Z, so Z = 0. The particle with mass number 1 and no charge is a neutron. This is in fact the historic reaction in which Chadwick discovered the neutron.

Mass numbers must balance: 27 + 4 = 30 + A, so A = 1, and atomic numbers must balance: 13 + 2 = 15 + Z, so Z = 0. The emitted particle X is therefore a neutron with A = 1 and Z = 0. This was the first artificially induced nuclear reaction in which a radioactive isotope, phosphorus-30, was produced.

Beta Decay and Half-Life

Beta rays are fast electrons, or in beta-plus decay positrons, that are created inside the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton, or a proton changes into a neutron. They are therefore charged particles emitted by the nucleus itself. They are not the orbital electrons of the atom, and unlike gamma rays they are not electromagnetic radiation.

Each alpha emission lowers the mass number by 4, and the mass number falls by 200 - 168 = 32, so the number of alpha particles is 32 / 4 = 8. These 8 alpha emissions would lower Z by 16, from 90 to 74, but the final Z is 80, so 6 beta-minus emissions, each raising Z by 1, must also have occurred. The decay therefore emits 8 alpha particles and 6 beta particles.

Ten years is two half-lives, so the fraction of nuclei surviving is (1/2) x (1/2) = 1/4, that is 25 percent. The fraction that decays is therefore 100 - 25 = 75 percent. For a single nucleus this surviving fraction is read as a probability, so the probability that it decays within ten years is 75 percent.

In beta decay a neutron inside the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron, and the electron is emitted as the beta particle. The total number of nucleons, protons plus neutrons, does not change, so the mass number A remains the same. Only the atomic number Z changes, increasing by 1 in beta-minus decay, so a new element is formed.

In beta-plus decay a proton inside the nucleus changes into a neutron and a positron, and the positron is emitted. The number of protons therefore falls by one, so the atomic number Z decreases by 1, while the mass number stays unchanged. The daughter nucleus is an isotope of the element one place lower in the periodic table.

Four hundred days contains 400 / 100 = 4 half-lives, so the mass is halved four times: 16 g becomes 8 g, then 4 g, then 2 g and finally 1 g. In formula form the remaining mass is 16 x (1/2)^4 = 16 / 16 = 1 g. The rest of the material has been transformed into the decay products.

Binding Energy and the Nuclear Reactor

The binding energy per nucleon rises rapidly for light nuclei, reaches a maximum of about 8.8 MeV near iron with A about 56, and then falls slowly for heavier nuclei. This curve explains why energy is released both when light nuclei fuse and when very heavy nuclei undergo fission. It also shows that nuclei near the peak of the curve are the most stable.

Neutrons produced in fission are fast, and slow or thermal neutrons are far more likely to be captured by uranium-235 nuclei and cause further fission. A moderator such as ordinary water, heavy water or graphite slows the neutrons by repeated collisions without absorbing many of them. This keeps the chain reaction going steadily in the reactor core.

mcqs.q: In Be-9 (Z=4) + He-4 (Z=2) -> C-12 (Z=6) + x, balancing A: 9+4=12+A and Z: 4+2=6+Z gives particle x as:
options: A neutron with A = 1 and Z = 0
mcqs.why: Mass numbers give A = 13 - 12 = 1 and atomic numbers give Z = 6 - 6 = 0, so x is a neutron; this is the historic reaction in which Chadwick discovered the neutron.

mcqs.q: In Al-27 (Z=13) + He-4 (Z=2) -> P-30 (Z=15) + X, the emitted particle X is:
mcqs.why: Mass numbers give 27 + 4 = 30 + A so A = 1, and atomic numbers give 13 + 2 = 15 + Z so Z = 0; X is therefore a neutron, and phosphorus-30 was the first artificially produced radioactive isotope in this reaction.

mcqs.q: Beta rays emitted by a radioactive material are best described as:
options: Charged particles emitted by the nucleus itself
mcqs.why: Beta rays are fast electrons, or positrons in beta-plus decay, created inside the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton or vice versa; they are charged particles from the nucleus, not orbital electrons and not electromagnetic radiation.

mcqs.q: In the decay X-200 (Z=90) -> Y-168 (Z=80), the numbers of alpha and beta-minus particles emitted are:
mcqs.why: A falls by 32, so alpha particles = 32/4 = 8; these would lower Z by 16 to 74, but the final Z is 80, so 6 beta-minus emissions, each raising Z by 1, must also have occurred.

mcqs.q: A substance has half-life 5 years. For one nucleus, the probability of decaying within 10 years is:
mcqs.why: Ten years is two half-lives, so the surviving fraction is (1/2)x(1/2) = 1/4 = 25 percent; the decayed fraction, read as the probability for a single nucleus, is 100 - 25 = 75 percent.

mcqs.q: Emission of a beta-minus particle affects the mass number A of an element by:
options: Leaving A unchanged while Z increases by 1
mcqs.why: In beta-minus decay a neutron changes into a proton and an electron, so the total number of nucleons is unchanged and A stays the same, while Z increases by 1 and a new element is formed.

mcqs.q: Emission of a beta-plus particle affects the atomic number Z of an element by:
options: Decreasing Z by 1 while A stays unchanged
mcqs.why: In beta-plus decay a proton changes into a neutron and a positron, so the number of protons falls by one: Z decreases by 1 while the mass number A stays unchanged.

mcqs.q: An element has half-life 100 days. After 400 days, 16 g of it will be reduced to:
mcqs.why: 400 days contains 400/100 = 4 half-lives, so 16 g halves four times: 8 g, 4 g, 2 g, 1 g; in formula form 16 x (1/2)^4 = 16/16 = 1 g.

mcqs.q: The binding energy per nucleon is maximum, about 8.8 MeV, near:
mcqs.why: Binding energy per nucleon rises rapidly for light nuclei, reaches a maximum of about 8.8 MeV near iron with A about 56, then falls slowly, which is why both fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei release energy.

mcqs.q: A moderator in a nuclear reactor slows down neutrons in order to:
options: Increase the probability of nuclear fission by uranium-235
mcqs.why: Slow or thermal neutrons are far more likely to be captured by uranium-235 and cause further fission; moderators such as water, heavy water or graphite slow neutrons by repeated collisions without absorbing many of them.

lessons.title: The Nucleus, Radioactive Decay and Reactors
lessons.notes_html:
Why Protons and Neutrons Are Both Needed for a Stable Nucleus

Protons repel one another strongly because they all carry positive charge, so a nucleus of protons alone would fly apart at once. Neutrons carry no charge but attract both protons and neutrons through the strong nuclear force, which acts over the very short range inside the nucleus. By adding attraction without adding repulsion, and by keeping the protons slightly farther apart, neutrons hold the nucleus together. A suitable balance of protons and neutrons is therefore necessary, and nuclei with a badly unbalanced ratio are unstable and radioactive.

Isotopes and Why Their Differences Matter

Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons and electrons but different numbers of neutrons, so they have the same atomic number Z but different mass numbers A. Their chemical properties are almost identical, because chemistry depends on the electrons, but their nuclear properties differ greatly: some isotopes are stable while others are radioactive with different half-lives. These differences are significant because radioactive isotopes are used as tracers in medicine and industry, in radiotherapy, and in dating old materials, while the heavy isotope uranium-235, unlike uranium-238, can sustain a fission chain reaction.

Two Methods of Controlling a Chain Reaction

The first method is the use of control rods made of a neutron-absorbing material such as boron or cadmium, which are pushed into or pulled out of the reactor core to absorb more or fewer neutrons and so control the rate of fission.
