The second method is the use of a moderator, such as ordinary water, heavy water or graphite, which controls the speed of the neutrons and hence the probability that they will cause further fission. Together these methods keep the multiplication factor at exactly one for steady working. In an emergency the control and safety rods are dropped fully in to stop the reaction quickly.

Why Nuclear Decay Is Spontaneous and Random

Nuclear decay is called spontaneous because it happens by itself, without any external cause, and it is not affected by temperature, pressure or chemical state of the material. It is called random because it is impossible to predict which particular nucleus will decay next or exactly when any one nucleus will decay. We can only state the probability that a nucleus decays in a given time, expressed through the decay constant and the half-life. For a very large number of nuclei this probability gives the accurate average behaviour described by the decay law.

What Happens During Nuclear Fusion

In nuclear fusion two light nuclei, such as hydrogen isotopes, come so close together that the strong nuclear force joins them into a single heavier nucleus. To overcome the repulsion between their positive charges the nuclei must move at very high speed, which needs temperatures of millions of kelvin as in the interior of the Sun. Because the product nucleus has a smaller mass than the two original nuclei together, the mass lost appears as energy according to E = mc2. Fusion of hydrogen into helium is the source of energy of the Sun and the stars, and of the hydrogen bomb.

Activity and Decay Constant

The activity of a sample is the number of nuclei decaying per second, and it is directly proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei N present at that time. The constant of proportionality is the decay constant lambda, so activity A = lambda N, measured in becquerel. The decay constant is the probability that one nucleus decays in one second, so a large lambda means a rapidly decaying, short-lived material. As N decreases with time, the activity decreases in the same exponential way, A = A0 e raised to -lambda t.

Binding Energy and Binding Energy per Nucleon

The binding energy of a nucleus is the energy that must be supplied to break the nucleus completely into its separate protons and neutrons, and it equals the mass defect of the nucleus multiplied by c2. It is a measure of how strongly the nucleus is held together by the nuclear force. The binding energy per nucleon is this total binding energy divided by the mass number A. It tells the average energy needed to remove one nucleon, and the higher its value, the more stable the nucleus; it is maximum, about 8.8 MeV, near iron.

Why Half-Life Is Important

Half-life gives a simple and fixed measure of how fast a radioactive substance decays: it is the time in which half of the nuclei present, and hence half of the activity, disappear. It allows us to calculate how much of a sample will remain after any time and how active a source will be when it is used. Choosing an isotope with a suitable half-life is essential in medicine, where the source must work long enough for treatment but not remain active in the body for too long. Half-life is also the basis of radioactive dating, for example carbon-14 dating of fossils.

Positron Emission

Positron emission, or beta-plus decay, occurs in nuclei that have too many protons compared with neutrons. A proton inside the nucleus changes into a neutron, a positron and a neutrino, and the positron and neutrino are emitted from the nucleus. As a result the atomic number Z decreases by 1 while the mass number A stays the same, and the nucleus moves towards stability. The emitted positron soon meets an ordinary electron and the two annihilate, producing two gamma ray photons of 0.51 MeV each, which is the effect used in PET scanning in medicine.

mcqs.q: Why are neutrons needed together with protons for a stable nucleus?
options: Neutrons add strong-force attraction without adding electric repulsion and keep protons slightly farther apart
mcqs.why: Protons alone would fly apart through mutual repulsion; neutrons carry no charge but attract protons and neutrons through the short-range strong force, adding attraction without repulsion and holding the nucleus together.

mcqs.q: Isotopes of an element have:
options: The same atomic number Z but different mass numbers A, with almost identical chemical properties
The same mass number but different atomic numbers
mcqs.why: Isotopes have the same number of protons and electrons but different numbers of neutrons, so Z is the same and A differs; chemistry, which depends on electrons, is almost identical while nuclear properties differ greatly.

mcqs.q: Control rods used to control a chain reaction are made of neutron-absorbing material such as:
mcqs.why: Control rods of boron or cadmium are pushed into or pulled out of the core to absorb more or fewer neutrons and control the fission rate, keeping the multiplication factor at exactly one for steady working.

mcqs.q: Nuclear decay is called spontaneous because it:
options: Happens by itself without external cause and is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state
Can be predicted exactly for each nucleus
mcqs.why: Decay is spontaneous because it happens by itself with no external cause and is not affected by temperature, pressure or chemical state; it is random because which nucleus decays next cannot be predicted, only the probability can be stated.

mcqs.q: During nuclear fusion, energy is released because:
options: The product nucleus has greater mass than the reactants
The product nucleus has smaller mass than the two original nuclei together, and the lost mass appears as energy E = mc^2
mcqs.why: In fusion two light nuclei join into a heavier nucleus whose mass is less than the sum of the original masses; the mass lost appears as energy according to E = mc^2, as in hydrogen fusing to helium in the Sun.

mcqs.q: The activity A of a radioactive sample is related to the number of undecayed nuclei N by:
options: A = lambda N, measured in becquerel
mcqs.why: Activity is the number of decays per second and is directly proportional to N, with A = lambda N in becquerel; lambda is the probability that one nucleus decays in one second, so a large lambda means a short-lived material.

mcqs.q: The binding energy of a nucleus equals:
options: Its mass defect multiplied by c^2, the energy needed to break it into separate protons and neutrons
mcqs.why: Binding energy is the energy that must be supplied to break the nucleus completely into separate protons and neutrons, and it equals the mass defect multiplied by c^2; per nucleon it is maximum, about 8.8 MeV, near iron.

mcqs.q: Why is the concept of half-life important?
options: It gives the exact decay time of one nucleus
It lets us calculate how much sample and activity remain after any time, choose medical isotopes and date old materials
It applies only to stable isotopes
mcqs.why: Half-life is the fixed time in which half the nuclei and half the activity disappear; it allows remaining amounts to be calculated, suitable half-lives to be chosen in medicine, and radioactive dating such as carbon-14 dating of fossils.

mcqs.q: In positron emission, a proton inside the nucleus changes into:
options: A neutron only, so A decreases by 1
A neutron, a positron and a neutrino, so Z decreases by 1 and A stays the same
mcqs.why: In beta-plus decay a proton changes into a neutron, a positron and a neutrino; Z decreases by 1 while A stays the same, and the emitted positron later annihilates with an electron producing two gamma photons of 0.51 MeV each, used in PET scanning.

mcqs.q: Which statement about isotopes is significant for applications?
options: Radioactive isotopes are used as tracers, in radiotherapy and in dating, and uranium-235 unlike uranium-238 can sustain a fission chain reaction
Uranium-238 sustains fission better than uranium-235
mcqs.why: Radioactive isotopes are used as tracers in medicine and industry, in radiotherapy and in dating old materials, while uranium-235, unlike uranium-238, can sustain a fission chain reaction, showing why isotopic differences matter.

lessons.title: Radioactive Decay, Fission and Fusion
lessons.notes_html:
Radioactivity and the Law of Radioactive Disintegration

Radioactivity is the spontaneous disintegration of an unstable nucleus with the emission of alpha, beta or gamma radiation, forming a new element. The law of radioactive disintegration states that the rate at which nuclei disintegrate at any instant is directly proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present at that instant, that is -dN / dt = lambda N, where lambda is the decay constant. Integrating this relation from N0 nuclei at t = 0 to N at time t gives ln (N / N0) = -lambda t, or N = N0 e raised to -lambda t. Because N contains the exponential factor e raised to -lambda t, the number of nuclei, and with it the activity, falls exponentially and never quite reaches zero. Putting N = N0 / 2 gives the half-life T half = 0.693 / lambda, which is constant for a given substance.

Alpha, Beta and Gamma Emissions Compared

Alpha emission is the loss of a helium nucleus, with A = 4 and Z = 2, from a heavy nucleus; it decreases A by 4 and Z by 2, has a range of only a few centimetres in air, is stopped by paper, and is strongly ionising. Beta emission is the loss of a fast electron or positron created inside the nucleus; it leaves A unchanged but changes Z by 1, travels up to a few metres in air, is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium, and is moderately ionising. Gamma emission is electromagnetic radiation of very short wavelength emitted when an excited nucleus falls to a lower energy state; it changes neither A nor Z, travels at the speed of light with a long range, is stopped only by thick lead, and is weakly ionising but highly penetrating. Alpha and beta particles are deflected by electric and magnetic fields in opposite senses appropriate to their charges, while gamma rays are not deflected at all.

How a Fission Reactor Produces Energy

In the reactor core, a slow neutron striking a uranium-235 nucleus makes it unstable, and it splits into two lighter nuclei of comparable mass, called fission fragments, together with two or three fresh neutrons and a large amount of energy, about 200 MeV per fission. The mass of the products is slightly less than the original mass, and this mass defect appears mainly as the kinetic energy of the fragments and neutrons. Collisions of these particles inside the fuel rods convert the kinetic energy into heat. This heat is carried away by a coolant to a heat exchanger, where it raises steam that drives a turbine and generator in the usual way. Control rods and a moderator keep the chain reaction steady at the required power level.

Q-Value of a Nuclear Reaction

The Q-value of a nuclear reaction is the net energy released in the reaction, equal to the total kinetic energy of the products minus the total kinetic energy of the reacting particles. By the mass-energy relation it is also Q = (total mass of reactants - total mass of products) multiplied by c2, expressed in MeV when masses are in atomic mass units using 1 u = 931.5 MeV. A positive Q means the reaction is exothermic and releases energy, while a negative Q means the reaction is endothermic and can occur only if the incoming particles bring at least that much kinetic energy. The Q-value therefore tells us whether a proposed reaction can supply energy, as in reactors and stars, and how much energy each reaction will give.

Construction and Working of the GM Counter

A Geiger-Muller counter consists of a metal tube acting as the cathode, filled with a low-pressure gas such as argon with a small amount of a quenching vapour, and a fine wire along its axis acting as the anode. A potential difference of about 400 to 500 V, just below the breakdown voltage, is applied between the wire and the tube, and radiation enters through a thin mica window at one end. When an ionising particle enters, it ionises some gas atoms; the electrons produced rush towards the wire and, in the strong field near it, ionise many more atoms by collision, causing an avalanche and a sudden pulse of current. This pulse is amplified, counted by a scaler and can also produce a click in a loudspeaker, so the counter records the number of ionising events per unit time. The quenching vapour prevents continuous discharge, so after a short dead time the tube is ready for the next particle.

Nuclear Reactions Induced by Neutrons

Neutrons induce many important nuclear reactions because, having no charge, they can enter a nucleus without being repelled by its positive charge, and they produce reactions such as fission of uranium-235, capture reactions forming new isotopes, and the production of artificial radioisotopes. Slow, thermal neutrons are especially effective for fission, while fast neutrons are used in other reactions and in breeding new fuel. Charged particles such as protons and alpha particles must be given high energy in accelerators to overcome the Coulomb barrier before they can reach the nucleus. Neutrons face no such barrier and can react even at very low energies. For this reason neutron-induced reactions are the working basis of nuclear reactors and of most practical production of radioisotopes.

Nuclear Reactions: Fission and Fusion

A nuclear reaction is a process in which a nucleus is changed by striking it with a particle such as a neutron, proton or alpha particle, producing new nuclei and usually releasing or absorbing energy; both A and Z are balanced on the two sides of the reaction equation. In fission a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 splits, after absorbing a neutron, into two medium nuclei with the release of more neutrons and about 200 MeV of energy, and the escaping neutrons can produce a chain reaction. In fusion two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, and the mass lost appears as energy; this needs extremely high temperature to overcome the repulsion between the nuclei. Fission is used in nuclear reactors and the atomic bomb, while fusion powers the Sun and the hydrogen bomb and is being developed for future power stations.

How the Sun and Stars Produce Energy: The Proton-Proton Cycle

The Sun and stars produce energy by nuclear fusion in their extremely hot, dense cores, where hydrogen nuclei are converted into helium and the mass lost appears as radiant energy according to E = mc2. In the proton-proton cycle, which dominates in the Sun, two protons first combine to form a deuteron with the emission of a positron and a neutrino. The deuteron then captures another proton to form light helium-3, and finally two helium-3 nuclei combine to form ordinary helium-4 and release two protons back. The net result is that four protons are converted into one helium-4 nucleus, two positrons, two neutrinos and about 25 MeV of energy, the positrons annihilating with electrons to add further energy. This energy slowly travels to the surface of the Sun and is radiated into space as light and heat, sustaining life on Earth.

N = N0 e^(-lambda t) ; T(1/2) = 0.693 / lambda

mcqs.q: The law of radioactive disintegration states that -dN/dt equals:
options: lambda N, proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present
mcqs.why: The rate of disintegration at any instant is directly proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present, -dN/dt = lambda N, where lambda is the decay constant.

mcqs.q: Integration of the decay law gives the number of nuclei remaining as:
mcqs.why: Integrating -dN/dt = lambda N gives ln(N/N0) = -lambda t, or N = N0 e^(-lambda t), so the number of nuclei and the activity fall exponentially and never quite reach zero.

mcqs.q: The half-life is related to the decay constant by:
mcqs.why: Putting N = N0/2 in N = N0 e^(-lambda t) gives T(1/2) = 0.693/lambda, which is constant for a given radioactive substance.

mcqs.q: Alpha emission from a heavy nucleus decreases A and Z by, respectively:
options: A by 4 and Z by 2, with range of a few cm in air and stopped by paper
mcqs.why: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus with A = 4 and Z = 2, so emission decreases A by 4 and Z by 2; alpha radiation has a range of only a few centimetres in air, is stopped by paper and is strongly ionising.

mcqs.q: Beta emission leaves A unchanged but changes Z by 1. It is stopped by:
options: A few millimetres of aluminium, with range up to a few metres in air
mcqs.why: Beta emission is the loss of a fast electron or positron created inside the nucleus; it travels up to a few metres in air, is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium and is moderately ionising.

mcqs.q: Gamma emission changes A and Z by:
options: Neither A nor Z; it is highly penetrating and stopped only by thick lead
mcqs.why: Gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation emitted when an excited nucleus falls to a lower state; they change neither A nor Z, are weakly ionising but highly penetrating, and are stopped only by thick lead.

mcqs.q: In electric and magnetic fields, alpha, beta and gamma radiations behave as follows:
options: Alpha and beta are deflected in opposite senses according to their charges, while gamma rays are not deflected at all
Alpha and gamma are deflected the same way
mcqs.why: Alpha and beta particles carry opposite charges and are deflected in opposite senses appropriate to their charges, while gamma rays carry no charge and are not deflected at all.

mcqs.q: A slow neutron striking uranium-235 in a reactor produces fission fragments, 2 or 3 fresh neutrons and energy of about:
mcqs.why: Uranium-235 splits into two lighter fission fragments with two or three fresh neutrons and about 200 MeV per fission, the mass defect appearing mainly as kinetic energy of the fragments and neutrons.

mcqs.q: In a fission reactor, the heat that drives the turbine is produced when:
options: Collisions of fission fragments and neutrons inside the fuel rods convert their kinetic energy into heat, carried by a coolant to a heat exchanger
Steam is produced directly in the core without heat transfer
mcqs.why: The kinetic energy of fragments and neutrons becomes heat through collisions inside the fuel rods; a coolant carries this heat to a heat exchanger where it raises steam that drives a turbine and generator.

mcqs.q: The Q-value of a nuclear reaction is defined as:
options: Total mass of products times c^2
Total kinetic energy of products minus total kinetic energy of reactants, equal to (mass of reactants - mass of products) x c^2
mcqs.why: Q is the net energy released, equal to the kinetic energy of the products minus that of the reacting particles, and also Q = (total mass of reactants - total mass of products) x c^2, using 1 u = 931.5 MeV.

mcqs.q: A positive Q-value means the reaction is:
options: Endothermic and needs incoming kinetic energy
A decay with no energy change
mcqs.why: A positive Q means the reaction is exothermic and releases energy, while a negative Q means it is endothermic and can occur only if the incoming particles bring at least that much kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: A Geiger-Muller counter operates with a potential difference of about:
options: 400 to 500 V, just below the breakdown voltage
mcqs.why: The GM tube has a metal cathode and a fine axial wire anode with about 400 to 500 V applied, just below the breakdown voltage, and radiation enters through a thin mica window.

mcqs.q: When an ionising particle enters a GM counter, the output pulse is produced because:
options: Freed electrons rush to the wire and ionise many more atoms by collision, causing an avalanche and a sudden pulse of current
The scaler generates the pulse itself
mcqs.why: The particle ionises gas atoms; the electrons rush towards the wire and in the strong field near it ionise many more atoms by collision, causing an avalanche and a pulse that is amplified, counted by a scaler and heard as a click.

mcqs.q: Neutrons are preferred for inducing nuclear reactions because:
options: Having no charge, they can enter a nucleus without Coulomb repulsion and can react even at very low energies
mcqs.why: Neutrons face no Coulomb barrier, unlike protons and alpha particles which need accelerator energies; slow thermal neutrons are especially effective for uranium-235 fission, making neutron reactions the basis of reactors and radioisotope production.

mcqs.q: In the proton-proton cycle, the net result is that four protons are converted into:
options: One helium-4 nucleus, two positrons, two neutrinos and about 25 MeV of energy
mcqs.why: Two protons form a deuteron with a positron and neutrino, the deuteron captures a proton to form helium-3, and two helium-3 nuclei form helium-4 releasing two protons back; the net result is 4 protons to helium-4 plus two positrons, two neutrinos and about 25 MeV.

lessons.title: Worked Examples
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example 1

In 9.0 days the number of radioactive nuclei decreases to one-eighth the number present initially. What is the half-life (in days) of the material?

Step 1: Given: time t = 9.0 days, final number N = N0 / 8, half-life T = ?

Step 2: Formula: after each half-life the number halves, so N = N0 x (1/2) raised to (t / T), that is 1/8 = (1/2) raised to (t / T)

Step 3: Substitution: (1/2)^3 = (1/2) raised to (9.0 / T), because 1/8 = (1/2)^3

Step 4: Calculation: comparing powers, 9.0 / T = 3, so T = 9.0 / 3 = 3.0 days

The half-life of the material is 3 days.

Worked Example 2

The P-32 (Z = 15) isotope of phosphorus has a half-life of 14.28 days. What is its decay constant in units of s-1?

Step 1: Given: half-life T = 14.28 days, decay constant lambda = ?

Step 2: Formula: lambda = 0.693 / T, with T expressed in seconds

Step 3: Substitution for T in seconds: T = 14.28 x 24 x 3600 = 1.234x10^6 s

Step 4: Calculation: lambda = 0.693 / 1.234x10^6 = 5.62x10^-7 per second

The decay constant of phosphorus-32 is 5.62x10^-7 s-1, meaning each nucleus has this probability of decay in one second.

Worked Example 3

Find the binding energy (in MeV) for lithium Li-7 (Z = 3) (atomic mass = 7.016003 u).

Step 1: Given: Li-7 has Z = 3 protons and N = 4 neutrons, atomic mass of Li-7 = 7.016003 u, mass of a hydrogen atom = 1.007825 u, mass of neutron = 1.008665 u, and 1 u = 931.5 MeV

Step 2: Formula: mass defect dm = (Z x mass of hydrogen atom + N x mass of neutron) - atomic mass, and binding energy BE = dm x 931.5 MeV

Step 3: Substitution: dm = (3 x 1.007825 + 4 x 1.008665) - 7.016003 = (3.023475 + 4.034660) - 7.016003

Step 4: Calculation: dm = 7.058135 - 7.016003 = 0.042132 u, so BE = 0.042132 x 931.5 = 39.25 MeV

The binding energy of lithium-7 is about 39.2 MeV, or about 5.6 MeV per nucleon.

Worked Example 4

The binding energy of a nucleus is 225.0 MeV. What is the mass defect of the nucleus in atomic mass units?

Step 1: Given: binding energy BE = 225.0 MeV, mass defect dm = ?, and 1 u of mass corresponds to 931.5 MeV

Step 2: Formula: BE = dm multiplied by c2, so dm = BE / 931.5 in atomic mass units

Step 3: Substitution: dm = 225.0 / 931.5

Step 4: Calculation: dm = 0.2415 u

The mass defect of the nucleus is 0.2415 u, that is, the nucleus is lighter than its separate nucleons by this amount.

Worked Example 5

A copper penny has a mass of 3.0 g. Determine the energy (in MeV) that would be required to break all the copper nuclei into their constituent protons and neutrons. Ignore the energy that binds the electrons to the nucleus and the energy that binds one atom to another in the structure of the metal. For simplicity, assume that all the copper nuclei are Cu-63 (Z = 29) (atomic mass = 62.939598 u).

Step 1: Given: mass of penny = 3.0 g, Cu-63 has Z = 29 and N = 34, atomic mass = 62.939598 u, hydrogen atom mass = 1.007825 u, neutron mass = 1.008665 u, Avogadro number = 6.022x10^23 per mol, 1 u = 931.5 MeV

Step 2: Formula: mass defect per nucleus dm = (29 x 1.007825 + 34 x 1.008665) - 62.939598, binding energy per nucleus = dm x 931.5 MeV, number of nuclei = (3.0 / 62.939598) x 6.022x10^23, and total energy = binding energy per nucleus x number of nuclei

Step 3: Substitution for mass defect: dm = (29.226925 + 34.294610) - 62.939598 = 63.521535 - 62.939598 = 0.581937 u

Step 4: Calculation of binding energy per nucleus: BE = 0.581937 x 931.5 = 542.1 MeV

Step 5: Calculation of number of nuclei: N = (3.0 / 62.939598) x 6.022x10^23 = 2.87x10^22 nuclei

Step 6: Calculation of total energy: E total = 542.1 x 2.87x10^22 = about 1.5x10^25 MeV

About 1.5x10^25 MeV (the book gives 1.51249x10^25 MeV) would be needed to break all the copper nuclei in the penny into separate protons and neutrons.

Worked Example 6

Write the beta-plus decay process for each of the following nuclei with their proper chemical symbols including Z and A for each daughter nucleus: (a) F-18 (b) O-15.

Step 1: Given: in beta-plus decay a proton changes into a neutron, so A stays the same and Z decreases by 1, and a positron e+ and a neutrino are emitted

Step 2: Rule applied to part (a): fluorine F-18 has Z = 9, so the daughter has Z = 8 and A = 18, which is oxygen

Step 3: Equation for part (a): F-18 (Z = 9) changes to O-18 (Z = 8) + e+ + neutrino

Step 4: Rule applied to part (b): oxygen O-15 has Z = 8, so the daughter has Z = 7 and A = 15, which is nitrogen

Step 5: Equation for part (b): O-15 (Z = 8) changes to N-15 (Z = 7) + e+ + neutrino

The two decay processes are F-18 to O-18 plus a positron and a neutrino, and O-15 to N-15 plus a positron and a neutrino, with A unchanged and Z reduced by 1 in each case.

Worked Example 7

A device used in radiation therapy for cancer contains 0.50 g of cobalt Co-60 (Z = 27) (59.933819 u). The half-life of Co-60 (Z = 27) is 5.27 years. Determine the activity of the radioactive material.

Step 1: Given: mass = 0.50 g, molar mass of Co-60 = 59.933819 g per mol, half-life T = 5.27 years, Avogadro number = 6.022x10^23 per mol, activity A = ?

Step 2: Formula: number of nuclei N = (mass / molar mass) x Avogadro number, decay constant lambda = 0.693 / T, and activity A = lambda N

Step 3: Substitution for N: N = (0.50 / 59.933819) x 6.022x10^23 = 5.02x10^21 nuclei

Step 4: Substitution for lambda: T = 5.27 x 365 x 24 x 3600 = 1.66x10^8 s, so lambda = 0.693 / 1.66x10^8 = 4.17x10^-9 per second

Step 5: Calculation of activity: A = 4.17x10^-9 x 5.02x10^21 = 2.09x10^13 decays per second

The activity of the cobalt source is about 2.10x10^13 Bq, which is why cobalt-60 is a strong and useful source for radiotherapy.

mcqs.q: In 9.0 days the number of radioactive nuclei falls to one-eighth of the initial number. The half-life is:
mcqs.why: 1/8 = (1/2)^3, so 9.0/T = 3 and T = 9.0/3 = 3.0 days; three half-lives elapse in 9.0 days, halving the number three times.

mcqs.q: For the material that falls to one-eighth in 9.0 days, how many half-lives have passed?
mcqs.why: After each half-life the number halves, and (1/2)^3 = 1/8, so exactly 3 half-lives have passed in the 9.0 days, giving T = 9.0/3 = 3.0 days.

mcqs.q: Phosphorus-32 has half-life 14.28 days. Its decay constant lambda = 0.693/T is:
mcqs.why: T = 14.28 x 24 x 3600 = 1.234x10^6 s, so lambda = 0.693 / 1.234x10^6 = 5.62x10^-7 s^-1, the probability that one P-32 nucleus decays in one second.

mcqs.q: The half-life of P-32, 14.28 days, expressed in seconds is:
mcqs.why: T = 14.28 days x 24 hours/day x 3600 s/hour = 1.234x10^6 s, which must be used in lambda = 0.693/T to obtain lambda in units of s^-1.

mcqs.q: For lithium-7 (Z=3, N=4, atomic mass 7.016003 u), the mass defect dm = (3x1.007825 + 4x1.008665) - 7.016003 is:
mcqs.why: The separate masses sum to 3.023475 + 4.034660 = 7.058135 u, so dm = 7.058135 - 7.016003 = 0.042132 u, the amount by which the nucleus is lighter than its separate nucleons.

mcqs.q: The binding energy of lithium-7, from dm = 0.042132 u and 1 u = 931.5 MeV, is:
mcqs.why: BE = dm x 931.5 = 0.042132 x 931.5 = 39.25 MeV, about 39.2 MeV, which is the binding energy of the lithium-7 nucleus.

mcqs.q: The binding energy per nucleon of lithium-7 (BE about 39.2 MeV, A = 7) is about:
mcqs.why: BE per nucleon = 39.25 / 7 = 5.6 MeV per nucleon, found by dividing the total binding energy of lithium-7 by its mass number A = 7.

mcqs.q: A nucleus has binding energy 225.0 MeV. Its mass defect dm = BE/931.5 is:
mcqs.why: dm = 225.0 / 931.5 = 0.2415 u, so the nucleus is lighter than its separate nucleons by 0.2415 atomic mass units.

mcqs.q: For copper-63 (Z=29, N=34, atomic mass 62.939598 u), the mass defect per nucleus is:
The binding energy per copper-63 nucleus, from dm = 0.581937 u, is:
mcqs.why: BE = 0.581937 x 931.5 = 542.1 MeV per nucleus, which is the energy needed to break one copper-63 nucleus into separate protons and neutrons.

mcqs.q: The total energy needed to break all copper nuclei in a 3.0 g penny (2.87x10^22 nuclei, 542.1 MeV each) is about:
mcqs.why: Total energy = 542.1 x 2.87x10^22 = about 1.5x10^25 MeV (the book gives 1.51249x10^25 MeV), with the number of nuclei found from (3.0/62.939598) x 6.022x10^23.

mcqs.q: In beta-plus decay, fluorine-18 (Z=9) changes into:
options: Oxygen-18 (Z=8) plus a positron and a neutrino, with A unchanged
mcqs.why: In beta-plus decay A stays the same and Z decreases by 1, so F-18 (Z=9) becomes O-18 (Z=8) plus a positron e+ and a neutrino.

mcqs.q: In beta-plus decay, oxygen-15 (Z=8) changes into:
options: Nitrogen-15 (Z=7) plus a positron and a neutrino, with A unchanged
mcqs.why: In beta-plus decay A stays the same and Z decreases by 1, so O-15 (Z=8) becomes N-15 (Z=7) plus a positron e+ and a neutrino.

mcqs.q: A 0.50 g cobalt-60 source (molar mass 59.933819 g/mol) contains N = (0.50/59.933819) x 6.022x10^23 nuclei, equal to about:
mcqs.why: N = (0.50 / 59.933819) x 6.022x10^23 = 5.02x10^21 nuclei, the number of cobalt-60 nuclei present in the 0.50 g therapy source.

mcqs.q: Cobalt-60 has half-life 5.27 years, giving lambda = 4.17x10^-9 per second. The activity A = lambda N of the 0.50 g source is about:
mcqs.why: A = lambda N = 4.17x10^-9 x 5.02x10^21 = 2.09x10^13 decays per second, about 2.10x10^13 Bq, which is why cobalt-60 is a strong radiotherapy source; lambda used T = 5.27 years = 1.66x10^8 s.

lessons.title: The Standard Model, Quarks and Particle Detectors
lessons.notes_html:
Fermions, Bosons and Quark Flavours

In the Standard Model all elementary particles are divided by their spin into fermions, which have half-integer spin and make up matter, and bosons, which have integer spin and carry the fundamental forces. Quarks and leptons are the two families of fermions. Hadrons, baryons and mesons are composite particles made of quarks, not a basic division of elementary particles.

The six quark flavours are up, down, charm, strange, top and bottom. The electron is not a quark at all; it is a lepton, an elementary particle that does not feel the strong nuclear force. Quarks are never found alone, whereas the electron exists freely, for example in cathode rays and beta radiation.

The up quark carries a fractional charge of +2/3 e, while the down quark carries -1/3 e. These fractions always combine in groups of two or three to give whole-number charges for observable particles. For example, a proton, made of two up quarks and one down quark, has charge 2/3 + 2/3 - 1/3 = +1 e.

The Higgs boson is the particle of the Higgs field, and it is through their interaction with this field that fundamental particles such as quarks, electrons and the W and Z bosons acquire their mass. The photon, which does not interact with the Higgs field in this way, remains massless. The Higgs boson was detected at CERN in 2012, confirming this part of the Standard Model.

Colour Charge, Confinement and Hadrons

Quark confinement means that the strong force between quarks does not weaken with distance, so the energy needed to pull a quark out of a hadron grows until it is enough to create a new quark-antiquark pair instead. As a result quarks are only ever observed inside hadrons, as baryons of three quarks or mesons of a quark and an antiquark. No isolated free quark has ever been detected, in agreement with this idea.

Color is the name given to the charge of the strong nuclear force carried by quarks and gluons; it has nothing to do with ordinary visible colour. Quarks carry one of three color charges, called red, green and blue, and antiquarks carry the matching anticolors. Observable particles are always color neutral, either by combining all three colors in a baryon or a color with its anticolor in a meson.

A meson is a hadron built from one quark and one antiquark held together by the strong force, examples being the pion and the kaon. A baryon, by contrast, is made of three quarks, like the proton and the neutron. Leptons and neutrinos are elementary particles and are not made of quarks at all.

Quarks carry electric charge, color charge and also take part in weak interactions, so they feel the electromagnetic, strong and weak forces alike. Leptons and electrons feel the electromagnetic and weak forces but not the strong force. The neutrino feels only the weak force (and gravity), which is why it passes through ordinary matter almost undisturbed.

Detecting Ionising Radiation

A Geiger-Muller counter detects ionising radiation: a particle entering the gas-filled tube ionises the gas, and the resulting avalanche of charge produces an electrical pulse. Counting these pulses gives the number of ionising particles or photons arriving in a given time. The counter does not measure the velocity or energy of the particles, and it cannot create particles or magnetic fields.

The tube of a Geiger-Muller counter is commonly filled with argon at low pressure, together with a small amount of a quenching vapour. Argon is easily ionised by a passing charged particle or photon, which starts the avalanche that produces the output pulse. The quenching vapour stops the discharge after each pulse so that the tube is ready to count the next event.

mcqs.q: In the Standard Model, elementary particles are divided by spin into:
options: Fermions with half-integer spin, which make up matter, and bosons with integer spin, which carry forces
mcqs.why: Fermions have half-integer spin and make up matter, while bosons have integer spin and carry the fundamental forces; quarks and leptons are the two families of fermions, and hadrons are composite, not a basic division.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a quark flavour?
mcqs.why: The six quark flavours are up, down, charm, strange, top and bottom; the electron is not a quark at all but a lepton that does not feel the strong force and exists freely.

mcqs.q: The electric charges of the up quark and the down quark are respectively:
mcqs.why: The up quark carries +2/3 e and the down quark carries -1/3 e; these fractions combine in groups of two or three to give whole-number charges for observable particles.

mcqs.q: A proton made of two up quarks and one down quark has total charge:
mcqs.why: Proton charge = 2/3 + 2/3 - 1/3 = +1 e, exactly the proton charge, showing how fractional quark charges combine to a whole-number charge.

mcqs.q: The primary role of the Higgs boson in the Standard Model is:
options: Giving mass to other particles through interaction with the Higgs field
mcqs.why: Through interaction with the Higgs field, particles such as quarks, electrons and the W and Z bosons acquire mass, while the photon does not interact this way and remains massless; the Higgs boson was detected at CERN in 2012.

mcqs.q: Quark confinement means that:
options: Quarks are easily isolated in the laboratory
The energy needed to pull a quark out grows until a new quark-antiquark pair is created, so quarks are only observed inside hadrons
mcqs.why: The strong force between quarks does not weaken with distance, so pulling a quark out needs enough energy to create a new pair instead; quarks are only ever observed inside baryons or mesons and no free quark has been detected.

mcqs.q: Observable particles are always colour neutral. This is achieved by:
options: Combining all three colours in a baryon or a colour with its anticolour in a meson
mcqs.why: Quarks carry red, green or blue colour and antiquarks carry anticolours; a baryon combines all three colours and a meson combines a colour with its anticolour, so freely observed particles are colour neutral.

mcqs.q: A meson is a hadron built from:
options: One quark and one antiquark, such as the pion and the kaon
mcqs.why: A meson is one quark plus one antiquark held together by the strong force, examples being the pion and the kaon, whereas a baryon such as the proton or neutron is made of three quarks.

mcqs.q: Which particle feels only the weak force (and gravity) and passes through ordinary matter almost undisturbed?
mcqs.why: Quarks feel electromagnetic, strong and weak forces, and electrons feel electromagnetic and weak forces, but the neutrino feels only the weak force (and gravity), which is why it passes through matter almost undisturbed.

mcqs.q: The gas commonly used in a Geiger-Muller counter to detect ionising radiation is:
options: Argon at low pressure with a small amount of quenching vapour
mcqs.why: The GM tube is commonly filled with argon at low pressure plus quenching vapour; argon is easily ionised by a passing particle or photon to start the avalanche, and counting the pulses gives the number of ionising events, not their velocity or energy.

lessons.title: Quarks, Leptons, Forces and Detectors
lessons.notes_html:
Bosons and Fermions and Their Roles in the Fundamental Forces

Fermions are particles with half-integer spin, such as quarks, electrons and neutrinos, which obey the Pauli exclusion principle and form the matter of the universe. Bosons are particles with integer spin, such as the photon, gluon and W and Z particles, which do not obey the exclusion principle in the same way. The fundamental forces arise from the exchange of bosons between fermions: photons carry the electromagnetic force, gluons the strong force, and W and Z bosons the weak force. In short, fermions are the particles of matter and bosons are the carriers, or field particles, of the forces between them.

Quarks and Leptons Compared

Quarks and leptons are both elementary fermions with spin 1/2, and each family has six members arranged in three generations. Quarks carry fractional electric charge, +2/3 e or -1/3 e, and also carry color charge, so they feel all three forces: strong, electromagnetic and weak. Leptons carry whole-number charge, such as -e for the electron or zero for the neutrinos, and they carry no color charge, so they do not feel the strong force. Quarks are always confined inside hadrons, while leptons such as electrons and neutrinos can exist freely on their own.

Leptons: Definition, Examples and Properties

A lepton is an elementary fermion that does not take part in the strong nuclear interaction; the name comes from a word meaning light or small. The leptons are the electron, muon and tau, together with their three matching neutrinos: the electron neutrino, muon neutrino and tau neutrino. They have spin 1/2, the charged leptons each carry charge -e, and the neutrinos are neutral and have extremely small mass. In the Standard Model leptons form, together with quarks, the basic matter content of the universe, and the electron is essential to the structure of every atom.

Colour Charge and the Colour-Neutral Nature of Protons and Neutrons

Color charge is the charge of the strong force, carried by quarks in three forms called red, green and blue, and exchanged between quarks by gluons, which carry the strong interaction. It is significant because the strong force binds quarks into hadrons and, as a leftover effect, binds protons and neutrons together inside the nucleus. A proton or a neutron contains three quarks, one of each color, and the three colors combine to give a color-neutral, or white, total. In the same way a meson combines a color with its anticolor, so all particles observed freely in nature are color neutral, as confinement requires.

Quark Structure of the Proton and the Neutron

A proton is a baryon made of three quarks: two up quarks and one down quark, written uud, held together by gluons through the strong force. Its charge is +2/3 + 2/3 - 1/3 = +1 e, exactly the proton charge. A neutron is made of one up quark and two down quarks, written udd, and its charge is +2/3 - 1/3 - 1/3 = 0, so it is electrically neutral. Only the lightest quarks, up and down, are involved in ordinary protons and neutrons, and the three colors of the three quarks combine to make each particle color neutral.

Structure of the Standard Model

The Standard Model organises all known elementary particles into fermions, which form matter, and bosons, which carry forces. The fermions consist of six quarks (up, down, charm, strange, top and bottom) and six leptons (electron, muon, tau and three neutrinos), arranged in three generations of increasing mass, each quark and lepton having an antiparticle. Quarks combine as baryons of three quarks and mesons of a quark-antiquark pair to form the hadrons, while leptons exist freely. The gauge bosons are the photon, the eight gluons, and the W, Z and Higgs bosons, the Higgs giving mass to other particles through the Higgs field. The model classifies three fundamental forces in this scheme: the electromagnetic force carried by photons, the strong force carried by gluons between color charges, and the weak force carried by W and Z bosons, responsible for beta decay. Gravity is not included in the Standard Model, which is its best known limitation.

The Fundamental Forces and Their Field Particles

The gravitational force, the weakest but longest-range force, acts between all masses and is described by general relativity; its proposed carrier, the graviton, has not been detected and lies outside the Standard Model. The electromagnetic force acts between electric charges, has infinite range, and is carried by the massless photon. The strong nuclear force acts between color charges of quarks, is the strongest force but has a very short range, and is carried by the eight gluons, binding quarks in hadrons and nucleons in the nucleus. The weak force acts on quarks and leptons over an extremely short range and is carried by the massive W and Z bosons; it is responsible for beta decay and for changing quark flavour. A boson is a particle of integer spin, 0, 1 or 2. Bosons are called field particles because in quantum field theory every force field has its own boson, and the force between two particles is pictured as the exchange of these bosons between them.

Operating Principle of the Geiger-Muller Counter and Its Limitations

The Geiger-Muller counter works on the ionisation of a gas by radiation: a metal tube filled with argon at low pressure has a central wire anode held a few hundred volts positive, just below the self-discharge voltage. Radiation entering through a thin mica window ionises gas atoms, and the freed electrons, accelerated in the intense field near the wire, produce an avalanche of further ionisation, giving one large standard pulse for each entering particle. The pulses are amplified and counted by a scaler, so the count rate measures the activity or intensity of the radiation reaching the tube. Its limitations are that every pulse has the same size, so it gives no information about the energy or type of the radiation, and it cannot distinguish alpha, beta and gamma events by itself. It also has a dead time after each pulse during which new events are missed, so it undercounts at very high rates, and weakly penetrating alpha particles can enter only through the thin window.

The Wilson Cloud Chamber and How It Visualises Tracks

The Wilson cloud chamber makes the paths of charged particles visible and was used in classic discoveries such as the positron and several particles from cosmic rays. The chamber contains air saturated with water or alcohol vapour, and a sudden expansion cools the vapour into a supersaturated state in which it is ready to condense but needs ions as centres. A passing charged particle ionises the vapour along its path, droplets condense on these ions, and a thin white track of droplets appears and can be photographed. In a magnetic field the curvature of the track shows the charge and momentum of the particle, and the thickness of the track indicates its ionising power. Its performance is affected by the degree of supersaturation and the speed and timing of the expansion, by temperature and cleanliness of the chamber, and by the need to photograph the tracks in the brief moment before the droplets grow and fall.

mcqs.q: Fermions and bosons differ in that:
options: Fermions have integer spin and carry forces
Fermions have half-integer spin, obey the Pauli exclusion principle and form matter, while bosons have integer spin and carry forces
Bosons form matter and fermions carry forces
mcqs.why: Fermions such as quarks, electrons and neutrinos have half-integer spin, obey the Pauli exclusion principle and form matter; bosons such as the photon, gluon and W and Z have integer spin and are the carriers of the forces between fermions.

mcqs.q: The carriers of the electromagnetic, strong and weak forces are respectively:
options: Photons, gluons and W and Z bosons
mcqs.why: Forces arise from exchange of bosons between fermions: photons carry the electromagnetic force, gluons the strong force, and W and Z bosons the weak force.

mcqs.q: Quarks differ from leptons in that quarks:
options: Carry fractional charge and colour charge, feel the strong force and are confined in hadrons, while leptons carry whole-number charge, no colour and exist freely
mcqs.why: Both are spin-1/2 fermions with six members in three generations, but quarks carry +2/3 e or -1/3 e plus colour and feel all three forces, while leptons carry -e or zero, no colour, do not feel the strong force and can exist freely.

mcqs.q: The six leptons are:
options: Up, down, charm, strange, top and bottom
Photon, gluon, W, Z, Higgs and graviton
Electron, muon and tau, together with the electron, muon and tau neutrinos
mcqs.why: A lepton does not take part in the strong interaction; the leptons are the electron, muon and tau with charge -e and spin 1/2, together with their three matching neutral neutrinos of extremely small mass.

mcqs.q: Colour charge is carried by quarks in three forms called:
mcqs.why: Colour is the charge of the strong force, carried as red, green and blue by quarks and exchanged by gluons; it has nothing to do with ordinary visible colour but binds quarks into hadrons and nucleons into the nucleus.

mcqs.q: The quark composition and charge of the proton are:
mcqs.why: A proton is a baryon of two up quarks and one down quark, uud, held together by gluons; its charge is +2/3 + 2/3 - 1/3 = +1 e and its three quark colours combine to colour neutral.

mcqs.q: The quark composition and charge of the neutron are:
mcqs.why: A neutron is one up quark and two down quarks, udd, with charge +2/3 - 1/3 - 1/3 = 0, so it is electrically neutral; only the lightest up and down quarks occur in ordinary protons and neutrons.

mcqs.q: The best known limitation of the Standard Model is that it does not include:
mcqs.why: The Standard Model classifies the electromagnetic force carried by photons, the strong force carried by gluons and the weak force carried by W and Z bosons responsible for beta decay, but gravity is not included in the model.

mcqs.q: The gauge bosons listed in the Standard Model structure include:
options: The photon, the eight gluons, and the W, Z and Higgs bosons
mcqs.why: The fermions are six quarks and six leptons in three generations with antiparticles, while the gauge bosons are the photon, the eight gluons, and the W, Z and Higgs bosons, the Higgs giving mass through the Higgs field.

mcqs.q: The proposed carrier of gravity, which has not been detected and lies outside the Standard Model, is the:
mcqs.why: Gravity is the weakest but longest-range force, described by general relativity; its proposed carrier, the graviton, has not been detected and lies outside the Standard Model.

mcqs.q: The strong nuclear force is best described as:
options: The strongest force with very short range, carried by eight gluons between colour charges
The weakest force with infinite range
mcqs.why: The strong force acts between colour charges of quarks, is the strongest force but has a very short range, and is carried by the eight gluons, binding quarks in hadrons and nucleons in the nucleus.

mcqs.q: The weak force is responsible for:
options: Beta decay and changing quark flavour, acting over an extremely short range via massive W and Z bosons
mcqs.why: The weak force acts on quarks and leptons over an extremely short range and is carried by the massive W and Z bosons; it is responsible for beta decay and for changing quark flavour.

mcqs.q: Bosons are called field particles because:
options: In quantum field theory every force field has its own boson, and the force is pictured as the exchange of these bosons between particles
mcqs.why: A boson has integer spin 0, 1 or 2, and bosons are called field particles because every force field has its own boson whose exchange between two particles is pictured as the force between them.

mcqs.q: A limitation of the Geiger-Muller counter is that:
options: Every pulse has the same size, so it gives no information about the energy or type of radiation and cannot distinguish alpha, beta and gamma by itself
mcqs.why: Every GM pulse is one large standard pulse, so the counter gives no energy or type information and cannot distinguish alpha, beta and gamma by itself; it also has a dead time after each pulse during which new events are missed.

mcqs.q: A Wilson cloud chamber visualises charged-particle tracks because:
options: Droplets condense on ions left along the particle path in supersaturated vapour, forming a thin white track
Particles change the colour of the gas permanently
mcqs.why: Sudden expansion cools saturated vapour to a supersaturated state; a passing charged particle ionises the vapour along its path, droplets condense on the ions, and a photographable white track appears whose curvature in a magnetic field shows charge and momentum.
